Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible, kept closer to the author’s own Bible where his argument rests on its wording; capitals for God in quotations (He, His) follow the BSB. “You+” marks every plural “you” (the older “ye”); a plain “you” is singular or general.

The Epistle Dedicatory

TO THE RIGHT HONORABLE, RIGHT Worshipful, and my other beloved parishioners, inhabitants of the precinct of Blackfriars, LONDON: such sufficiency of grace as may bring them to fullness of glory.

If noble birth, high honor, great wealth, true piety, generous charity, a good esteem of God’s word and ministers, and in particular a whole-hearted love of the author, are reasons for choosing a patron for his work, then I for my part need not go far for a patron. In my own parish are all these. To you+ therefore (Right Honorable, Right Worshipful, and my other beloved parishioners, most worthy of all due respect) I dedicate these poor labors of mine on domestical duties. To testify to the equal duty which I owe and the impartial respect which I bear to you+ all, I make you+ all one patron. You+ were the first over whom I ever had any ministerial charge. To this charge I was called by your+ free choice. Among you+ I have spent1 almost two full apprenticeships. You+ have always so accepted my labors and respected my person that I never had any cause to repent of my accepting this place and calling, but rather cause to thank God for it. My desire is (if it may seem good to the divine providence) to spend all my days among you+, and, while I am among you+, to help forward your+ spiritual edification. This is the chief end of my calling. It is the mark I have aimed at, as in the ordinary course of my ministry, so in publishing these eight treatises of domestical duties and dedicating them to you+. As I have preached these duties in your+ hearing, and published them in your+ name, in testimony of love and duty, so do you+ show your+ kind acceptance of my former and my latter labors by conscientiously observing them, so far as they agree with God’s word, so that all who know you+ may know by that clear demonstration how well you+ have relished and approved them. In this way you+ will gain much profit, and I much comfort, by my labors. Oh, if the head and the separate members of a family would each be persuaded to be conscientious in performing their own particular duties, what a sweet society and happy harmony there would be in houses! What excellent nurseries families would be for church and commonwealth! It is necessary that good order be first set in families. For as families came before other states, so they are somewhat more necessary;2 and good members of a family are likely to make good members of church and commonwealth. The subject matter of these treatises is therefore worth handling, if I were able to handle it according to its worth. I have endeavored to do what I could in it, though I have not attained to what I would. Be like God, who, if there is first a willing mind, accepts according to what a man has, and not according to what he does not have. Though for such a matter as is handled in these treatises the work may seem at first sight too long, yet I hope the observant reader will not find it too tedious. It is the variety of many points,3 not the long-windedness of a few, which has made this book swell to the size it has. The first treatise (which is a fourth part of the book) contains a commentary on that part of Scripture out of which domestical duties are raised. In it the apostle, setting forth Christ and the church as patterns to husbands and wives, vividly declares the great love of Christ to his church and the near union between them, together with other deep mysteries; and the unfolding of these has kept me a little longer. But as I have dwelt for a while on main matters of great weight, so I have passed very briefly over other points. The other treatises, in which the duties themselves are handled, are each much shorter than the first. In them I have simply set forth and briefly proved the truth and fairness of the separate duties, except some choice points which are of special use, or at least are much questioned through disuse; and these I have handled more fully. And because contraries laid side by side4 set each other forth in their true colors, I have joined to every duty the contrary fault and straying from it. For many who hear the duties think all is well enough, until they also hear the contrary vices, by which they are most convicted in their consciences. Concerning the many faults and vices of bad husbands, wives, parents, children, masters and servants, censured in these treatises, let me entreat you+ not to apply them too generally to all husbands, wives, parents, children, masters and servants. Has not wise Solomon much censured the flightiness, shrewishness, pride, flattery, and other vices of women? And shall sober, meek, humble, chaste women think themselves censured by it? By the same reasoning unchaste harlots, untrustworthy gossips, restless shrews, and proud dames might think themselves commended by those excellent commendations which he gives of good women. Let every one, as their conscience (an impartial judge) bears them witness, make a right application of everything to themselves. In this way we ministers will be freed from many evil suspicions. I remember that when these domestical duties were first delivered from the pulpit, much exception was taken against the application of a wife’s subjection to restraining her from disposing of the common goods of the family without, or against, her husband’s consent. But surely those who took those exceptions did not consider well the cautions and limitations which were delivered then, and are now expressly noted again. They are these: that the restraint mentioned is not to be extended to the wife’s own goods,5 no, nor too strictly to such goods as are set apart for the use of the family,6 nor to extraordinary cases,7 nor always to an express consent,8 nor to the consent of such husbands as are incapable, or far and long absent.9 If any other warrantable caution is shown to me, I will be as willing to admit it as any of these. Now, so that my meaning may not always be twisted, I pray you+, in reading of the restraint on a wife’s power in disposing of the goods of the family, always bear those cautions in mind. Other exceptions were taken against some other particular duties of wives. For many who can hear their duties declared in general terms patiently enough cannot bear to hear those generals illustrated in their particular branches. This comes too near the quick, and pierces too deep. But (to interpret all according to the rule of love, in the better sense) I take the main reason for the many exceptions which were taken to be this. Wives’ duties were handled in the first place (according to the apostle’s method), and so it was taught (as it must have been taught, unless the truth were to be betrayed) what a wife is bound to, in the uttermost extent of that subjection under which God has put her, in case her husband will insist on the uttermost of his authority. This was taken as if I had taught that a husband might and ought to exact the uttermost, and that a wife was bound, in that uttermost extent, to do all that was delivered as duty, whether her husband exacted it or not. But when I came to deliver husbands’ duties,10 I showed that he ought not to exact whatever his wife was bound to (in case it were exacted by him), but that he ought to make her a joint governor of the family with himself, and leave the ordering of many things to her discretion, and carry himself toward her with all honorable and kind respect. In a word, I have so set down a husband’s duties that, if he is wise and conscientious in observing them, his wife can have no just cause to complain of her subjection. What makes a wife’s yoke heavy and hard is a husband’s abuse of his authority, and his pressing his wife’s duty more than performing his own, which is directly contrary to the11 apostle’s rule. I have been forced to make this just defense so that I might not forever be judged (as some have censured me)12 a hater of women. Now, so that I might give some ease in all those places where a wife’s yoke may seem to pinch most, I have made a reference, in the margin beside every head of wives’ duties, to the duties of husbands that answer to it, and marked the reference with this sign *, so that it may be turned to more readily. Indeed, I have further set side by side, and laid evenly one against another in one view, the heads of husbands’ and wives’ duties, as they answer each other, and in the same way the contrary failings, with a reference to the particular sections where they are handled. So on the one side it may appear that, if both are conscientious and careful to perform their own duty, the yoke of marriage will lie so evenly on both their necks that the wife will be pinched by it no more than the husband, but it will be like Christ’s spiritual yoke, light and easy;13 and on the other side it may be clear that there is commonly as much failing by husbands in their duties as by wives in theirs. This parallel, setting out evenly the duties of each and the contrary failings, I have placed next to this epistle. And I have further added to it a table of the separate heads of the points that are handled in the eight following treatises, so that by this help you+ may more readily find such particular points as you+ most especially desire to read. To show that the duties prescribed to husbands, wives, parents, children, masters, and servants are such as they are bound to in conscience, I have endeavored to show how they are grounded on the word of God and gathered from it. To avoid long-windedness, I have put most of the quotations in the margin. If your+ leisure allows, you+ would do well to search them out. Two things have been special helps to me for finding out the many duties noted in these treatises, and the vices contrary to them: observation and disposition. Observation, both of such duties as the Scripture commends and such contrary vices as it condemns, and also of such commendable virtues as I liked well in those husbands, wives, parents, children, masters, and servants among whom I came, and such unseemly vices as I disliked in them; and disposition of one point after another in the best order that I could. My method and manner of proceeding brought many things to my mind which otherwise might have slipped by. For by method many separate points belonging to one matter are drawn out, as in a chain one link draws up another. There is no better way to find many observations in a text than by a methodical analysis of it. As method is a help to invention, so also to retention. It is like the thread or wire on which pearls are strung, which keeps them from scattering. And if a man is cast into a labyrinth by an abundance of matter, by the help of method he may easily and readily find his way out again. In these respects method is fitly called the14 mother of the mind and mistress of memory. If you+ mark well the order of the points and how one depends on another, you+ will find as great a help in understanding and remembering15 them as I did in finding them out and setting them in order.

Because there is no one word that includes both masters and mistresses under it, as fathers and mothers are included under parents, and sons and daughters under children, I have, according to the Scripture’s way of speaking, included mistresses under masters, so that the duties enjoined to masters belong to mistresses, so far as may stand with their sex. To conclude, in recompense for all my labors I heartily pray you+ all to pray heartily for him who daily prays for you+, even16

The watchman of your+ souls, WILLIAM GOUGE.

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9

Serving Each Other in the Fear of the Lord

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 1–6

Eph 5:21.

Submit to one another in the fear of God.

§. 1. Of the apostle’s transition from general duties to particular ones.

There are two callings to which it has pleased God to call every one. The one is general. By virtue of it, certain common duties are required, which are to be performed by all men (such as knowledge, faith, obedience, repentance, love, mercy, justice, truth, etc.). The other is particular. By virtue of it, certain special duties are required of separate persons, according to the distinct places in which the divine providence has set them, in commonwealth, church, or family. As there are these two, so God’s ministers ought to be careful to instruct God’s people in both kinds of duties: both those which concern their general calling, and those also which concern their particular calling. Accordingly Saint Paul (who, like Moses,17 was “faithful in all the house of God”) first instructed God’s church sufficiently in those general duties which belong to all Christians, of whatever sex, state, degree, or condition they may be. After that he goes on to lay down certain particular duties, which belong to particular callings and conditions. Among these he chooses those which God has established in a family. With excellent skill he passes from those generals to these particulars, laying down a transition between them in these words: “Submitting to one another in the fear of God.” These words refer both to what goes before and to what follows after. The form and manner in which this verse is set down, with a participle, submitting, shows that it depends on what went before, and so refers to it. Again, the word itself is the very same as the one used18 in the next verse. This shows that this verse contains the sum of what follows, and so refers to it as a general refers to its particulars. This manner of passing from one point to another by a perfect transition, which looks both ways, both to what is past and to what is coming, is very elegant, and it is also frequent with this apostle of ours. By it he teaches us19 to give heed to what follows in such a way that we do not forget what is past. As we must give diligent attention to what remains, so we must retain well what we have heard, and not let it slip. Otherwise, if one precept makes another be forgotten (as one nail drives out another), it will be altogether in vain to add line to line, or precept to precept.

§. 2. Of joining service to men with our praise of God.

As this verse refers to what was delivered before concerning our duty to God, it teaches us this lesson:

It is the duty of Christians, as to set forth the praise of God, so to be serviceable to one another. For this purpose, in the20 Ten Commandments, the second table, which declares the service that we owe to one another, is added to the first table, which prescribes the duty that we owe to God. And he who said, “The first and great commandment is this: You shall love the Lord,”21 etc., also said, “The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor,” etc. For this reason the22 apostle, declaring what those sacrifices are with which God is well pleased, joins these two together: to give thanks to God, and to do good to man. The service which we perform to one another in the fear of God is a clear and real demonstration of the respect we bear to God. “Our goodness does not extend to God.”2324 He is so high above us, so perfect and complete in himself, that we can neither give to him, nor can he receive from us. But in his own stead he has placed our brother, who is like ourselves. As we may do him hurt,25 so by our faithful service we may do him much26 good, and in doing it God is much honored.

This exposes the hypocrisy of those who make a great show27 of praising God, and yet are scornful and disdainful to their brethren, and lazy to do any service to man. “These men’s religion is worthless.”28 By this mark the prophets in their time, and Christ and his apostles in their time also, exposed the hypocrisy of those among whom they lived, and so may we also in our times. For there are many who often sing praise to God in their houses and in the midst of the congregation, and perform other parts of God’s outward worship, but toward one another are proud, haughty, envious, unmerciful, unjust, slanderous, and very slow to do any good service. Surely the outward service which they claim to perform to God does not so much wipe out the spot of profaneness, as their neglect of duty to man brands their foreheads with the stamp of hypocrisy.29

For our part, let us not think to shift off one duty on the pretext of another, though that one may seem to be the weightier, lest that fearful woe which Christ pronounced against the scribes and Pharisees fall on our heads. As God is careful to instruct us how to carry ourselves both toward his own Majesty and also toward one another, so let us approve ourselves to him in both. Let us remember what Christ said to the Pharisees: “These you+ ought to have done, without neglecting the others.” The same Lord who requires praise to his own Majesty enjoins mutual service to one another. The neglect of this, as well as of that, shows too light a regard for his will and pleasure. “Therefore what God30 has joined together, let man not separate.”

§. 3. Of everyone’s submitting himself to another.

Again, as this verse refers to what follows, it declares the general sum of all, which is to submit ourselves mutually to one another in the fear of God. Its parts are two:

  1. An exhortation.
  2. A direction.

In the exhortation are noted both the duty itself, in this word submit, and also the parties to whom it is to be performed, one another.

Both branches of the exhortation, that is, the duty and the parties, joined together, give us this doctrine:

It is a general, mutual duty belonging to all Christians31 to submit themselves to one another. For this precept is as general as any of the former ones, belonging to all sorts and degrees whatever, and this word one another32 implies as much. In the same extent the apostle in another place exhorts us to “serve one another,” and again, every man to seek33 “the good of others.”

Concerning inferiors, it is clear without question that34 they ought to submit themselves to their superiors. Indeed, concerning equals no great question can be raised: they must go before one another in giving honor,35 and so submit themselves. But concerning superiors, a fair question may be raised, whether it is a duty required of them to submit themselves to their inferiors.

To resolve this doubt, we must first distinguish between36 the subjection of reverence and the subjection of service.

Subjection of reverence is that by which one acknowledges a preeminence and superiority in those whom he reverences. He does it in speech, by giving them titles of honor; or in gesture, by some kind of bow; or in action, by readily obeying their commands. This belongs to inferiors only.

Subjection of service is that by which one, in his place, is37 ready to do what good he can to another. This is common to all Christians. It is a duty which even superiors owe to inferiors, according to the extent of this word one another named before. In this respect even the highest governor on earth is called a minister, for the good of those who38 are under him.

Secondly, we must make a difference between the work itself39 and the manner of doing it. A work which in itself is a work of superiority and authority may, in the manner of doing it, be a work of submission: that is, if it is done in humility and meekness of mind. The magistrate, by ruling with meekness and humility, submits himself to his subject. In this respect the apostle exhorts, “Do nothing” (no, not the highest and greatest works that40 can be) “out of empty pride, but in humility.”

Thirdly, we must distinguish between the different places in which men stand. For even those who are superiors to some41 are inferiors to others, like the one who said, “I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me.” The master who has servants under him may be under the authority of a magistrate. Indeed, God has so ordered each one’s place that there is not any one who is not in some respect under another. The wife, though a mother of children, is under her husband. The husband, though head of a family, is under public magistrates. Public magistrates are one under another, and all under the king. The king himself is under God, and under his word delivered by his ambassadors, to which the highest are to submit themselves. And ministers of the word, as subjects, are under their kings and governors. He who says, “Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities,”42 does not except ministers of the word. And he who says, “Obey your+ leaders and submit to them,”43 does not except kings. The only difference is this: the authority of the king is in himself, and in his own name he may command obedience to be performed to himself; but the authority of a minister is in Christ, and only in Christ’s name may he require obedience to be performed to Christ.

The reason why all are bound to submit themselves to one44 another is this: every one is set in his place by God, not so much for himself as for the good of others. For this reason the apostle exhorts, “No one should seek his own good, but the good of others.”45 Even governors are raised to places of dignity and authority more for the good of their subjects than for their own honor. Their callings are in truth offices of service, indeed burdens, to which they must willingly put their shoulders, being called by God. And they must give an account of them, concerning the good which they have done to others. To bring that good about, they need to submit themselves.

Therefore let every one, high and low, rich and poor,46 superior and inferior, magistrate and subject, minister and people, husband and wife, parent and child, master and servant, neighbors and fellows, all of all sorts in their different places, take notice of their duty in this point of submission, and make it a matter of conscience to put it into practice. Let magistrates do it by securing the welfare and peace of their people, as Mordecai did;47 ministers, by making themselves servants to their people, not seeking their own profit but the profit of many, that they may be saved, as Paul did;48 fathers, by bringing up their children well, and taking heed that they do not provoke them to wrath, as David did;49 husbands, by living with their wives with understanding, giving honor to the wife as to the weaker vessel, as Abraham did;50 masters, by doing what is just and fair to their servants, as the centurion did.51 Let every one do it by being of the same mind toward one another, and by serving one another in love, according to the apostle’s rule.52 Let this duty of submission first be well learned, and then all other duties will be better performed.

Do not be high-minded, nor swell against one another.53 Though in outward condition some may be higher than others, yet in Christ all are one, whether slave or free;54 all are members of one and the same body.55 Now consider the mutual affection (if I may so speak) of the members of a natural body toward one another. Not one of them will puff itself up and rise against another. The head, which is the highest and of greatest honor, will submit itself to the feet in performing the duty of a head, as well as the feet to the head in performing their duty; and so with all the other parts. Nor is it implied by this that those who are in a place of dignity and authority should forget or give up their place, dignity, or authority, and become like inferiors under authority, any more than the head does. For the head, in submitting itself, does not go on the ground and bear the body, as the feet do; but it submits itself by directing and governing the other parts, and that with all the humility, meekness, and gentleness that it can. So must all superiors do. Much more must equals and inferiors learn to perform their duty with humility and meekness,56 without scorn or disdain. This is what the apostle expressly mentioned before, and here hints at again: none are exempted or excused from it. We know that it is unnatural and unbecoming for the head to scorn the feet and to swell against them, but it is worse than monstrous for one hand to scorn another. What then shall we say if the feet swell against the head? Surely such scorn and disdain among the members would cause not only great disturbance, but also utter ruin to the body. And can it be otherwise in a political body? But on the contrary, when all of all sorts willingly submit themselves to one another (as has been shown before), the whole body and every member of it will reap good by it. Indeed, by this mutual submission, as we do good, so we shall receive good.

§. 4. Of the fear of God.

So much for the exhortation. The direction follows: In the fear of the Lord. This clause is added to declare partly the means by which men may be brought to submit themselves readily to one another, and partly the manner in which they ought to submit themselves. The fear of the Lord is both the efficient cause that moves a true Christian willingly to perform every duty to man, and also the end to which he refers everything that he does. For the better understanding of this, I will briefly declare

  1. What this fear of the Lord is.
  2. How the Lord is the proper object of it.
  3. What its extent is.
  4. Why it is so much urged.

First, the fear of God is a reverent awe of the divine Majesty.57 At times it arises from faith in the mercy and goodness of God. For when the heart of man has once felt a sweet taste of God’s goodness, and found that all happiness consists in his favor alone, it is struck with such an inward awe and reverence that it would not displease58 his Majesty for anything, but would rather do whatever it may know to be pleasing and acceptable to him. For these are the two effects which arise from this kind of fear of God:

1. A careful endeavor to please God. In this respect59 good King Jehoshaphat, having exhorted his judges to execute the judgment of the Lord rightly, adds this clause as a motive to it: “May the fear of the Lord be upon you+.”60 By this he implied that God’s fear would make them endeavor to approve themselves to God.

2. A careful avoiding of such things as offend the Majesty of God and grieve his Spirit. In this respect the wise man says, “To fear the Lord is to hate evil.”61 And of Job it is said that he was “fearing God and shunning evil.”62

At other times, again, awe and dread of the divine Majesty arise from distrust. For when a man’s heart doubts God’s mercy and expects nothing but vengeance, the very thought of God strikes an awe, or rather a dread, into him, and so makes him fear God.

From this double cause of fear, the one contrary63 to the other, has arisen that common distinction between a filial or son-like fear and a servile or slavish fear. This distinction is grounded on these words of the apostle: “You+ did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you+ to fear” (this is64 a servile fear), “but you+ received the Spirit of sonship,65 by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” This causes a filial fear. Filial fear is the kind of fear that dutiful children bear toward their fathers. But servile fear is the kind that slaves bear toward their masters. A son fears simply to offend or displease his father, so that66 his fear is accompanied with love. A slave fears nothing but the punishment of his offense, so that his fear is joined with hatred; such a one does not fear to sin, but fears to burn in hell for sin. Faithful Abraham, like a gracious child, feared God (as God’s angel bears witness, Gen 22:12) when he was ready to sacrifice his only son rather than offend God by refusing to67 obey his command. But faithless Adam, like a servile slave, feared God (as he himself testifies against himself, Gen 3:10) when, after he had broken God’s command, he hid himself from the presence of God. This slavish fear is plainly a devilish fear (for the devils68 fear so that they tremble). It makes men wish there were no hell, no day of judgment, no judge, indeed no God. This is the fear without which we must serve the Lord.69 To submit oneself in this fear is not at all acceptable to God. It is therefore the filial fear which is meant here.

Secondly, God is the proper object of this fear, as is evident from70 this testimony and many more in Scripture, where the fear of God and of the Lord is mentioned. This fear has so proper a relation to God that the Scripture, by a kind of special right, gives God this title, Fear. For where Jacob mentions “the Fear of Isaac,”71 he means the Lord whom Isaac feared.

Is it then unlawful to fear any but God?72

No. Men also may be feared, such as princes, parents, masters,73 and other superiors. For the apostle, exhorting us to give every one his due,74 gives this instance: “fear to whom fear is due.” Yet God may nevertheless be said to be the proper object of fear, because all the fear that is in any way due to any creature is due to him in and for the Lord, whose image he carries. So in truth it is not so much the person of a man that is to be feared, as the image of God placed in him by virtue of some authority or dignity belonging to him. If any such opposition should arise between God and man that in fearing man our fear would be withdrawn from God, then the rule of Christ is to prevail, which is this: “Do not fear those who75 kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell.”

Thirdly, the extent of this true filial fear of God is76 very large. No one point throughout the whole Scripture is urged more than this fear of the Lord. It is often added to other duties, as that by which they are seasoned, and without which they cannot be performed well. That is why we are commanded to “serve the Lord with fear,”77 to be “perfecting holiness in the fear of God,”78 and to work out our salvation “with fear.”79 And the churches are commended for “living in the fear of the Lord,”80 and so likewise particular men, such as Abraham,81 Joseph,82 Job,83 and many others. Indeed, the whole worship of God is often summed up under this branch of fear. So when our Savior Christ cites this text, “Fear the Lord your God,”84 he expresses it this way: “Worship the Lord your God.”85 And again, where the Lord says by his prophet Isaiah, “Their fear86 of Me is but rules taught by men,” Christ quotes that text this way: “They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine87 the precepts of men.” From these places compared together it is evident that under the fear of God is included the worship of God. Indeed, all the duty which we owe to God and man is summed up under this title, the fear of God. For when David would declare in one word the sum and substance of all that a minister ought to teach his people, he says, “I will teach you+ the fear of88 the Lord.”89

Fourthly, the reason why the Holy Spirit so much urges the fear of God, and that in so large an extent as has been shown, I take to be this: to show a difference between the integrity and perfection of God’s image which was first planted in man at his creation, and the renewal of it while he lives here in this world. So complete and perfect was God’s image in man then that he needed no other motive but love to stir him up to any duty. That is why, when the Holy Spirit would set forth that perfection of God’s image first planted in man, he adds this title love to other duties, whether they concern God or man. Concerning God, Moses exhorts Israel “to love the90 Lord your God and to serve Him,” and again, “to love the Lord your God, to walk in91 His ways, and to keep His commandments,” etc. Concerning man, the apostle exhorts us to “serve one another in love,”92 and to “do everything in love.”93 Indeed, at times the Holy Spirit is pleased to sum up all duties under love. In this respect Christ calls this commandment (“You shall love the Lord”) “the94 great commandment,” which includes all the commandments of the first table under it. And for the second table, Saint Paul says that “love is the fulfillment of the law.”95 But by Adam’s fall, and the corruption with which it infected man’s nature, the love of God has grown cold in man. And though the saints are created anew according to that image of God, yet while they live in this world that image is not as perfect as it was; the flesh remains in the best of them. In this respect God has firmly fixed this feeling of fear in man’s heart, and by it he both restrains him from sin and also stirs him up to every good duty.

§. 5. Of the fear of God moving us to do service to men.

Having briefly declared the nature, object, extent, and use of fear, I return to the point in hand, that is, to show 1. how it is laid down here as a motive to stir men up to perform the duty required here. For by this clause, in the fear of the Lord, the apostle implies that

It is the fear of God which moves men to submit96 themselves to one another as a matter of conscience. This made David97 rule the people of God so well, and Joseph98 deal so well with his brothers. Indeed,99 this is noted as the cause of the righteous rule of Christ himself. That good King Jehoshaphat knew this well. Therefore, when he appointed judges over his people, he said to them, as a motive to stir them up to execute the judgments of the Lord rightly, “May the fear of the Lord be upon you+.”100 So also Saint Peter, to move subjects to honor their king, sets this exhortation first: “Fear God.”101

By fear of man one may be brought to submit himself102 to another. A magistrate may be moved to deal justly and mildly with his people through fear of insurrections and rebellions. Subjects may be brought to submit themselves by severe laws and tyranny. And so may other inferiors also, by threats, by harsh treatment, and by other self-serving motives.

1. Though fear of man is a motive, it does not follow103 that the fear of God is therefore no motive. It may be another motive, and a better motive.

2. The submission which is performed through fear of104 man is a forced and slavish submission, not at all acceptable to God. But the submission which is performed through a true filial fear of God is a free, willing, ready, cheerful, conscientious submission. It is such a submission as will stir us up to do by it the best good we can to those to whom we submit ourselves. So it is more acceptable to God, by reason of its cause, and more profitable to man, by reason of its effect and fruit.

For a true fear of God makes us regard what105 God requires and commands more than what our corrupt heart desires and suggests. It subdues our unruly passions and brings them within the bounds of duty. It makes us deny ourselves and our own desires. And though through the corruption of our nature and our inborn pride we are loath to submit, yet God’s fear will bring down that proud mind, and make us humble and gentle. It will keep those who are in authority from tyranny, cruelty, and excessive severity. And it will keep those who are under subjection from pretense, deceit, and secret conspiracies.

See how necessary it is that a true fear of the Lord106 be planted in men’s hearts: in the hearts of kings and all governors, in the hearts of subjects and all people, whether superiors or inferiors. Where there is no fear of God, there will be no good submission to man. Abraham107 thought that the men of Gerar would have no respect for him or his wife, nor make a matter of conscience of common uprightness, nor keep from shedding innocent blood, because he saw that there was “no fear of God in this place.” And the apostle, having listed108 many notorious effects of man’s natural corruption, concludes them all with this, as the cause of all: “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” Therefore let magistrates, parents, masters, and all in authority take special care that their subjects, children, servants, and all under them may be taught and brought to fear the Lord. I dare affirm that inferiors who are taught to fear God will do better service to their superiors than those who fear their superiors only as men, and do not fear God. Let ministers especially urge and press a fear of God on the consciences of men. Let all inferiors pray that the fear of the Lord may be planted in the hearts of their superiors, so that they may live a quiet and peaceable life under them in all godliness and dignity. Happy is that kingdom where magistrates and subjects fear the Lord. Happy is that church where ministers and people fear the Lord. Happy is that family where husband and wife, parents and children, master and servants fear the Lord. In such a kingdom, church, and family, every one will submit himself to the others, for the mutual good of one another. But if those who do not fear God submit themselves, whether they are superiors or inferiors, it is for their own ends and advantages, and not for the good of those to whom they submit themselves.

§. 6. Of limiting all duty to man within the bounds of the fear of God.

Again, as this clause (In the fear of the Lord) declares the manner of submission, it shows that

No submission is to be performed to man except that which109 may stand with the fear of God. By this we show that we have respect to God, and labor above all to approve ourselves to him. So David is commanded to “rule in the110 fear of God,” and other magistrates to perform their duty111 “in the fear of the Lord”; and Nehemiah, that good governor,112 was careful to do so. So also subjects are to obey in the fear of the Lord. The apostle implies this by setting113 this precept, “Fear God,” before that one, “honor the king”; as if he had said, “So honor the king that in it, and by it, you+ may show your+ fear of God. Do not let this latter cross the former.” Servants likewise are commanded to be obedient to their masters with this proviso: “fearing the Lord.”114 Such phrases as these, “for the Lord’s sake,” “as to the Lord,” “in the115 Lord,” “as servants of Christ,” and the like, joined to116 the duties of inferiors, imply as much.

There is great reason that all service should be limited117 by the fear of God. For God is the highest Lord, to whom all service is due first and chiefly. Whatever service is due to any man, high or low, is due in and for the Lord. The Lord has set superiors in their places of preeminence, in which they bear the image of God. The Lord has also set inferiors in their places, and entrusted them as his charge to the government of those who are over them. He who does not obey those who are over him in the fear of God shows no respect for God’s image. And he who does not govern those who are under him in the fear of God shows no respect for God’s charge.

Besides, God is that great Judge to whom all of all sorts,118 superiors and inferiors, must give an account of their service. However well we have approved ourselves to men by our service, yet if we have not had respect to God in it, and approved ourselves to him, with what face can we appear before his dreadful judgment seat?119 Can the favor of those whom we have pleased in this world protect and shelter us from the fury of God’s displeasure?

See the folly of those governors who wholly give themselves to the whims of their people, even though it is against the Lord and his word. This was Adam’s folly, who120 ate of the forbidden fruit at his wife’s urging. This was Aaron’s folly, who set up an121 idol to please the people. And this was Saul’s folly, who, against God’s express122 prohibition, allowed his people to take some of the spoil of the Amalekites. The same may be said of Joash, who123 listened to his princes and set up idols, and of Pilate, who,124 to please the people, delivered Christ to be crucified against his conscience. The fearful outcome of this submission of theirs, not seasoned with the fear of God but contrary to it, may be a warning to all superiors to take heed how they seek to please those who are under them more than God who is above them. The outcome of Adam’s, Aaron’s, Saul’s, and Joash’s base submission is noted by the Holy Spirit in their separate histories. Of Pilate it is recorded that, being125 brought into extreme distress, he laid violent hands on himself.

Nor is it to be counted folly only in superiors to submit themselves to their inferiors against the Lord, but also in inferiors to submit to their superiors against him. For by it they show that they fear man more than God, which Christ expressly126 forbids his friends to do. The captains who went127 to fetch Elijah obeyed their king in it; but what did they gain by it? Was the king able to save them from the fire which God sent down from heaven on them? The women128 who were rebuked for burning incense to the Queen of Heaven did not do it without their husbands; yet they were not excused by that. The children and others in the family129 submitted themselves to Dathan and Abiram in standing at the door of their tents in defiance of Moses; but because it was not in the Lord, but against him, they were not exempted from the judgment. Therefore let all of all sorts set the fear of God before them as a mark to aim at in all their actions. Let superiors130 neither do anything to please their inferiors,131 nor allow anything to be done for their sakes by their inferiors, which cannot stand with the fear of God. And let inferiors132 neither do,133134 nor forbear to do, at the will of their superiors, anything that swerves from the fear of God. But let every one “submit to one another in the fear of God.”

Particular Callings and the Wife’s Submission

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 7–13

§. 7. Of performing the duties of particular callings.

Eph 5:22.

Wives, submit yourselves+ to your+ own husbands as to the Lord.

From that general direction about mutual submission, the apostle comes to certain particulars, by which he gives examples of it. And he teaches us that

It is not enough to perform the general duties of Christianity,135 unless we are also conscientious in performing the particular duties of our separate callings. A conscientious performance of those particular duties is one part of our walking “worthy of the calling” we have received.136 Therefore the apostle, to illustrate this and give examples of it, lists various particulars, both in this and137 other epistles. So do138 other apostles. And Titus139 is charged to teach them. God himself has given a pattern of this in his law: for the main aim of the fifth commandment140 is to instruct us in the particular duties of our separate callings.

By this much credit is brought to our profession of faith, and “the teaching about God our Savior” is adorned.141 And by this much good is both shared with one another and received from one another. For our particular places and callings are the bonds by which persons are firmly and fitly knit together, as the members of a natural body are knit by nerves, arteries, sinews, veins and the like, by which life, sense and motion are passed from one to another.

Therefore let notice be taken of the particular callings142 in which God has set us, and of the separate duties of those callings, and let conscience be used in practicing them. He is no good Christian who is careless in this. A bad husband, wife, parent, child, master, servant, magistrate or minister is no good Christian.

§. 8. Of the lawfulness of private functions in a family.

Among other particular callings, the apostle chooses those which God has settled in private families. He is exact in reciting their separate and distinct orders (for a family consists of these three orders, husbands, wives, parents, children, masters, servants, all of which he lists). Yes, he is also full and earnest in urging the duties which belong to them. From this we may well infer that

The private vocations of a family, and the functions belonging143 to it, are such as Christians are called to by God, and in exercising them they may and must employ some part of their time. For can we think that the Holy Spirit (who, as the philosophers say of nature, does nothing in vain) would set down these private duties so distinctly, and urge them so forcibly, if they did not well become Christians and closely concern them? All the places in Scripture which require family duties are proofs of the truth of this doctrine.

The reasons for this doctrine are clear. For the family is144 a seedbed of the church and commonwealth. It is like a beehive, in which is the stock, and out of which many swarms of bees are sent. For in families all sorts of people are bred and brought up, and out of families they are sent into the church and commonwealth. The first beginning of mankind, and of its increase, was out of a family. For God first joined Adam and Eve in marriage and made them husband and wife, and then gave them children. So husband and wife, parent and child (which are parts of a family) existed before magistrate and subject, minister and people, which are the parts of a commonwealth and a church. When all public societies were destroyed by the universal flood, a family, the family of Noah, was preserved, and out of it kingdoms and nations were raised again. That great people of the Jews, which could not be numbered for multitude, was raised out of the family of Abram. Yes, even to this day all sorts of people have come from families, and so they will to the end of the world. From this it follows that a conscientious performance of domestic and household duties tends to the good ordering of church and commonwealth, as being a means to fit and prepare men for them.

Besides, a family is a little church and a little commonwealth,145 or at least a lively representation of them. By it a trial may be made of those who are fit for any place of authority, or of subjection, in church or commonwealth. Or rather, it is like a school in which the first principles and grounds of government and subjection are learned, so that men are fitted for greater matters in church or commonwealth. That is why the146 apostle declares that a bishop who cannot rule his own house is not fit to govern the church. So we may say of inferiors who cannot be subject in a family: they will hardly be brought to yield such subjection as they ought in church or commonwealth. Take as an instance Absalom and Adonijah, David’s sons.

This is to be noted for the satisfaction of certain weak147 consciences, who think that if they have no public calling, they have no calling at all, and from this conclude that all their time is spent without a calling. If that conclusion were good and sound, what comfort in spending their time would most women have, who are not admitted to any public function in church or commonwealth? Or servants, children and others who are wholly employed in the private affairs of the family? But the doctrine named above shows how unsound that conclusion is. Besides, who does not know that the preservation of families tends to the good of church and commonwealth? So a conscientious performance of household duties, in regard to its end and fruit, may be counted a public work. Yes, if domestic duties are well and thoroughly performed, they will be quite enough to take up a man’s whole time. If a master of a family is also a husband of a wife and a father of children, he will find work enough. This may easily be proved by those particular duties which we will show later to belong to masters, husbands and parents. So a wife likewise, if she is also a mother and a mistress, and faithfully endeavors to do what she is bound to do by virtue of those callings, will find enough to do. As for children under the government of their parents, and servants in a family, their whole calling is to be obedient to their parents and masters, and to do what they command them in the Lord. Therefore, if those who have no public calling are all the more diligent in the functions of their private callings, they will be as well accepted by the Lord as if they had public offices.

Yet there are many who, having no public employment, think they may spend their time as they please, either in idleness148 or in following their vain pleasures and delights day after day, and so cast themselves out of all calling. Such are many masters of families, who commit all the care of their house either to their wives or to some servant, and misspend their whole time in idleness, dissipation and sensual pleasure. Such are many mistresses, who spend their time lying in bed, dressing themselves and gossiping. Such are many young gentlemen living in their fathers’ houses, who, partly through the excessive indulgence and negligence of their parents, and partly through their own headstrong desires and rebellious will, run without restraint wherever their corrupt lusts lead them. These, and others like them, though by God’s providence they are placed in callings, in lawful callings, and in callings that give them matter enough of employment, yet make themselves to be of no calling. Now what blessing can they look for from the Lord? The Lord is accustomed149 to give his blessing to men while they are busy in their callings. Jacob’s150 faithful service to his uncle Laban moved God to bless him. Joseph’s151 faithfulness to his master Potiphar was remembered by God, who advanced him to be ruler in Egypt. Moses152 was keeping his father-in-law’s sheep when God appeared to him in the bush and appointed him a prince over his people. David153 was sent for from the field, where he was keeping his father’s sheep, when he was anointed to be king over Israel. Elisha154 was plowing when he was anointed to be a prophet.155 The shepherds were watching their sheep when the glad tidings were brought to them that the Savior of the world was born. Not to dwell on any more particulars, the promise of God’s protection is limited to our callings: for156 the charge which God has given to the angels concerning man is to guard him in all his ways.

As for those who have public offices in church or157 commonwealth, they must not on that account think themselves exempt from all family duties. These private duties are necessary duties. Though a man is a magistrate or a minister, yet if he is a husband, or a father, or a master, he must not neglect his wife, children and servants. Indeed, those who are free from public functions are bound to attend all the more to the private duties of their families, because they have more leisure for them. But no one ought wholly to neglect them. Joshua,158 who was a captain and prince of his people, and very much employed in public affairs, yet did not neglect his family: for he professes that he and his house would serve the Lord. It seems that Eli159 was negligent in performing the duty of a father, and David160 also. But what followed from it? Two of Eli’s sons proved sacrilegious and wicked priests. Two of David’s sons proved very bad members of the commonwealth, even plain traitors.

§. 9. Of the apostle’s order in laying down the duties of husbands and wives in the first place.

There being three special degrees or orders in a family,161 (as we heard before) the apostle places husband and wife in the first rank, and declares their duties first, and that not without good reason. For

First, the husband and wife were the first couple that162 ever were in the world. Adam and Eve were joined in marriage, and made man and wife, before they had children or servants. So it happens for the most part even to this day in setting up or bringing together a family: the first couple is ordinarily a husband and a wife.

Secondly, most usually the husband and his wife are the163 chief in a family, and all under them are single persons: they are the governors of all the rest in the house. Therefore it is most fitting that they should first know their duty and learn to practice it, so that they may be an example to all the rest. If they fail in their duty to one another, they give occasion to all the rest under them to be careless and negligent in theirs. Let a husband be churlish to his wife and despise her, and he gives an occasion to children and servants to despise her likewise and to be disobedient to her. Yes, he gives them occasion to be churlish and perverse to one another, especially to those under them. Let a wife be untrustworthy and unfaithful to her husband, let her filch and pilfer from him, and children and servants will soon take courage, or rather boldness, from her example to steal secretly what they can from their father and master. So their breach of164 duty is a double fault: one in respect of the party whom they wrong and to whom they deny duty, the other in respect of those to whom they give occasion of sinning.

Know therefore, O husbands and wives, that you+, above165 all others in the family, are most bound to a conscientious performance of your+ duty. Your+ condemnation will be greater if you+ fail in it. Look to it above the rest, and by your+ example draw your+ children and servants (if you+ have any) to perform their duties. They will surely do this more readily when they see you+ as guides going before them, and making conscience of your+ joint and separate duties.

§. 10. Of the apostle’s order in setting down the duties of inferiors in the first place.166

In handling the duties of the first couple named above, the apostle begins with wives, and lays down their particular duties in the first place. I take the reason for this order to be the inferiority of the wife to her husband. I take it so all the more because I observe this to be his usual method and order: first to declare the duties of inferiors, and then those of superiors. For in handling the duties of167 children and parents, and of168 servants and masters, he begins with the inferiors, both in this and169 in other epistles. Peter170 also observes this order. Yes,171 the law itself mentions the inferiors’ duty in the first place, and that expressly, only implying the superiors’ duty to follow as a just consequence, which is this: If the inferior must give honor, and by virtue of it perform such duties as belong to it, then the superior must carry himself as worthy of honor, and by virtue of it perform corresponding duties.

Question. Why should inferiors’ duties be more fully172 expressed, and placed in the first rank?

Answer. Surely because, for the most part, inferiors are most unwilling to undertake the duties of their place. Who is not more ready to rule than to be subject?

I do not deny that it is a far more difficult and hard matter to govern well than to obey well. For to rule and173 govern requires more knowledge, experience, wisdom, care, watchfulness, diligence and other such virtues than to obey and be subject. He who obeys has his rule laid before him, which is the will and command of his174 superior in things lawful and not against God’s will. But the superior who commands has to consider not only what is lawful, but also what is most fit, proper, suitable and in every way the best. Yes, he must also look ahead to the time to come, and observe, as far as he can, whether what is fit enough for the present may not be dangerous for the time to come, and in that respect unfit to be pressed. From this it follows that the superior in authority may sin in commanding what the inferior in subjection may do at his command without sin. Who can justly charge Joab with sin in numbering the people,175 when David urged him to do it by virtue of his authority?176 Yet David did sin in commanding it. Without any question Saul did sin in charging the people by an oath to eat no food on the day that they pursued their enemies (a time when they most needed to be refreshed with food, as Jonathan’s words imply). And yet the people did not177 sin in abstaining: witness what followed on Jonathan’s eating, though he did not know his father’s charge. Who does not see by this that it is a matter of much more difficulty to rule well than to obey? This is still further evident from God’s wise, disposing providence in ordering who should govern and who obey. Commonly the younger178 in age, the weaker in sex, the lower in condition, the more ignorant in understanding, and the like, are in places of subjection; but the elder, stronger, wealthier, wiser and similar persons are for the most part, or at least should be, in places of authority. “Woe to you, O land179 whose king is a youth,” says Solomon. And Isaiah180 denounces it as a curse on Israel: “I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them.” And he complains181 that “women rule over them.”

Now to return to the point: though it is true that governors have the heaviest burden laid on their shoulders, yet inferiors who are under subjection think their own burden the heaviest. They are the most reluctant to bear it and the most willing to cast it off. For by nature there is in everyone much182 pride and ambition. Like dust thrown in the eyes of their understanding, it puts out their sight, and so makes them desire superiority and authority over others, and makes them stubborn under the yoke of subjection. This is why in all ages, both by divine and by human laws, penalties and punishments of various kinds have been ordained to keep inferiors within the bounds of their duty. And yet (such is the pride of man’s heart) all this will not serve. What age, what place was there ever, which has183 not had just cause to complain of subjects’ rebellion, servants’ stubbornness, children’s disobedience and wives’ presumption? It is not without cause, therefore, that the apostle first declares the duties of inferiors.

Besides, the apostle would teach by this those who are under authority how to move those who are in authority over them to deal fairly and kindly with them, not harshly and cruelly: namely, by endeavoring to perform their own duty first. For what is it that provokes wrath, rage and fury in governors? What makes those who have authority deal roughly and rigorously? Is it not, for the most part, disobedience and stubbornness in those who are under government? Some in authority are so proud, so savage and inhumane that no honor done to them, no performance of duty, can satisfy and content them, but they will (like David’s184 enemies) repay goodness with evil. Even so, the best general direction that can be prescribed to inferiors, to provoke their governors to deal well with them, is that the inferiors themselves be careful and conscientious in doing their duty first. If their governors on earth are not moved by it at all, yet the highest Lord in heaven will graciously accept it.

Lastly, men must first learn to obey well before they185 can rule well. For those who scorn to be subject to their governors while they are under authority are likely to prove intolerably insolent when they are in authority.

Learn, all you+ who are under authority, how to win your+ governors’ favor: how to make your+ yoke easy and your+ burden light, and how to prevent many harms which might otherwise fall on you+ because of the power your+ superiors have over you+. First do your+ duty.

There are many weighty reasons to move governors186 to be the first to begin doing their duty. For,

First, by virtue of their authority they bear God’s image; therefore in doing their duty they honor that image.

Secondly, because of their place they ought to go before those who are under them.

Thirdly, a faithful performance of their duty is a special means to keep their inferiors within the bounds of theirs.

Fourthly, their failing in duty sets an example: it causes others under them to fail in theirs, and so it is a double sin.

Fifthly, their reckoning will be the greater: for of those who have received more, more will be required.

It is therefore to be wished that superiors and inferiors would strive over who should begin first,187 and who should perform his own part best, and in this kind strive to excel, as runners in a race strive to outrun one another.

But if the question is raised who will begin, I advise inferiors not to hold out in this contest, but to consider that the apostle188 urges them first, and that it is safest for them to begin. For in this contest inferiors are likely to fare the worst, because of the power which superiors have over them. And though it is more against our corrupt, proud and stubborn nature to be subject and obey, yet let us endeavor all the more to yield duty in this kind. For it is a special part of spiritual prudence to observe what our corrupt nature is most prone to, and where it most swells up, so that there we may strive most to beat it down. Nature is contrary to grace, and “the mind of the flesh is hostile to God.”189

§. 11. Of the reasons why wives’ duties are taught first.

Question. Why, among other inferiors, are wives brought first into the school of Christ to learn their duty?

Answer. Many good reasons may be given for the apostle’s order even in this point.

First, of all the other inferiors in a family, wives are by far the most excellent, and therefore they are to be placed in the first rank.

Secondly, wives were the first to whom subjection was commanded. Before there was child or servant in the world, it was said to the woman, “Your desire will be subject to your husband.”190

Thirdly, wives are the fountain from which all the other degrees spring, and therefore they ought to be cleansed first.

Fourthly, this subjection is a good pattern for children and servants, and a great means to move them to be subject.

Fifthly, I may further add as a truth, which experience makes all too plain in every place, that among all the parties from whom the Holy Spirit requires subjection, wives for the most part are191 the most backward in yielding subjection to their husbands. But you+ wives who fear God, be careful of your+ duty. Though it may seem somewhat contrary to192 the common course and practice of wives, yet “you shall not follow the crowd in wrongdoing.” Though it is harsh to corrupt nature,193 yet beat down that corruption. Yes, though your+ husbands are backward in their duties, yet be eager, and strive to go before them in yours+. Remember what the Lord says (Matt 5:46, 47): “If you+ love those who love you+, what are you+ doing more than others?” Remember also what the apostle says (1 Tim 2:14): that the woman was first in the transgression,194 and first had her duty given to her, and that the woman was made for the man, and not man for the woman.195

So you+ will deserve that commendation of good wives: “Many have done noble things, but you+ surpass them all.”196

Having so far handled the general instructions named above, I will go on to a more distinct explanation of the words, gather the observations which arise from them, and then declare in particular the separate duties which the three orders in a family owe to each other.

§. 12. Of wives’ subjection.

Eph 5:22.

Wives, submit yourselves+ to your+ own husbands as to the Lord.

The197 word by which the apostle has set out the duties of wives is in the middle voice. It may be translated passively, as198 many have done, or199 actively, as our English Bible does (submit yourselves), and that most fitly: for there is a double subjection.

1. A necessary subjection, which is the subjection of order.

2. A voluntary subjection, which is the subjection of duty. The necessary subjection is that degree of inferiority in which God has placed all inferiors, and by which he has subjected them to their superiors, that is, set them in a lower rank. By virtue of it, though inferiors seek to exalt themselves above their superiors, yet they are subject to them: their ambition does not take away the order which God has established. A wife is in an inferior degree, however much she domineers over her husband.

The voluntary subjection is that dutiful respect which inferiors carry toward those whom God has set over them, by which they show a willingness to yield to the order which God has established. Because God has placed them under their superiors, they will show, in all duty, the subjection which their place requires.

Because it is a duty that is required here, the voluntary subjection must be meant here. And to express this, it is set down this way: submit yourselves.

Though the same word is used here as in the previous verse, yet it is limited to a narrower compass, namely to200 the subjection of reverence.

Here learn that voluntary subjection must be added to necessary201 subjection: that is, duty must be performed according to the order and degree in which God has set us. This is to make a virtue of necessity.

Under this phrase (submit yourselves) all the duties which a wife owes to her husband are included, as I will202 show more distinctly later.

§. 13. Of the persons to whom wives must be subject.

In setting down the persons to whom wives owe subjection, the apostle notes a word of limitation203 (own), and he does so to show that a wife ought to have only one husband. This is expressed more plainly in another place by the same phrase: “each woman” is to have “her own husband,” that204 is, only one, her own. So

It is unlawful for a wife to have more than one husband at once.

A wife must submit herself only to that one205 husband of her own, and to no other man (as she is a wife and yields the duty of a wife). So the subjection of adulteresses is excluded here, and the duty required is that

A wife must yield a chaste, faithful, matrimonial subjection206 to her husband.

Here, by the way, note the foolish207 inference of Adamites, Familists and such licentious libertines. From the general words which the apostle uses (men208 and women) they infer that all women are as wives to all men, and that there is no need for any such close union of one man with one woman. This beastly opinion is contrary to the current of Scripture and to the ancient law of marriage (“the two will become one flesh”), and so also to this clause (their own husbands). The apostle, in using those general words, followed the Greek idiom, which puts those two words (men, women) for husbands and wives. So also do other languages, yes, and our English. The particular relation between the persons meant by those two words plainly shows how they are to be taken, and when they are to be limited to man and wife. To take away that ambiguity, our English has well translated them husband and wife.

To direct wives to their duty and stir them up to it, the apostle adds this clause (as to the Lord), which is both a rule and a reason for wives’ subjection. It directs wives by noting the limit of their obedience and its manner.

The limit is in this: that wives ought to obey their husbands in such a way209 that at the same time they obey the Lord; but no further. They must not be subject to their husbands in anything that cannot stand with their subjection to the Lord.

The manner is in this: that wives ought to yield such a kind of subjection210 to their husbands as may be approved by the Lord.

So the apostle himself explains this phrase, in ch. 6, v. 5, 6.

It stirs wives up to submit themselves to their husbands by noting the place of a husband, which is to be in the Lord’s stead, bearing his image, and in that respect having a fellowship and partnership with the Lord. So

Wives, in subjecting themselves rightly to their husbands, are subject to the Lord. And on the other side,211

Wives, in refusing to be subject to their husbands, refuse to be subject to the Lord.212
