Headship in Marriage and the Church

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 14–25

§. 14. How a husband is his wife’s head.

Eph 5:23.

For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the church; and He is the Savior of the body.

The place of a husband, hinted at in the last clause of the previous verse, is more plainly expressed and fully explained in this verse. His place is expressed under the metaphor of a head, and amplified by his likeness in this to Christ.

The particle of connection (FOR) shows that this verse is added as a reason. It may fitly be referred both to the duty itself and to the manner of performing it.

The metaphor of a head enforces the duty.

The amplification of it, by the likeness that is drawn to Christ, enforces the manner of performing the duty.

A wife must submit herself to a husband, because he is her head; and she must do it as to the Lord, because her husband is to her as Christ is to the church.

The metaphor of a head declares two points: the dignity and the duty of a husband.

1. As a head is more eminent and excellent than the body, and placed above it, so is a husband to his wife.

2. As a head, by the understanding that is in it, governs, protects, preserves and provides for the body, so the husband governs, protects, preserves and provides for his wife; at least he ought to do so, for this is his office and duty. This is noted here to show the benefit that a wife receives from her husband. So two motives are included under this metaphor.

The first is taken from the husband’s prerogative. From it note that

Subjection must be yielded to those who are over us. For this is a main end of the difference between one party and another.213 To what end is the head set above the body, if the body is not subject to it?

The second is taken from the benefit that a wife reaps from her husband’s superiority, and it shows that

Those who will not submit themselves to their superiors are214 injurious to themselves, as the body would be injurious to itself if it would not be subject to the head.

§. 15. Of the resemblance of a husband to Christ.

To enforce the reason given above all the more, the apostle adds the likeness there is between a husband and Christ, as this note of comparison215 (as) shows. From this it follows that

It is as fitting for a wife to submit herself to her husband as216 for the church to submit itself to Christ. This amplification is added especially for Christians. Heathens may be moved to subject themselves to their governors by the likeness taken from a natural body. How much more ought Christians to be moved by the likeness taken from the mystical body of Christ?

These words, “and He is the Savior of the body,” as they declare the office of Christ and the benefit that the church reaps, so they note the end for which a husband is appointed to be the head of his wife: namely, that by his provident care he may be as a savior to her. It is noted here rather to show the benefit that a wife reaps from her husband than the duty that he owes, for the apostle declares that afterwards (v. 25, etc.). The meaning, then, is this: as Christ was given to be a head of the church, which is his body, so that he might protect it and provide all needful things for it, and so be a Savior to it, even so,217 for that very end, husbands are appointed to be the head of their wives.

On this ground the apostle infers the conclusion in the next verse.

§. 16. Of the resemblance between the church’s relation to Christ and a wife’s to her husband.

Eph 5:24.

Therefore, as the church is subject to Christ, so let wives be subject to their own husbands in everything.

This conclusion sets forth not only the duty itself, but also another reason and another rule to stir up and direct wives to perform their duty, and that under the pattern of the church.

The reason may be framed thus: What the church does to Christ, a wife must do to her husband. But the church is subject to Christ. Therefore a wife must be subject to her husband.

The proposition is grounded on the likeness there is between the church in relation to Christ and a wife in relation to her husband. For a husband is to his wife what Christ is to the church; therefore a wife must be to her husband as the church is to Christ.

The rule notes both the manner218 (as) and also the extent of a wife’s subjection219 (in everything).220

Question. Is mortal and sinful man to be obeyed as the Lord Christ, the eternal Son of God?

Answer. This extent is to be limited to the whole range of the things in question. So it is in other places. Where the apostle says, “All things are lawful for me,”221 he means all things neither commanded nor forbidden, for his speech in that place was of them. And where again he says, “Eat anything set before you+,”222 he means any good and wholesome food, for that was what he spoke of.

Thus much of the main drift of the apostle in setting before wives the example of Christ, whom husbands resemble in dignity, and the example of the church, which wives ought to resemble in duty.

I will further consider these examples of Christ and the church more distinctly by themselves, without any relation to man and wife, and from them note such general instructions as concern all Christians.

§. 17. Of the relation between Christ and the church.

Eph 5:23, 24.

23. Christ is the head of the church; and He is the Savior of the body. 24. The church is subject to Christ in everything.

See here the mutual relation between Christ and the church.

In this, note concerning Christ:

  1. His preeminence over the church, (he is her head.)
  2. His goodness to her, (he is her Savior.)

Note also concerning the church:

  1. Her prerogative, (she is the body of Christ.)

  2. Her duty. In setting this down, there is noted

    1. What it consists in (the church is subject to Christ)
    2. How far it extends, (in everything.)

The title Head is given to Christ in two respects.

  1. In regard to his223 dignity and dominion over the church.
  2. In regard to the224 close union between him and the church.

This union is more fully expressed afterwards, in v. 30.

The dignity of Christ is chiefly intended here, so that Christ is the highest in authority over the church. The titles225 Lord,226 father, master, teacher,227 Prophet,228 Firstborn,229 and the like, being attributed to him by a kind of excellence, as properly his own, prove as much.

The causes of this are

  1. The good pleasure of God his Father.
  2. The dignity of his person, being God-man.
  3. The merit of his sacrifice, by which he has redeemed and purchased his church for himself.
  4. The omnipotence of his power, by which he is able to protect it.
  5. The all-sufficiency of his Spirit, by which he is able to give every member all needful grace.

Until the Pope of Rome can show as good a reason for this230 title (Supreme head of the whole church), we will account him a blasphemous usurper of it.

Objection. He is not accounted an imperial head as Christ is,231 but only a ministerial head.

Answer.

  1. This distinction is without any ground or warrant of Scripture.
  2. It implies a plain contradiction. For to be a ministerial head is to be a head and a minister, which is all one with being a head and a member in relation to the same thing.
  3. Though by these two words (imperial, ministerial) they may seem to advance Christ above the Pope, yet in their own interpretation of these words they make the Pope equal232 to Christ, if they do not advance him above Christ. For they say that Christ is an imperial head, to give life to the church inwardly, and the Pope a ministerial head, to govern it outwardly. First, let it be noted how little this exposition agrees with the words expounded. Does this word (imperial) suggest a life-giving power? Does this word (ministerial) imply a governing power? No; is there not great incongruity in this, that Christ should be the imperial head, and yet the Pope a head to govern? Besides, does this not tear apart two of Christ’s offices, leaving one to Christ and giving another to the Pope, and so make him equal with Christ? If the particular branches of this government that papists give to the Pope by virtue of his headship are observed, we shall find verified in him what the apostle foretold concerning Antichrist, that “he will seat himself in the temple of233 God, proclaiming himself to be God.” For they give him the keys of heaven and hell, to shut or open the one or the other as234 he pleases. They give him power to dispense with God’s laws, to coin articles of faith, to make laws to bind men’s consciences directly and immediately, to give pardon for sin, to free subjects from allegiance to their sovereigns, to canonize saints, and who knows what else. But to let these impious blasphemies pass: besides the fact that this prerogative of Christ (to be head of235 the church) is incommunicable (for by it the apostle proves Christ to be advanced “far above all rule and authority, power and dominion, and every name,” etc.), Christ needs no vicar or deputy for the execution of his office in it. For as head he “fills all in all,” and by his eternal spirit he is in heaven, on earth, and in every place where any of his members are, according to his236 promises made to his church.

This must surely give much comfort and great confidence237 to all who have assurance that they are of this body. For having so mighty, so wise, so merciful a head, a head so sufficient every way, who can instruct, direct, guide, govern, protect and help them in all their needs whatever, what need they fear? When we are assaulted by Satan, or set upon in any way by any of his instruments, or are in any distress or need, let us lift up the eyes of our faith higher than we can lift the eyes of our body, and in heaven behold this our head, who is invisible; and we cannot but receive much comfort and encouragement from there.

§. 18. Of the benefit of Christ’s headship.

The goodness of Christ is set down in these words: “and He is the Savior of the body.” Almost every word has its emphasis.

1. The joining particle (AND) shows that

The good that Christ does for his church, he does because238 he is its head.

O how happy a thing it is for the church that it has such a head! A head that does not tyrannize over it, nor trample it under foot; a head that does not fleece or strip the church, but procures peace and safety for it. When Naomi sought to make a match between Boaz and Ruth,239 that he might be her head, what did she say? “Should I not seek rest for you, that it may be well with you?” It is therefore the office of a head to be a savior, to procure rest and prosperity for the body whose head it is.

Happy it would be for kingdoms, commonwealths, cities, churches, families, wives, and all that have heads, if they had such heads: heads that, because they are heads, would endeavor to be saviors.

§. 19. Of Christ as a sufficient Savior.

In setting out the goodness of Christ, three things are noted.

  1. The kind of goodness, which is salvation (the Savior)
  2. The person who performs it (he himself.)
  3. The parties for whom he performs it (the body.)

1. The Greek word translated240 Savior is so emphatic that other tongues can hardly find a fit word to express its emphasis. Being attributed to Christ, it implies that

Christ is a most absolute and perfect Savior; he is every way a sufficient Savior,241 “able to save completely,” even to the very uttermost. He saves soul and body. He saves from all manner of misery, which is suggested by that particular thing from242 which he saves, namely sin: “He will save His people from their sins.” Sin is the greatest and most grievous evil; indeed, it is the cause of all misery. Those who are saved from it are saved from all evil, for there is nothing hurtful to man but what is caused by sin or poisoned by it.

Before sin seized on man, he was most happy, free from all misery; and so he will be after the contagion, guilt, punishment, dominion and remainder of sin are removed. But he who remains in the bondage of sin is in a most woeful plight. In that Christ saves from sin, he saves from the wrath of God, the curse of the law, the venom of all outward crosses, the tyranny of Satan, the sting of death, the power of the grave, the torments of hell, and much else besides.

The purity of Christ’s nature and the excellence of his person243 are what make him so sufficient a Savior. The apostle himself notes this reason: for where he says that Christ is “able to save completely,” he adds, as proof of it, that he244 is “holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens.”

This supplies245 us with great matter for rejoicing and for confidence. When the angel first brought this news, “A Savior has been born to you+,” he said, “Behold, I bring you+ good news of great joy.” This made the Virgin Mary say, “My spirit rejoices in God my Savior,” and for this Zechariah blessed God, who “has … redeemed His people” and “raised up a horn of salvation.”246 When the eyes of old Simeon had seen this salvation, he desired to live no longer, but said, “Sovereign Lord, … You now dismiss Your servant247 in peace.”

Those who believe in this Savior will be of like mind. As they rejoice in him, so they will trust in him, and say with the apostle, “we are more than conquerors through Him248 who loved us,” etc.

This being so, what end does the supposed treasury of249 the church serve, in which are said to be stored up indulgences, pardons, merits, works of supererogation, and I know not what trash, to add to the satisfaction of this Savior? Either Christ is not a sufficient Savior, or these things are (to say the least) vain. But vain they are; and that is an empty, filthy, detestable treasury, which God will destroy with all who trust in it.

§. 20. Of Christ as the only Savior.

This relative particle250 (HE) also has its emphasis. For as it points out Christ the head of the church, so it restricts this great work to him. It may be translated thus: he himself; that is, he in his own person, he by himself, he and none but he. So, to speak properly,

Christ is the only Savior of men. In this respect he is251 called “a horn of salvation,”252 indeed, “salvation”253 itself. These titles are given to him by way of excellence, as properly his own; and in the same respect the name Jesus254 was given to him.

Here, by the way, note the blasphemous arrogance of those great sectarians among the papists who style themselves Jesuits, taking that name which belongs only to this great office of Jesus Christ.

Objection. Why is this name more blasphemous than the title Christians?

Answer. One of their own religion resolves that objection thus: “We are called Christians from Christ, but not Jesuits from Jesus, because we share in the thing signified by the name Christ, that is, anointing; for (as the apostle says) ‘we have all received from His fullness.’ But he has not shared with us the thing signified by the name Jesus, for it belongs to him alone to save; as the Scripture says, ‘He will save His people,’ as if he should say, he alone, and no other.” A Christo dicimur255 Christiani, non autem à Iesu Iesuani, seu Iesuitae: quia rem signatam nomine Christus, scil. vnctionem nobis communicauit. Nam, ut ait Apostolus, omnes nos de plenitudine eius accepimus: sed rem significatam nomine Jesus256 non communicauit: nam saluare ipsi soli conuenit: ipse enim (vt dicitur in scriptura) saluum faciet257 populum suum: ac si diceret, ipse solus, & non alius. Guil. Lindwood in Prouinc. siue Constitut. Angl. lib. de Consuetud.

But to return to our matter: Saint Peter most plainly and fully proves the doctrine named above in these words spoken of Jesus Christ: “Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.”258 None is able,259 none is worthy, to do so great260 a work. He must do it, or it cannot be done. But261 he is so262 able, and so worthy, that he can do it by himself, and needs none to assist him.

What folly it is to trust in other saviors! Papists have legions of263 saviors to whom they flee in their need. All the angels in heaven, and all whom their popes have at any time canonized as saints (and they are many millions), are made saviors by them. “Be stunned by this, O heavens,” for they “have committed two evils: They have forsaken” Christ, “the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns—broken cisterns that cannot hold water.”264

Let us for our part flee to this Savior only, and wholly265 rely on him, as we desire to be saved. In this way we shall honor him by preferring him before all, indeed, by rejecting all but him; and in this way we shall be sure to bring help, ease and comfort to our own souls.

§. 21. Of the church as the body of Christ.

The persons who receive any benefit from this Savior are all comprised under this metaphor, the body, by which the same thing is meant as was meant before by the church.

Church, according to the derivation of the Greek word, signifies266 an assembly called together. In Scripture it is given, as properly theirs, to those who are called to God.

This calling is twofold:

1. Outward, which is common to all who make profession267 of the gospel. In this respect it is said, “many are called, but few are chosen.”

2. Inward, which belongs only to the elect. None but they, and all of them in their time, shall both be called outwardly by the word to a profession of Christ, and also inwardly and effectually by the spirit to believe in Christ and obey his gospel. This is styled “the heavenly calling,”268 which269 belongs only to the saints. These make up that church of which Christ is properly the head; and therefore, in relation to that metaphor of a head, they are called the body, and that in these respects:

  1. They are under Christ, as a body under the head.
  2. They receive spiritual life and grace from Christ, as a natural body receives sense and vigor from the head.
  3. Christ governs them, as a head governs the body.
  4. They are subject to Christ, as a body to the head.

§. 22. Of the extent of Christ’s goodness to all his body.

This metaphor, by which the persons who reap the benefit of Christ’s office are set forth, notes two points.

1. All who are once incorporated into Christ will be saved. The body comprises all the parts and members under it: not only arms, shoulders, breast, back and the like, but also hands, fingers, feet, toes and all. Since Christ their head is their Savior, who can doubt of their salvation?

2. None but those who are incorporated into Christ will be saved. For this privilege is reserved for the body.

The former point is clearly set forth by a comparison that the apostle makes between Adam and Christ, thus: “just as the trespass of one brought condemnation for all men,270 so also the righteousness of one brought justification and life for all men.” Here two roots are noted: one is Adam, the other is Christ. Both of them have their number of branches, to all of which they convey what is in them, as the root conveys the sap that is in it into all the branches that sprout from it. The first root, Adam, conveys sin and death to all who come from him; and the other root, Christ, conveys grace and life to every one who is given to him. For he says, “Everyone the Father271 gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away.” And a little after, he gives this reason: “this is the will of Him who sent Me, that I shall lose none of those He has given Me,272 but raise them up at the last day.”

Objection. Christ himself makes an exception of one, where he says, “Not one of them has been lost, except the son of perdition.”273

Answer. That phrase, son of perdition, shows that Judas was never of this body. For can we imagine that Christ is a Savior of a son of perdition?

Objection. Why then is he excepted?

Answer. By reason of his office and calling he seemed to be of this body, and until he was made known, no one could judge otherwise of him. In this respect Saint Peter says, “He was274 one of our number.”

2. Answer. Christ speaks there in particular of the twelve apostles, and to be an apostle of Christ was in itself only an outward calling.

This is a point of wonderful comfort to those who have assurance275 of their incorporation into Christ: they may rest on the benefit of this office of Christ, that he is a Savior. We need not think of climbing up to heaven and searching God’s records to see if our names are written in the book of life. Let us only test whether we are of this body or not.276 For our help in this, let us know that this metaphor of a body implies two things.

  1. A mystical union with Christ.

  2. A spiritual communion with the saints.

    1. By virtue of that union, those who are of Christ’s body

      1. Receive grace and life from him.277
      2. Are guided and governed according to his will.278
      3. Seek to honor him in all things they do.279
      4. Are offended and grieved when he is dishonored by others.280

    2. By reason of their communion with the saints, being fellow members,

      1. They love the brethren.281
      2. They are ready to help those who are in distress.282
      3. They will edify one another.283
      4. They keep a mutual sympathy, rejoicing and mourning with one another.284

§. 23. Of limiting the benefit of Christ’s headship to those only who are of his body.

That none but those who are of Christ’s body will share in the benefit of his office is clear from other like titles of restriction, such as his people285 and his sheep,286 but especially from his denying to the world the benefit of his intercession: “I do not ask on behalf of the world,”287 he says. In this respect this position, (out of the church, no salvation), is true without exception. For the body is the true, invisible universal church. He who is not a member of this church, but is out of it, does not have Christ to be his head288 and Savior; from where, then, can he have salvation?

The former point is not more comforting to those who have assurance that they are members of this body than this one is terrible to those who give too much evidence that they are no members of it. All those do so who do not have the spirit of Christ ruling in them, but rather rebel against him, and who bear no love to the saints, but rather hate them and do them all the spite they can.

§. 24. Of the church’s subjection to Christ.

Eph 5:24.

The church is subject to Christ in everything.

The duty that the church performs to Christ her head, by way of thankfulness for this great benefit, that he is her Savior, is subjection. Under this word is comprised all the obedience and duty of any kind that Christ requires of the church, in and by the word.

Question. Is it possible for that part of the church which is here on earth to yield such obedience?

Answer. It will faithfully endeavor to do what it can; and that sincere and utmost endeavor Christ graciously accepts as a perfect performance of all.

In that it is taken for granted here that “the church is subject to Christ,” I may infer, as from a general to a particular, that

Whoever is of the true universal church is subject to Christ, and yields obedience to his word. “We will run after you,”289290 says the church to Christ. “My sheep listen to My voice … and they follow Me,”291 says Christ of that flock, which is his church.

For Christ conveys his own spirit into his mystical body the church, and into every member of it; and this spirit is292 much more operative and full of life than the soul of man. If, therefore, man’s soul, giving life to every part of the natural body, makes them subject to the head, much more will the spirit of Christ bring the members of his mystical body into subjection to himself. “If the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead is living in you+, He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead293 will also give life to your+ mortal bodies through His Spirit, who lives in you+.”

By this let trial be made of particular visible churches and of particular persons, whether they are indeed of this true universal294 church or not. Those visible churches that refuse to be governed by Christ’s word and are wholly governed by human traditions, that rise against Christ and play the adulteress by committing idolatry, are not of this universal church which is subject to Christ. No more are infidels who defy Christ, heretics who deny him, ignorant persons who do not know his will, profane persons who despise him, worldlings who think lightly of him, or any who persecute or scorn him in his members. By this we may see that many have a name for being of the church who indeed are not.

Objection. Many such persons may belong to God’s election, and so be of that body of which Christ is a Savior.

Answer. Election indeed gives them a title to Christ, but they cannot reap any benefit by that title until they have possession of Christ by virtue of their spiritual union with him. Nor can they have any assurance of their election until they find, by the life-giving power of the spirit, that they are united to Christ. Therefore, so long as men remain destitute of the Spirit of Christ and are possessed by a contrary spirit, they may well be judged, for the present, to be none of this body and to have no part in Christ; their future state is left to him who alone knows what it will be.

§. 25. Of the extent of the church’s subjection.

The extent of the church’s subjection to Christ is without any restriction at all: in everything. For there is nothing that Christ requires of her but she may yield to it with a good conscience, and must yield to it in obedience. Just and pure and perfect are all his commandments; there is no error in any of them; no injury or harm can follow from keeping them. This extent being taken for granted here, I may further infer that

Those who are of the true universal church will yield complete295 obedience to Christ: they will obey him in each and every one of his commandments. David “had not turned aside from anything296 the Lord commanded.” Josiah “turned to the Lord with all his297 heart … according to all the Law.” And Zechariah and Elizabeth walked “in all the commandments” of God. All these were of this church, and all others who are of this church are of their mind.

For the spirit of Christ which is in them works a thorough298 reformation. Even as the flesh leads a natural man on to every sin, so the spirit of Christ stirs him up to every good duty. In this respect it is said that “anyone born of God299 does not commit sin.”

Objection. The best saints in all ages have transgressed in many300 things.

Answer. Their sins, though grievous, have not been committed willfully, in open rebellion against Christ; rather, they have fallen into them partly through their own weakness, and partly through the violence of some temptation. So what the apostle says of himself may be applied to all who are of the body of Christ: “What I do, I do not approve. … In that case,301 it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it.”

This extent is a good proof of the truth of subjection, for302 in this lies a main difference between the upright and the hypocrite, indeed between restraining and renewing grace. The restraining grace that is in many hypocrites stirs them to do many things that Christ commands, at least if those things do not cross their honor, profit, ease and the like. Herod, that notorious hypocrite,303 “did many things.” There is none who bears the name of the church but will be subject in some things. But none but the upright, who are indeed renewed by the sanctifying spirit of Christ, will make Christ’s will their rule in all things and hold close to it in everything, preferring it before their pleasure, profit, preferment, or any other outward allurement. Those who do so give good evidence that they are of the body of Christ, and may rest assured that Christ is their Savior.

Husbands and the Love of Christ

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 26–33

§. 26. Of the sum of husbands’ duties.

Eph 5:25.

25. Husbands, love your+ wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.

From the duties of wives the apostle goes on to press the duties of husbands. And as he set before wives the example of the church as a pattern, so he sets before husbands the example of Christ; and304 he adds to it the pattern of a man’s own self, in regard of that natural affection which he bears to his body. So he adds pattern to pattern,305 and he presses husbands’ duties the more fully and earnestly, because husbands have a more honorable place, and so their failing in duty is the more heinous, scandalous, and dangerous.

The apostle limits the duties of husbands to their306 own wives, as he did the duties of wives to their307 own husbands. For though the same word is not used here as was used before, yet a word of like emphasis is used; and there is as good reason that our English translators should have put this particle (own) into this verse as into the 22nd verse. For proof of this, read 1 Corinthians 7:2, where308 these two words are used, and both of them are translated own.

I have noted this all the more because many who hold that a wife must have only one husband imagine that a husband may have more wives than one; and this particle (own) wipes that notion away. All the duties of a husband are comprised under this one word309 love. So that a husband might be the better directed in this love, and the more stirred up to it, the example of Christ named before, and of his love to the church, is set forth very vividly: first in general in these words, “just as Christ loved the church,” and then more particularly in the words that follow.

§. 27. Of the example of Christ’s love.

The note of comparison310 (just as) requires no equality, as if it were possible for a husband to love his wife in the same measure as Christ loved his church (for as Christ exceeds man in excellence and greatness, so he does in love and tenderness). But it notes an equity, and a like quality.

An equity, because there is as great reason that husbands, by virtue of their place, should love their wives, as that Christ, by virtue of his place, should love the church.

A like quality, because the love which Christ bears to the church is in every way without exception, and it is a love which turns to the good and benefit of the church. From this, note two points.

1. Husbands must come as near as they can to Christ in loving their wives. In this respect, because they can never love as much as Christ did, they must never think they have loved enough.

2. Though their love cannot equal Christ’s love in measure, yet in its manner it must be like Christ’s: a love that goes before, a true, free, pure, exceeding, constant love.

The measure and manner of Christ’s love are set out distinctly in Treatise 4, §. 61, etc., and the love which a husband owes his wife is there compared with it and applied to it. The same application may also be made of that mutual Christian love which we owe one another.

The love of Christ to the church is amplified:

  1. By an effect of it, in these words: “gave Himself up for her.”
  2. By the end of that effect, set down at length in v. 26, 27.

The effect is noted partly to confirm the truth, partly to declare the measure of Christ’s love.

The act (he gave) shows that his love was in deed and in truth, not only in show and pretense.

The object (himself) shows that he loved his church more than his own life. A greater evidence of love could not be given, for “greater love has no one than this, that he311 lay down his life for his friends.”

The end of Christ’s love (set forth in v. 26, 27) is noted to show that he loved his church so for her good and happiness, rather than for any advantage to himself.

As this example of Christ’s love to his church is set before husbands, so it may and ought also to be applied to all Christians, and that in a double respect.

1. As a motive to stir them up to love both Christ himself and also their brethren.

2. As a pattern to teach them how to love.

It is a motive to love Christ, because love deserves love, especially such a love, from such a person, as the love of Christ is. Indeed, our love of Christ is an evidence that we are loved by Christ, as smoke is a sign of fire. Therefore, both in thankfulness to Christ for his love to us, and for the assurance of our own souls of Christ’s love to us, we ought in all things that we can to testify our love to Christ.

It is also a motive to love our brethren, because, Christ being in heaven, “our goodness does not extend to him”;312 but our brethren on earth stand in his place, and the love we show to them we show to him, and he accepts it as done to him. “You+ fed Me, you+ visited Me,”313 says Christ to those who fed and visited his brethren. This love too, the314 love of our brethren, is an evidence that we are loved by God. Therefore, “if Christ so loved us, we also ought to love one another.”315

How the love of Christ is a pattern I will316 show later.

§. 28. Of Christ’s giving himself.

Eph 5:25.

And gave Himself up for her.

This fruit and effect of Christ’s love extends to all317 the things that Christ did or suffered for our redemption: that he came down from heaven, took our nature on himself, and became a man; that he subjected himself to the law, and perfectly fulfilled it; that he made himself subject to many temptations of the devil and his instruments; that he took our infirmities on himself; that he became a King to govern us, a Prophet to instruct us, a Priest to make atonement for us; that he subjected himself to death, the cursed death of the cross, and so made himself an oblation and sacrifice for our sins; that he was buried; that he rose again; that he ascended into heaven, and sits there at God’s right hand to make intercession for us. For after Christ had taken it on himself to be our head and Savior, he set himself apart wholly for our use and our benefit. So his person, his offices, his actions, his sufferings, his humiliation, his exaltation, the dignity, the purity, the efficacy of all of them, belong to the church, and they all tend to her good. This in general is the extent of this fruit of Christ’s love: he “gave Himself up for her.”

More particularly, we may note these three points:

  1. The action, what he did (he gave.)
  2. The object, what he gave (himself.)
  3. The end, why he gave himself (for her), for the church’s good.

The action, having relation to the object, points most especially to the death of Christ. The318 Greek word is a compound word, and signifies to give up. It implies two things:

1. That Christ died willingly: the simple word (gave) indicates that much.

2. That his death was an oblation, that is, a price of redemption, or a satisfaction: the compound word (gave up) indicates that much.

§. 29. Of the willingness of Christ to die.

That Christ died willingly is evident from the circumstances noted about his death. When Peter counseled him to spare himself, and not to go to Jerusalem (where he was to be put to death),319 he called him Satan, and said that he was “a stumbling block” to him. When Judas went out to betray him,320 he said to him, “What you are about to do, do quickly.”321 When Judas had gone out to get a company to arrest him, he went to the place where he usually went, so that Judas might readily find him. Indeed, he went halfway to meet those who came to take him, and he asked them whom they were seeking, though he knew whom they sought. And when they said, “Jesus of Nazareth,” he answered, “I am He.” When they came to him, he drove them all backward with a word of his mouth, and yet he would not escape from them.322 He could have prayed to the Father to have more than twelve legions of angels to guard him against those who arrested him, but he would not.323 When his adversaries provoked him to come down from the cross, though he could have done so, he would not.324 At the very instant of giving up his spirit he cried with a loud voice, which shows that his life was not then spent: he might have kept it longer if he had wished. And from this the centurion gathered that he was the Son of God.325 When he was actually dead, and laid in a grave, he rose again. These and other such circumstances verify what Christ said of his own life: “No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord.”326 It was therefore no necessity that compelled him to die, but his voluntary obedience.

Christ is327 the Lord, Prince and Author of life, and he has absolute power over his own life, as over the life of others.

So then we see that his sacrifice was a voluntary and free gift: its cause was his own will and good pleasure.

This greatly commends the love of Christ, and assures us that his sacrifice is all the more acceptable to God, who “loves a cheerful giver.”328

Let us, in imitation of our head, do the things to which329 we are called willingly and cheerfully, however330 disgraceful they may seem to the world, or grievous to our weak flesh.

§. 30. Of the kind of Christ’s death, an oblation.

That Christ’s death was an oblation, and a price of redemption, is evident from the death of the beasts which were offered up as sacrifices, and in that were a type of Christ’s death. But this apostle notes it expressly where he says that Christ “gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,”331 and again, that Christ “gave Himself as a ransom.”332 The phrases redeeming,333 purchasing,334 buying,335 and the like, attributed to Christ and his blood, confirm the same further.

Learn by this to consider Christ’s death, not as the death of336 a private man, but of a public person, of a surety, of a pledge, who in our place and stead was made “to be sin”337 and became “a curse”338 to redeem us from our sins, and from the curse which had fallen on us through sin. The comfort and benefit of Christ’s death is lost if this is not known and believed. In this lies a main difference between the death of Christ and that of all other men, not excepting the most righteous martyrs. Their death was only a duty and a debt: no oblation making satisfaction, no price, no ransom, as Christ’s was.

§. 31. Of the infinite value of the price of our redemption.

The object, the thing which Christ gave as a ransom, was himself: not his body alone, nor his body and soul only, but his person, consisting of his two natures, human and divine.

Question. How could his divine nature be given up? Could it339 suffer? Could it die?

Answer. 1. The Deity, considered simply in and by itself, could not die; but that person who was God both could die and did die. For the Son of God took a human nature into the unity of his divine nature, and united them together340 without confusion, alteration, division, separation, in one person. So what is done by one nature is done by the person, and in that respect the Scripture often attributes it to the other nature: as where it is said that they “crucified the Lord of glory,”341 and that God “purchased” the church “with His own blood.”342

2. Though the divine nature of Christ did not suffer, yet it upheld the human nature, and added dignity, worth and efficacy to the sufferings of that nature.

3. Christ’s divine nature had its own proper and distinctive works in the work of redemption, such as to sanctify his human nature, to take away our sins, to reconcile us to God, and the like.

So then, in three respects the whole person of Christ was given to us.

1. In regard of the inseparable union of both natures.

2. In regard of the assistance of the Deity in the things which the human nature of Christ did.

3. In regard of some proper actions belonging to the Deity.343

Since the person of Christ, God-man, was given up,344 I gather that

The price of our redemption is of infinite value. Neither Christ345 nor God himself could give a greater. Heaven and earth and all things in them are not of like worth. Well, therefore, might Saint Peter call it “precious blood,” and prefer it before silver, gold, and all other things of price.

1. What place can be left for despair in those who know and believe the worth of this ransom?

2. What can be held too dear for him who, notwithstanding the infinite excellence of his person, gave himself for us? Can goods, can friends, can children, can liberty, can life, can anything else?

3. What just cause do we have to give ourselves up as “living sacrifices,346 holy and pleasing” to him who gave himself for us?

4. How ungrateful, how unworthy of Christ are those who for his sake will not forsake their unstable honors, fading wealth, vain pleasures, gaudy clothes, and such trash!

§. 32. Of Christ’s seeking the good of the church.

The end for which Christ gave himself was for the church, so347 that Christ in his death aimed at our good.348 He was made “sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God”;349 he became “a curse for us,” and “redeemed us from the curse of the law”;350 he gave himself “for our sins to rescue us”;351 he laid down his life “for the sheep.”

This proves Christ’s giving of himself to be a fruit of his love, for “love does not seek its own.”352

Let us learn by this to apply to ourselves all that Christ did. If he gave himself for us, then he, and353 all that belongs to him, is ours.

Let us also learn by this how to show love: namely, by seeking and procuring the good of others. “No one should seek his354 own good, but the good of others.” If this were practiced, would there be such oppressing, such undermining, such deceiving, such wronging of one another as there is? The apostle’s complaint is proved all too true in our days: “All seek355 their own.” But let that mind be in us which was in Christ Jesus, and let us show our love in this way, as we desire to share in this fruit of Christ’s love.

From this it follows by just consequence that Christ did not merit356 for himself. Was there any need for Christ to come down from heaven to earth to purchase anything for himself? When he was going out of the world, he prayed thus: “And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had357 with You before the world existed.” Did Christ, by anything which he did on earth, merit that glory which he had before the world existed? All the exaltation to which he was advanced, even in his human nature, was due to the dignity of his person.

1. Objection. He endured the cross “for the joy set358 before Him.”

Answer. He used that joy, which was due to him by right, as a help to support him in the weakness of his human nature, not as a recompense which he was to earn.

2. Objection. “He … became obedient to death, even death on a cross.359 THEREFORE God exalted Him to the highest place.”

Answer. That particle (therefore) does not declare the cause, but the order of his exaltation, noting a consequence that followed after his death: after he had humbled himself so low, he was most highly advanced.

3. Objection. Christ, being man, was bound to the law, and therefore he ought to fulfill it for himself.

Answer. If he had been merely a man, that would be true. But he united his human nature to his divine, and made one person of both, and that person was God as well as man; so he was bound to nothing further than what it pleased him to subject himself to voluntarily for our sakes.

2. If Christ had been bound to the law, he must have fulfilled it as a duty; and if he was to fulfill it as a duty, how could he merit by it so high a degree of honor as he is advanced to?

This notion of Christ’s meriting for himself greatly lessens the glory of Christ’s grace and goodness in giving himself.

§. 33. Of the particular ends for which Christ gave himself, and of the condition of the church before Christ took her.

Eph 5:26.

That He might sanctify her and cleanse her with the washing of water by the word.

The general end of Christ’s giving himself, intimated before in this phrase (for us), is set out particularly in this verse and the next, and that in two branches.

One concerns the state of the church in this world, v. 26.

The other concerns her state in the world to come, v. 27.

The latter of these two is the chief.

The former is subordinate to the latter, an end for accomplishing the other end: for the church is made pure here so that hereafter it may be made glorious.

In laying down the former, he notes

  1. The end at which Christ aimed.
  2. The means by which he effected what he aimed at.

That end is set forth in these words, “that He might sanctify her,360 having cleansed her” (so they may be translated word for word), so that what stands in the latter place in the order of the words stands in the first place in the order of the matter.

The word (cleansing) points to our justification.

The word (sanctifying) expresses our sanctification.

The means of effecting these are two.

  1. Baptism, comprised under this phrase, washing of water.
  2. The word.

The two branches of the former end, namely cleansing and sanctifying, imply two things in general.

  1. The condition of the church in itself.
  2. The alteration of it by Christ.

The condition is presupposed, which is that she was impure, polluted, in the common state of corrupt man. Things pure in themselves are not cleansed, but things foul and impure; persons who are of themselves freed and exempted from a common misery do not need another’s help to free and exempt them. Seeing, then, that the church stood in need of being cleansed and sanctified, surely

The church in herself was, like the world, polluted. This is set forth very vividly361 by the prophet Ezekiel under the picture of a362 wretched infant born of a cursed parentage, whose navel cord was not cut, who was not washed, salted, or swaddled, but cast out into the open field, polluted with blood.363 The apostle, when he sets forth the wretched state of the world, often notes of the true members364 of the church that “we too” were such.365366

The church consists of none other than those who came out of Adam’s loins. Now as all the brood that comes from vipers, adders, toads, spiders, and other such venomous mothers is infected with poison, so all the sons of Adam are polluted with sin. “That which is born of the flesh” (as every mother’s child is, not excepting the members of the church, for they have fathers and mothers of their flesh) “is flesh,” that is, polluted and corrupt. Therefore, when we are taken into the church, we are “born again.”367

This, our former state by nature, is to be thought of often and seriously,368 and that in respect of

  • Christ.
  • Ourselves.
  • Others.

1. In regard of Christ, to magnify his love all the more. Our former state, before he cast the wings of his mercy over us, shows our unworthiness, our vileness, and our wretchedness; and in that respect it opens our heart and mouth to think and say, “O Lord, our Lord, … what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?”369 “Lord, why are You going to reveal Yourself to us and not to the world?”370 The right knowledge of our former state, and a due consideration of it, makes us ascribe all the glory of our present dignity and happiness to Christ, who changed our state, as Saint Paul does: “I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me … I was formerly a blasphemer,” etc.371 Indeed, it makes us prize and value our present state all the more, as David did.372

2. In regard of ourselves this is to be thought of, to humble us, and to keep us from insolent boasting in those privileges which we share through Christ. To this purpose the apostle presses this point thus: “For who makes373 you different from anyone else? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” When a man is raised from a lowly place to a great one, and grows proud and insolent because of it, we say, he has forgotten where he came from. So the remembrance of our former condition is a means to preserve humility and to suppress insolence.

3. In regard of others it is to be thought of, to move us to pity all the more the woeful state of those who still remain as we once were; to hope that their state may be changed as well as ours was; and to pray, and to use what means we can, that it may be changed. To stir Christians up to show all meekness to those who were outside, the apostle gives this reason: “For at one time we too were foolish,”374 etc. Read how forcibly this is urged in Rom 11:18, 19, etc.

Love That Purifies the Unclean

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 34–47

§. 34. Of Christ’s grace that goes before.

In setting down how the condition of the church named before is changed, note:

  1. The manner of setting it forth.
  2. The matter, or substance, of it.

The manner is implied in this conjunction375 THAT (“that He might sanctify her”). Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, not because she was sanctified, but “that He might sanctify her.” This shows that

The grace which Christ shows to the church is a grace that goes before.376 Sanctification is no cause but an effect of Christ’s377 love, and it follows in order after his love. His love arose only and wholly from himself. In the parties loved there was nothing but matter for hatred before they were loved. Moses says this of the love of God to Israel: “The Lord did not set His love on you+ … because you+ were more numerous …, but because the Lord loved you+.” At first sight this may seem to be (as378 we say)379 a woman’s reason: that the Lord should set his love on them because he loved them. But when it is duly considered, we shall find the ground of God’s love excellently set forth here: it rests altogether in himself, and in his own good pleasure.380 Indeed, since this is noted as the end of Christ’s love, “that He might sanctify her,” it further shows that it was not any foresight of holiness in the church that moved him to love it. First he loved it, and then he sought how to make it lovely and worthy to be loved.

In this Christ’s love differs from the love of all men toward381 their spouses. For they must see something in them to move them to love. When Ahasuerus was to choose a wife, the maidens from whom he was to take one were first purified, and then he took the one in whom he most delighted. But Christ first loves his spouse, and then sanctifies her. Before he loved her, he saw nothing in her for which he should prefer her before the world.

Seeing that all the beauty382 and dignity of the church is “from Him and through Him and to Him,” “to Him be the glory forever!383 Amen.”

§. 35. Of Christ’s seeking to make his church pure.

The matter, or substance, of that subordinate end which Christ aimed at in giving himself up for the church is in these words (“that He might sanctify her, having cleansed her”). In general they show that

Christ seeks the purity of his church. For this end he has384 shed his own most pure and precious blood (for his blood “cleanses us from all sin”)385 and conveyed his Holy Spirit into his body, the church. The Spirit is called the Spirit of sanctification,386 because he renews and sanctifies those in whom he is.

Christ aims at this: that he might make his spouse like387 himself, pure as he is pure.

We who profess ourselves388 to be of this church must strive after that end which Christ aimed at. For “everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure.” Let us therefore use all good means to cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit.

Since this is the end which Christ aims at for the good389 of his church, to cleanse it, those who find themselves cleansed have good evidence that they are of this church. Those who are not cleansed can have no assurance of it.

How unworthy of this benefit are those who live as the390 world does, and like swine wallow in the mire at every occasion, being drawn into sin by every temptation! Do they not, as much as lies in them, make the death of Christ to be in vain, and pervert that main end which Christ aimed at in giving himself up?

But what may be thought of those who, like Ishmael, mock and scoff at those who labor to be cleansed?

§. 36. Of the church’s justification.

The two particular parts of the end named before, cleansing and sanctifying, set forth more distinctly the purity of the church even in this world. Cleansing has relation to the blood of Christ, and so points out our justification.

Sanctifying has relation to the Spirit of Christ, who works our sanctification.

From this cleansing of the church meant here, I gather that no sin lies upon the church. For the blood of Christ “cleanses391392 us from all sin.” This is to be taken of the guilt of sin, which is clean taken away by Christ’s death. So the sin which is in us is as if it were not in us, because it is not imputed to us.

See here the blessed condition of the church: “Blessed is393 he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed394 is the man whose iniquity the Lord does not impute to him.”

§. 37. Of the church’s sanctification.

From the sanctifying of the church mentioned here, I further gather that

The church is made holy and righteous. This is meant here of395 that inherent righteousness which the Spirit of Christ works in all the members of his body. In this respect they are called saints.396 So not only is the guilt of sin taken away, but the very “body of sin” is also so destroyed in them397 that it can no longer reign in them, nor can they obey it in its lusts. Instead of the dominion of sin, the Spirit of Christ reigns in them, and leads them into all righteousness.

See here the free condition of the church. Whereas the398 world lies under the slavery of sin and the tyranny of Satan, the church is “set free from sin” and has become a slave “to righteousness”;399 it is “dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.”

§. 38. Of the church’s purity before God and man.

From the joining together of these two benefits of Christ’s death, justification and sanctification, we see that the church is both spotless before God and blameless before men. The blood of Christ so cleanses her that in God’s sight she has no spot of sin. And the Spirit of Christ so sanctifies her that her righteousness shines before men. For “the grace of God”400 “instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age.” In this respect the church is said to be “all glorious within,” and her401 “gown” also to be “embroidered with gold.” And Zechariah and Elizabeth,402 members of this church, are said to be “righteous in the sight of God” and “blameless,” namely before men. There is no such purity in any as in the church. For true and perfect beauty403 is only in the body of Christ, which is the church, of which it is said, “You are altogether beautiful … there is no spot in you” (Song 4:7).

1. Question. Is it possible that neither God nor man should spy any fault in those who are of the true church, while they live here in this world?

Answer. Seeing that the flesh remains in the best while they remain404 in the world, it cannot be but that both God and man must spy many blemishes in the best. “Everything is405 uncovered and exposed before the eyes of Him.” If therefore any remnant of sin is in the saints (as there are exceedingly many in every one, so that “if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves,406 and the truth is not in us”), it is without question plain in his sight. Indeed, such is the imperfection and weakness of the best saints that the flesh, always lusting in them against the Spirit, often prevails, and so shows itself in some evil fruit or other, so that the eye of man spies it. Take as instances the examples of the best who ever lived in any age.

2. Question. How then are they spotless before God and407 blameless before men?

Answer. 1. God so fully discharges and acquits the church of all her sins that in his account she is as if she had no speck of sin at all. In this respect David uses the metaphor of covering sin,408 and explains his meaning by these two phrases, forgiving and not imputing sin.

2. It is the course of a man’s life, not this or that particular409 action, which makes a man blameworthy or blameless; just as it is the flock of swallows, and not one here or another there, which shows the spring. Now because the constant conduct of those who are of the church is blameless before men, they may justly be accounted so, even though some particular blameworthy things at times pass from them. See here how the true saints may boldly lift up their faces before God and man. The soundness of their faith gives them confidence before God. The testimony of their conscience gives them courage before men. Let all who desire this boldness join a sound faith and a good conscience together, and labor for assurance both of their cleansing by the blood of Christ and of their sanctifying by the Spirit of Christ.

§. 39. Of the order and dependence of justification and sanctification on one another.

The order and manner of knitting these two benefits together is worth noting.

The letter puts sanctification in the first place, but the sense presupposes justification. For this is how he says it: “that He might sanctify her,410 having cleansed her.” The cleansing spoken of here is an inward, invisible work, and the evidence of it is sanctification, which is an outward work, perceived by the senses. Therefore this is expressed first, and then that is inferred, as a thing that must necessarily be presupposed.

From this arise these doctrines. Our English, with this word having, fitly and properly renders the Greek active participles of the past (the preterperfect or finite) tenses. Because the Latin lacks these, Latin translators are forced to use the passive, or a roundabout phrase: as vt illam sanctificaret mundatam [that he might sanctify her, cleansed], Erasmus; Postquam eam purgasset [after he had cleansed her], Beza.

1. In order, justification goes before411 sanctification. I say “in order,” because at the very moment that Christ cleanses his church by his blood, he begins to sanctify her. But when he begins to sanctify her, he has already cleansed her: she is justified.

The grace of justification, then, is a most free grace. It is not wrought upon any righteousness of ours, for it comes before it.

2. Christ sanctifies those whom he has cleansed. The412 apostle proves this at length in the sixth chapter of Romans. Let none therefore boast of their cleansing by Christ’s blood until they find themselves renewed and sanctified by the Spirit of Christ. For note the apostle’s description of those who are justified by Christ, which for more clearness may be set down by question and answer. For whom is there no condemnation?413 For those who are in Christ Jesus. Who are they? Those “who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.”

3. Sanctification presupposes justification. Those who are sanctified414 may rest on this, that they are cleansed and justified.

For sanctification is a fruit of justification. In this respect James says that “we are justified by works,”415 that is, declared to be justified.

Wonderful is the comfort which the saints in this world416 reap from this. For their sanctification is imperfect, and the flesh abides in them and lusts against the Spirit. Indeed, sin is present with them when they would do good, so that they are often forced to complain and cry, “What wretched men we are!417 Who will rescue us from this body of death?” If they had no other ground on which to fasten the anchor of their hope but their sanctification, it could not hold them fast enough against the storms of Satan’s temptations. But because their sanctification is a fruit and evidence of their justification, they take heart, and thank God that with the mind they themselves serve the law of God, though with the flesh they serve the law of sin. And so, upheld and comforted, they go on striving against sin until it is clean rooted out of them, as well as forgiven.

§. 40. Of the sacramental washing of water.

One of the means which Christ uses for the cleansing and sanctifying of his church is expressed under this phrase: “with the washing of water.” Water is the outward element used in baptism; washing is the principal sacramental rite in it. Water sets forth Christ’s blood; washing points out its application and efficacy, which is the purging and cleansing of our souls. As water without washing makes nothing clean, so the blood of Christ, without a right application of it, cleanses no man’s soul.

Since this washing of water mentioned here is applied to an inward, spiritual cleansing, what else can it set forth but the sacrament of baptism, in which both water and washing are used?

Objection. There is but little washing used in the sacrament of baptism, nothing but sprinkling a little water on the face of the one who is baptized.

Answer. That sprinkling is enough to show the use of water.418 The one to be baptized is not brought to the font to have his face, or any other part of his body, made clean, but to have assurance of the inward cleansing of his soul. Now, so that our minds may not fasten too much on the outward thing done, but be wholly raised up to the mystery, the outward element is used no further than may serve to put us in mind of the inward thing signified by it. In the same way, in the Lord’s Supper not so much bread and wine is given and received as would satisfy one’s appetite, or slake his hunger and quench his thirst. Only a little bit of bread and a taste of wine are given, to declare the use of bread and wine, and so to draw the minds of the communicants to consider their spiritual nourishment by the body and blood of Jesus Christ.

§. 41. How baptism is a means of cleansing and sanctifying.

The manner of joining this sacramental washing to the sanctifying and cleansing of the church, “with the washing of water,” shows that

Baptism is a means of sanctifying and cleansing the church. All419 those places of Scripture that ascribe regeneration,420 justification,421 sanctification,422 or salvation423 to it prove as much. But so that the truth of it may be understood more fully and distinctly, I will briefly show:

  1. In what respect baptism is a means of our sanctifying and cleansing.
  2. What kind of means it is.
  3. How necessary it is.

It may be said to be a means, as stated above, in four special respects.

1. In that it most vividly represents and sets forth, even to the outward senses, the inward cleansing of our souls by the blood of Christ, and the sanctifying of us by the Spirit of Christ. Apply the use of water (by washing in which foul things are made very clean) to the power of Christ’s blood and the efficacy of his Spirit, and the truth of this will plainly appear. For better help in this application, read Romans 6:4, etc.

2. In that it truly sets forth and makes a tender, or offer, of the grace of justification and sanctification to the one baptized. In this respect it is described as “a baptism of repentance424 for the forgiveness of sins.”425 And Peter says to the same purpose, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you+, … for the forgiveness of your+ sins.”

3. In that it really holds out and gives and seals up to the conscience of the one who is baptized the graces named before, by which he is assured that he is made partaker of them. So Abraham “received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had426 by faith.” That is why the eunuch and others, when they were427 baptized, went on their way rejoicing.

4. In that it is a particular pledge, belonging to the one baptized, that he himself is made partaker of those graces. Therefore every one in particular is baptized for himself; indeed, though many are brought to the font at once, yet every one is baptized by name. To this purpose the apostle says, “Whoever has been baptized into Christ has clothed himself with Christ”:428 whoever, whether Peter, John, Thomas, or any other particular person. Ananias said to Paul in the singular number, “Be429 baptized, and wash your sins away.”

§. 42. Objections against the efficacy of baptism answered.

1. Objection. Many who are baptized receive no such grace at all. They are neither cleansed nor sanctified.

Answer. They are only outwardly washed with water; they are not baptized with the Holy Spirit. The fault is not that no grace accompanies that sacrament, but that they do not receive, but reject, the grace which belongs to it. “What if some did not have faith? Will their lack of faith nullify430 God’s faithfulness? Certainly not!”

2. Objection. Many receive the graces named before before they are baptized, as Abraham did before he was circumcised,431 and such as were baptized after they believed. How then is baptism a means of them?

Answer. Their spiritual cleansing is more vividly and fully shown by it, and they are the more assured of it.

3. Objection. Many who for a long time after their baptism have lived like swine in sin, and so have not been cleansed or sanctified, have yet been effectually called many years afterward. What means has baptism been of this?

Answer. The use and efficacy of baptism is not passing, as the act of it is, but lasting and perpetual, as long as the one baptized lives. Whenever a sinner sincerely repents and lays hold in faith on the promises of God, baptism, which is the seal of them, is as powerful and effectual as it could have been when it was first administered. For the efficacy of baptism consists in the free offer of grace. As long, therefore, as God continues to offer grace, so long may a man’s baptism be effectual. On this ground we are baptized only once for all. And as the432 prophets put the people in mind of their circumcision, so the apostles put them in mind of their baptism long after it was administered. Indeed, they speak of it (though the act was long past) as if it were being done in the present time: “baptism … now saves you+.”433

§. 43. What kind of means of grace baptism is.

II. Baptism is no physical or natural means of working434 grace, as if the grace which is sealed up by it were inherent in the water, or in the minister’s act of sprinkling it. (In medicines, salves, herbs, foods and the like, the power which comes from their use is inherent in them; when they are applied they have their effect, whether a man believes it or not.) Rather, it is only a voluntary instrument which Christ uses, as it pleases him, to work what grace, or what measure of435 grace, seems best to him. So grace only attends it; it is not enclosed in it. Yet in the right use of it, Christ by his Spirit works that grace which is received by it. In this respect the minister is said to “baptize with water,” but Christ “with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Matt 3:11).

§. 44. Of the necessity of baptism.

III. A means of working a thing may be said to be necessary436 in two ways.

1. Absolutely, so that the thing cannot possibly be without it. In this way the proper causes of a thing are absolutely necessary; as in this case God’s covenant, Christ’s blood, and the working of the Spirit are absolutely necessary for attaining any grace.

2. By consequence,437 so that, according to the course and order which God has set down, things cannot be without them.

Baptism is not absolutely necessary as a cause. For then it would be equal to God’s covenant, Christ’s blood, and the work of the Spirit. Indeed, then all who are baptized, without any exception, would be cleansed.

But it is necessary by consequence, and that in two438 respects:

  1. In regard of God’s ordinance.
  2. In regard of our need of it.

1. Since God has ordained this as a sacrament to be used, it is necessary that it should be used, if for no other end, yet to show our obedience. He who carelessly neglects, or willfully despises, any sacrament which God commands him to use, “that soul will be cut off.”439

2. Great is the need that we have of it, in regard of our dullness in understanding spiritual things, and of our weakness in believing invisible things. We are carnal and earthly, and we understand spiritual and heavenly things better by things that are earthly and perceived by the senses. Therefore God has ordained visible elements to be sacraments of invisible graces. Again, we are slow to believe such things as are promised in the word. Therefore, the more to help and strengthen our faith, God has added to his covenant in the word his seal in and by the sacrament, so “that by two unchangeable things” (God’s covenant and God’s seal) “in which it is impossible for God to lie, we … may be strongly encouraged.” Besides, though in general we do believe the truth of God’s word, yet we are doubtful about applying it to ourselves. So, for the better applying of God’s covenant to our own souls, God has added his sacrament to his word.

§. 45. Of the contrary extremes of papists and Anabaptists about the necessity and efficacy of baptism.

There are two extremes contrary to the points about baptism set down above.

One is in the excess: that of the papists, who ascribe too much to it, and make it a plain idol.

The other is in the defect: that of the Anabaptists and libertines, who440 take too much from it, and make it an idle ceremony.

The papists go too far in two things: in the necessity and in the efficacy of baptism.

They make it so absolutely necessary that if any die unbaptized, he cannot be saved. They pass this sentence on infants, even though they are deprived of it without any fault of their own, or even of their parents, being stillborn. It is a merciless sentence without any warrant from God’s word; indeed, it is against his word and against the order which he has prescribed. He has established441 his covenant, and promised to be the God of the faithful and of their seed. On this ground Peter says, “This promise belongs to442 you+ and your+ children.” And Paul says of “your+ children” that “now they are holy.”443 Shall all these privileges be made void by a lack444 of baptism that could not be helped? If so, would God have commanded circumcision (which was to the Jews what baptism is to Christians) to be put off to the eighth day, before which day many infants died? Or would Moses have allowed it to be left undone all the time that the Israelites were in the wilderness? If it is said that baptism is more necessary than circumcision, I answer that the Scripture lays no more necessity on it. If it were as necessary as they make it, then the power of Christ’s death would be less effectual since he was actually manifested than it was before. For before, it was effectual for infants without a sacrament, but now, it seems, it is not. Had the ancient churches thought so of the absolute necessity of baptism, they would not have had set times for administering it, nor would they have allowed it to be put off as long as they did.445 Some churches appointed it to be administered only at Easter.446 Some appointed it at Easter and Pentecost. And though many who gave evidence of their true faith died before they were baptized, yet447 they did not on that account judge them to be damned. This practice and judgment of the ancients has made448 many papists somewhat soften that absolute necessity, and say that “in this case God, who has not bound his grace to any sacrament, in respect of his own freedom, may and does accept as baptized those who either are martyred before they could be baptized, or else depart this life with a vow and desire to have that sacrament, but by some necessity that could not be remedied could not obtain it.” If a necessity that cannot be remedied can help the matter, what necessity is so beyond remedy as for a child to be stillborn?

Again, they add such efficacy to baptism that it gives grace by the work itself,449 that is, by the very work done. In this they make it equal to the very blood of Christ, and take away the proper work of the Spirit, and the use of faith, repentance, and such graces. What can there be more in the water of baptism than there was in the blood of the beasts that were offered up in sacrifice? But “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.”450 They themselves ascribe no such efficacy to the word preached, and yet they cannot show where the Holy Spirit has given more power to baptism than to the word. This text joins them both together (“that He might … cleanse her with451 the washing of water by the word”). What more can be said of a means than what is said of the word? “God was pleased through … what was preached to save those who believe.” “The gospel … is the power of God for salvation,” etc.

On the other side, the Anabaptists and such libertines esteem452 this holy and necessary ordinance of God too lightly. For they make it only a badge of our profession of faith, a mark of difference between the true and the false church, a sign of mutual fellowship, a bare sign of spiritual grace, a picture of mortification, regeneration, ingrafting into Christ, and the like, but no more. These indeed are some of the ends and uses of baptism. But in that they confine all its efficacy to these, they take away the greatest comfort and truest benefit which the church reaps by it, as may be gathered from the points noted453 before.

§. 46. Of the inward washing by baptism.454

In that Christ cleanses his church with this washing of water, I observe that

Whoever are fully baptized are cleansed from sin.

Fully, that is, powerfully and effectually: inwardly by the Spirit, as well as outwardly by the minister.

Cleansed, both from the guilt of sin by Christ’s blood, and from the power of sin by the work of his Spirit.

To this purpose tend the many emphatic phrases which the apostles apply to baptism: that we were “baptized into Christ Jesus,” “baptized into His death,” “buried with Him through baptism”; that “baptism … now saves you+”; that baptism is “the washing of regeneration,”455 and the like.

Vain is the rejoicing of many who boast of their baptism,456 and think themselves by virtue of it to be as good Christians as the best, and yet live and lie in their sin, more smeared and defiled with it than they were when they were first born. John says that Christ baptizes “with the Holy Spirit457 and with fire.” The apostle says that Christ cleanses “with the washing of water.” If that fire of the Holy Spirit does not burn up the dross of sin in you, and this water does not wash away the filth of sin, you were never fully baptized. It may be that the hand of some minister has sprinkled a little water on your face, but Christ’s blood has not yet been sprinkled on your soul. All the benefit which you reap from your baptism is that one day you will answer dearly for the abuse of so honorable an ordinance.

§. 47. Of joining the word with baptism.

The other means of sanctifying and cleansing the church expressed here is the word. Since this is applied to baptism and joined with it, it must be meant of the promise of grace sealed up in baptism, which is God’s promise of justifying us freely and sanctifying us effectually, plainly made known and truly believed. Since this means is added to this sacrament in this way, we may well infer that

It is necessary that the word and baptism go together. That is,458 where this sacrament is administered, its doctrine must be taught truly, plainly and understandably, so that its nature, efficacy, end and use may be made known, and the covenant of God sealed up by it may be believed. So Christ says, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them.”459 So the460 Baptist did, and the461 apostles: they preached the gospel to those whom they baptized.

1. A sacrament without the word is but an idle ceremony,462 no more than a seal without a covenant. For it is the word that makes known the covenant of God.

2. It is the word which makes the greatest difference between the sacramental washing of water and ordinary, common washing.

3. By the word the ordinary created things which we use are sanctified; much more the holy ordinances of God, of which baptism is one of the chief.

Question. Is it not lawful, then, to administer baptism without463 a sermon?

Answer. It is a very commendable and honorable manner of administering that sacrament to administer it at a time when the word is preached. Yet I do not think a sermon at that time to be so necessary that it would be unlawful to administer baptism without one. For the joining of the word and the sacrament spoken of here is this: that those who are baptized, or who present children to be baptized and answer for them, or who are present at the administering of baptism, or who live in the places where it is usually administered, should be instructed in the gospel, and taught the covenant which baptism seals up. Besides, the liturgy and public form prescribed for the administering of baptism, both in our church and in other Reformed churches, lays down the nature, efficacy, end, use, and other such points belonging to that sacrament, and plainly declares the covenant of God sealed up by it. So in our churches, and others like them, where such forms are prescribed to be always used, the word is never separated from baptism, though there is no sermon at the administering of baptism.

The Church of Rome directly transgresses against the464 rule set down above, of joining the word and baptism together. For though they have a public form prescribed, yet since it is in an unknown tongue, not understood by the people nor explained to them, it is all the same as if there were no form at all, no word at all. For what is not understood is all the same465 as if it were not spoken.

Much more heinous is the transgression of those who live under the gospel, where it is preached plainly to the understanding and capacity of the simplest, and yet are careless in coming to it or in attending to it. So they remain as ignorant as if they lived in places where the word is not preached at all, or is preached in an unknown tongue. Such ignorant persons, if they were not baptized, are not worthy, while they remain so ignorant, to be baptized, nor to present their children to be baptized, nor to be present at the baptism of others. As ministers who baptize ought to preach the word, so those who are baptized ought to be instructed in the word.
