The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 48–52

§. 48. Of the inference of glorification from justification and sanctification.

Eph 5:27.

That He might present her to Himself a glorious church, etc.

The chief end, in regard of the church’s good, at which Christ aimed when he gave himself for her, is her glorious state in heaven: this is the end of the end named before. For why did Christ give himself for the church? “That He might sanctify her, having cleansed her.” Why did he cleanse and sanctify her? “That He might present her to Himself a glorious church.” From this, note these three points.

  1. Justification and sanctification must go before glorification.
  2. The end for which the saints are cleansed and sanctified in this world is that they may be presented glorious to Christ in the world to come.
  3. The only means to make us glorious before Christ our spouse is righteousness.

1. All those places of Scripture which set our righteousness in this world before our glory in the world to come466 (as very many places do) prove the first point, that justification and sanctification must go before glorification.467 Among other proofs, note especially the order of the separate links of that golden chain which reaches from God’s eternal counsel before the world to our everlasting glory after this world: “Those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.”

1. Heaven, the place of our glorification, is “the holy city,”468 into which “nothing unclean will ever enter.”

2. In that place the church is to be married to Christ, and to be with him forever. She must therefore be pure, “just as Christ is469 pure,” for he will not endure the company of a foul, filthy spouse.

As we desire assurance of our glorification in heaven, so470 let us get, and give, evidence of our justification and sanctification on earth. The evidence of our justification is a sound and true faith. The evidence of our sanctification is a good and clear conscience.

The proofs and reasons named before also confirm the471 second point, that the end for which the saints are cleansed and sanctified in this world is that they may be presented glorious to Christ in the world to come.

It is therefore needful and fitting, not only in regard of472 Christ’s honor, but also of our own glory and happiness, that here, while we live on earth, we be sanctified and cleansed. If Christ for our sakes had an eye to our future and everlasting glory, and for that end prepared means to bring us to it, ought not we ourselves much more to have an eye to it, and both avoid all things which may hinder it, and use all means by which we may be assured of it? Moses “was looking ahead to his reward.” Indeed, Christ, “for the joy473 set before Him, endured the cross, scorning its shame.”

3. That righteousness is the only means to make us glorious474 before Christ our spouse is evident from this, that Christ gave himself to work and effect this means for this end. Christ himself, by his death, has consecrated this means and no other. If there is any other means than the one which Christ has procured by offering himself up, what need was there for Christ to be offered up? To show that this is the means to make the church glorious before Christ, the Holy Spirit likens “the righteousness of the saints” to “fine linen, bright and pure,”475 with which the wife of the Lamb is made ready for the day of the marriage.

Christ himself has “loved righteousness and hated wickedness”;476 therefore they, and none but they, who are arrayed with righteousness are glorious in his eyes.

I have noted this all the more against the notion of our adversaries,477 who place all the glory of the church in outward478 pomp. So their Pope, whom they make head of the church, and in a special manner the spouse of Christ, must have his triple crown, his scarlet robes, his throne raised above kings; men must be his horses to carry him, and kings and nobles must be his men to wait on him. Their priests too must be arrayed in glorious copes of the finest worked gold. Their temples must be decked with intricate, carved, gilded images. Their host is carried about in the manner of a triumph. Their people are all sprinkled with water. Their superstitious houses must be the finest buildings in a kingdom, and have the greatest revenues of a kingdom belonging to them; and the like.479

Is this glory fit for Christ’s spouse? Then it seems Christ has carnal eyes and ears, and is delighted with the things that delight the world. The wiser among the heathen scoffed at such base notions as their people had of their gods. Shall Christians think more basely of Christ than the heathen did of their gods? Most people dote far too much on outward, worldly glory, so much that they neglect true righteousness.

For our part, as we desire to appear before Christ in such a way that he480 may think us glorious, let us be arrayed with righteousness and holiness, “without which no one will see the Lord,” Heb 12:14.

§. 49. Of the enjoyment of Christ’s presence in heaven.

Eph 5:27.

That He might present her to Himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and without blemish.

Having noted how this verse follows from the one before, I will now handle it distinctly by itself. It contains a description of the glorious state of the church in heaven. This description must be meant here of that state,481 for on earth the church is not wholly without spot or wrinkle, though it is being prepared to be so.

This state is

  1. Set forth in general.
  2. Illustrated in particular.

In the general statement are noted

  1. Her condition (she is presented to Christ.)
  2. Her quality (glorious.)

The particular illustration of it is

1. Privative, by removing all deformity: noted in two words, spot and wrinkle.

2. Positive, by adorning her with beauty: noted also in two words, holy and blameless.

The word (present) is taken from the custom of solemnizing482 a marriage: first the spouse was wooed, and then set before her husband, so that he might take her as his wife, to be with him. So Eve483 was presented by God to Adam, so that he might take her as his wife; and Esther484 was presented to Ahasuerus among other virgins. This shows that485

The church in heaven will enjoy the presence of Christ.486 Christ himself says expressly to his disciples, “I am going there to prepare a place for you+ … so that you+ also may be where I am.” On this ground the apostle desired “to depart and be with Christ,”487 and “to be present with the Lord.”488

In heaven the marriage between Christ and the church is solemnized, which has been in preparation here on earth. God the Father has given his489 Son to the church, and the490 church to his Son. Indeed,491 Christ himself has purchased the church for himself by his blood, and492 promised marriage to her; and to assure the church all the more of his love, he has493 bestowed many gifts on her. He has further sent494 his ministers in his name to495 woo and496 beseech the church to give her consent, and to497 prepare her as a pure virgin for himself. On this the church has given her consent, for498 as a spouse she is subject to Christ as to a head. These things being so, how can it be thought that Christ will forsake her, and not receive her to be with him forever?

Can the thought of death be terrible to those who know and499 believe the truth of this? Will not the consideration500 of it rather make them, with the apostle, sigh and “desire to depart,” that they may be with the Lord? The highest degree of the church’s happiness consists in this enjoyment of the501 presence of her spouse; for so he becomes all in all to her, not by means, as in this world, but directly, by himself. So there will be no need of any minister, any sacrament, any ordinance to set forth Christ to us; no governor in family, church, or commonwealth to represent his person, or to keep us in subjection; no light to direct us, no food to sustain us: we will be so attended by Christ that we will need nothing. If those servants were happy who stood continually before Solomon,502 what are those who always stand in the presence of one who is infinitely greater than Solomon, not as servants, but as a wife? If it was a great grace and favor that Moses saw the back503 of God, what a grace and favor it is to behold Christ504 face to face! For “when Christ appears … we will see Him as He is.”505 Though we are now absent from the Lord, yet let us uphold ourselves with the expectation and assurance of this, that we will be presented before Christ.

§. 50. Of the glory of the church in heaven.

The quality of the church in heaven is as excellent as can be,506 and therefore it is said here to be glorious. All beauty, all comeliness,507 all grace, whatever may make the church lovely, attractive, or in any way to be desired or admired, is comprised under this word glorious. In this respect the saints are said to “shine,” and that “like a most precious jewel,”508 indeed, like “the brightness of the heavens,”509 like “the stars,” and like “the sun”;510 and to be “like Him,”511 Christ himself; and to “appear with Him in glory.”512

This glory of the saints extends to both soul and body, and to the whole person.

In regard of their souls, they will be all “glorious within,”513 for they are “the spirits of the righteous made perfect.”514515 Perfect knowledge, wisdom, and all manner of purity will be in them.

In regard of their bodies, they will be made “like His glorious body,”516 and that in incorruption, immortality,517 beauty, brightness, grace, favor, agility, strength, and the like. It is therefore truly said that the church at the end of the world expects what has already been shown beforehand in Christ’s body.

In regard of their person, as a wife is advanced to the honor and dignity of her husband, so will they be advanced to the honor and dignity of Christ, as far as they are capable of it: for they will be518 next to Christ, indeed519 one with him, and so520 above the most glorious angels.

Much more might be said of the glory of the church, but enough can never be said of it, no, not by the tongue of men or of angels: for “no eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.”521 When Paul was caught up into the third heaven, and saw only a glimpse of this glory,522 he “heard inexpressible words, which it is not possible for man to utter.” Therefore,523 when he speaks of it, he uses such a transcendent kind of phrase as cannot be fully expressed in any tongue. As well as we can, we translate it thus, by one degree of comparison upon another:524 “a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.”

Is this not enough to uphold us against all the reproach and disgrace which the world lays on us because we are525 of the church of Christ? The world has526 of old counted her forsaken and desolate, though Christ calls her “Hephzibah” (that is, my delight in her) and “Beulah” (that is, married); indeed, it has counted her527 “the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world.” Among the heathen, none were so vilely regarded as Christians; among papists, none so much as Protestants; and among carnal professing Christians, none so much as those who endeavor528 to purify themselves, “just as Christ is pure,” and to avoid the common sins of the world. When we are basely regarded for Christ’s sake, let us think of this.

§. 51. Of the church’s freedom from all deformity in heaven. Not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing.

The first point noted by the apostle in his illustration of the glory named before is the removing of all deformity. The word translated529 spot is used for a stain on a garment, and for a foul speck on a man’s face or another part of the body, or a scar or other blemish in his flesh from a sore, wound, blow, or the like. The other word530 (wrinkle) is used for a crease in the face through old age, for it signifies a gathering together of the skin by old age. By it is meant any kind of breaking (as we say) through age, sickness, trouble, pain, or the like. Because there may also be deformities in other ways, the apostle adds this clause (or any such thing.) These things, applied to531 the church, show that

No manner of deformity will cling to the church in heaven.532 There will be in her no stain or contagion of sin received from others, no scar of any infection arising from itself, no wrinkle, no lack of spiritual moisture, no sign of the old man, nor anything that may in any way make it seem deformed or uncomely in the sight of Christ. Not only great, heinous, capital sins (which are like ulcers and boils, and like open, wide sores, gashes and wounds), but all spots and specks, all wrinkles and defects, all manner of blemishes whatever, within or without, will be taken clean away. Sin will not only be subdued in us, but utterly rooted out of us: no relic, no sign of it will be left remaining. In this respect it is said that “God will wipe away every tear,”533 that is, he will take away all cause of mourning, sorrow, and grief. Now there is nothing that gives the saints more cause of sorrow than sin. The remnant of sin which was in the apostle, even after his regeneration, made him cry out thus: “What a wretched man I am!”534

Though this is only a privative good, yet it adds much to the heavenly happiness of the saints. If it were possible for us to enjoy the rest and glory prepared for the saints in heaven while the spots and wrinkles of sin still remained on us, these spots and wrinkles would be like the handwriting which appeared to Belshazzar535 in the midst of his revelry; they would be like gall mixed with wine; they would turn all our joy into heaviness, and take away the sweet relish of all our happiness. Therefore the consideration of this privative benefit cannot but breed, in the hearts of all who are members of this church, a longing desire for this perfect purging of them from all deformity.

§. 52. Of the perfect purity of the church in heaven.

But that she should be holy and without blemish.

The last branch by which the heavenly glory of the church is set forth is its perfect purity. The adversative particle (BUT) shows that the holiness spoken of here is no imperfect536 holiness, such as the sanctification of the saints is in this world, but an absolutely perfect holiness in all its parts and degrees: such as is without spot or wrinkle, without relic or sign of sin. And therefore, by way of explanation, there is added537 without blemish, or blameless: such that neither man, angel, nor God himself can find fault with it.538 This attribute is often applied to the person and blood of Jesus Christ,539 and therefore it must set forth perfect purity. From this we may observe that

The sanctification of the saints will be perfect in heaven. They will not only be justified by having their sins covered, nor only have their sanctification truly begun in them, but they will also have it absolutely perfected in every part, point, and degree. In this respect they are said to be “the righteous made540 perfect.” Adam in his innocence was not more pure than the saints will be in heaven; indeed, they will far surpass Adam, as in the measure of it, so in its stability and perpetuity.

In our endeavor after holiness let us keep an eye on this541 perfection, and not lose heart if we do not attain the measure which we desire. Perfection is reserved for the world to come. Yet let us know that the more holy and blameless we are, the nearer we come to that heavenly state; and the more spots and blemishes of sin we have, the more unlike it we are, and the less hope we have of enjoying that heavenly happiness.

All the separate points of the glorious state of542 the church in heaven named before should enrapture our spirits, and even break our hearts with a holy wonder at Christ’s goodness, and fill our mouths with praises for it, and make us sigh and long for it, and with all good conscience and diligence use all the means we can to attain it: no labor will be lost in this. Surely this is either not known, or not believed, or not remembered, or not duly and seriously considered by those who make light of it. Let what has been only briefly touched on here be meditated on further, and let us pray that “the eyes of our heart may be enlightened,543 so that we may know … the riches of the glorious inheritance of the saints.” If it were not for this hope, the saints would be544 the most miserable of all; whereas now they are the most happy.

Marital Love and Self-Love

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 53–67

§. 53. Of the application to husbands of the things that Christ has done for the church.

Eph 5:28.

So men ought to love their wives, etc.

The first clause of this verse serves both as an application of the former argument and as a transition to another argument.

The particle of relation (So) shows that what has been said before of Christ’s love to his church ought to be referred and applied to husbands. For as Christ loved his church, so husbands ought to love their wives.

Question. Why are these transcendent evidences of Christ’s surpassing love to his church set before husbands? Can any such things be expected from husbands toward their wives?

Answer. No,545 not in measure, but in likeness. For in this large declaration of Christ’s love there are two general points to be noted.

1. That the church in herself was in no way worthy of love.

2. That Christ so carried himself toward her that he made her worthy of much love.

This ought to be the mind of husbands toward their wives.

1. Though their wives are in no way worthy of love, yet husbands must love them.

2. They must endeavor, with all the understanding and wisdom they have, to make them worthy of love. I say endeavor because it is not wholly in the husband’s power to do the deed. Yet his faithful endeavor shall, on his part, be accepted for the deed.

I shall speak more fully of these points hereafter.

§. 54. Of the application to a husband of the love that a man bears to himself.

Eph 5:28.

So men ought to love their wives as their own bodies.

The forenamed particle (So) also has relation to another pattern, namely, that of a man’s self to his body. And so it is a transition from one argument to another.

There is more emphasis used here in setting down a husband’s duty than there was before, in v. 25.

There it was laid down by way of exhortation: “Husbands, love your+ wives.”

Here it is laid down with a stricter charge: husbands ought to love their wives. So this duty is not an optional matter, left to the husband’s will to do or to leave undone. A necessity is laid upon him: he must love his wife. Woe to him, therefore, if he does not do it.

In setting down this argument taken from a man’s self, the apostle likens a man’s wife to his body. In this he has relation to v. 23, where he said, “the husband is the head of the wife.” By this he shows that as a husband’s place is a motive to his wife to perform her duty, so it is to himself,546 to perform his duty.

He is her head; therefore she must be subject to him.

She is his body; therefore he must love her.

This example of a man’s self is both a reason, to move husbands the more to love their wives, and also a rule, to teach them how to love them.

The reason is implied in that near union which is between547 a man and his wife: she is as near to him as his own body; therefore she ought to be as dear to him. The body never disagrees with itself, nor the soul with itself. So neither should man and wife.

The rule is noted in the manner of a man’s loving his own body: as entirely as he loves his body, so entirely he ought to love his wife.

Of the manner of a man’s loving himself, see Treatise 4, §. 74, 76.

To enforce this comparison the more, the apostle adds, “He who loves his wife loves himself.”548

Two things are implied by this clause.

1. That a wife is not only as a man’s body, namely, his outward flesh, but as his person, his body and soul. She is as his body because she was taken out of his body,549 and because she is set under him as his body is under his head. She is as himself by reason of the bond of marriage, which makes one of two.550 In this respect a wife is commonly called a man’s second self.

2. That a husband in loving his wife loves himself, so that the benefit of loving his wife will redound to himself as well as to his wife.

§. 55. Of the amplification of a man’s love of himself.

Eph 5:29.

For no man ever yet hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as the Lord does the church.

The former pattern of a man’s self is further amplified here. For first the apostle proves that a man loves himself, and then he shows how he loves himself.

Two arguments are used to prove the point.

One is taken from the contrary: No man ever yet hated his own flesh. Therefore he loves it.

The other is taken from the effects of love: To nourish and cherish one’s flesh is a fruit of love. But every man nourishes and cherishes his flesh. Therefore he loves it.

This latter argument shows the manner of a man’s loving himself, and in this a man’s love of himself is a rule to teach him how to love his wife.

This indefinite phrase (no man) is to be restricted to such as have the understanding and feeling of a man in them, as if he had said, no man in his right mind. For furious, frantic, mad, desperate persons will cut their arms, legs and other parts, mangle their flesh, hang, drown, smother, choke and stab themselves. Even so, those who551 hate their wives, or hurt them in any way, are as men out of their minds. Indeed, it is the part of a madman to doubt that he loves himself and does good to himself.

These two words (to nourish and cherish) comprise under them a diligent providing of all things needful for a man’s body.

To nourish is properly to feed.552

To cherish is to keep warm.553

The former is done by food, the latter by clothing. Under554 food and clothing the apostle comprises all things needful for this life, where he says, “If we have food and clothing, let us be content with these.”555

Applied to a husband, this shows that he ought to have a provident care for the good of his wife in all things needful for her.

To press this point yet further, he returns again to the example of Christ (“just as the Lord does the church”). The apostle thought that this nail of love needed to be driven fast into the heads and hearts of husbands. Therefore he adds blow to blow to knock it in deep, even to the head. Before, he confirmed Christ’s example with the example of ourselves; here he confirms the example of ourselves with the example of Christ again. He does this for two special reasons.

1. To urge the point more forcibly. For two examples add weight to one another, especially this latter one, which is so far more excellent, as we heard from v. 25, 26, 27.

2. To give husbands better direction for their provident care toward their wives. They must nourish and cherish them not only as their own bodies, but as Christ nourishes and cherishes his church: not only with things temporal, but also with things spiritual and eternal.

§. 56. Of man’s natural affection toward himself.

Eph 5:28, 29.

So men ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no man ever yet hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as the Lord does the church.

Having briefly shown the general scope of the 28th and 29th verses, I will proceed to handle them more distinctly.

They set forth the natural affection of a man to himself.556

Two points are to be noted here.

1. The general proposition, that a man is well disposed toward himself.

2. The particular amplification and manifestation of that affection.

This is manifested in two ways.

Negatively: No man hates his own flesh. Affirmatively, and that in two branches: he nourishes and cherishes it.

Both these are justified by the like affection of Christ to the church, which is his body (“just as the Lord does the church”). In that the apostle sets forth the natural affection of a man’s self to his body as a motive and pattern to Christians to love their wives, and also justifies it by a like affection of Christ to his church, I observe that

Natural affection is a thing lawful and commendable. It is557 an affection which may stand with a good conscience. God’s word is so far from taking it away that it establishes it. For such as are558 “without natural affection”559 are directly condemned,560 and we are561 commanded to be as tenderly affectionate toward one another as562 we are toward ourselves. Indeed, the law in its strict rigor lays down the natural affection which is in a man toward himself as a rule for the love of his neighbor563 (“Love your neighbor as yourself”). Hence it is that the564 prophets,565 apostles, and Christ himself often call on us to have an eye to the affection which we bear to ourselves. Of this pattern Christ says, “This is the Law and the Prophets”:566 this is the brief sum of them; this is what they much urge and press.

1. Natural affection was at first created by God, and567 planted by him in man. So, as the soul and the body, and their powers and parts, are good things in their substance, this affection also is good in itself.

2. There are the same reasons to love ourselves as to love our brethren. For we ourselves are made in God’s image, redeemed by Christ’s blood, members of the same mystical body, and keepers of ourselves, who must give an account of the good or hurt we do to ourselves, and the like. In the law, under this word neighbor, we ourselves are included, and every commandment of the second table is to be applied to ourselves.

§. 57. Of natural self-love.

Objection. Lovers of themselves are condemned in God’s word, as 2 Tim 3:2, Phil 2:21, 1 Cor 10:24, Rom 15:1.

Answer. There is a double loving of a man’s self.568 One is good and commendable; the other is evil and damnable.

The good and commendable loving of a man’s self is

  1. Natural.
  2. Spiritual.

That which is natural is in all men by the very instinct of nature. It was created at first, and is always preserved in our nature by God’s providence, and that for the preservation of nature. If there were not such a natural love of himself in every one, a man would be as careless of himself as of others, and as unwilling to take pains for himself as for others. Therefore, so that every one might have care of at least one, namely himself, and so the world be better preserved, God has reserved in man this natural affection, notwithstanding his corruption by sin. Yes, further: because not every one is able to look after himself, at least when he is young, sick, old, or in any other way helpless, God by his wise providence has extended this natural affection toward others also, as they are closely linked to us by the bonds of nature. The nearest to a man’s self (by blood and the bond of nature) are his children. It is wonderful how much parents do for their children, which they would never do if there were not a natural affection in them toward their children. From children again this affection rises toward their parents, so that when parents grow old, helpless, or in any way unable to help themselves, they might have relief from their children. And because parents and children are not always together, or are not able to help one another, or are unnatural, God has extended this natural affection yet further, to brothers, kinsmen and other relatives. And to extend it further still, he has instituted marriage between those who are not of the same blood, and by virtue of that bond has raised a natural affection not only in husband and wife toward one another, but also in all the kindred by marriage that is made by it. Moreover, this affection is wrought in neighbors, friends, companions and others knit together by like bonds, so that the bow of God’s providence might have many strings, and if one breaks, another might hold. In all these kinds, the nearer a man comes to himself, the more this affection shows itself, according to the proverb, Near is my coat, but nearer is my skin. Since God has wrought this natural affection in its distinct kinds, and there are good ends and uses of it, it is not to be condemned.

§. 58. Of spiritual self-love.

Spiritual self-love is that which is wrought in man supernaturally by God’s Spirit. By it he is both enlightened to discern what is most excellent and best for him, and also moved to choose it, so that this serves to rectify the former. Hence it comes about that the chief care of such men is for their souls and for their eternal salvation. To further it they can be content, as need requires, to569 beat down their bodies, to570 deny them at times their ordinary refreshment by food, rest and other like means, and even to571 allow them to be imprisoned, racked and otherwise tortured, and life itself to be taken from them. Men do and suffer this,572 not for want of natural affection, but by reason of a spiritual affection which persuades them that it is good for them that it should be so. A man is not therefore to be said not to love the health and safety of his body because he loves something more. For though a covetous man loves his money, yet he can be content to part with it for bread to nourish his body. So though a spiritual man loves his life, yet he can be content to lose it for his soul’s salvation. For he loves himself sufficiently who does his best to enjoy the chief and truest good. This spiritual affection extends itself as573 far as natural affection, namely to wives, husbands, children, parents, brothers, kinsmen, friends, etc. It is much urged and pressed in the Scriptures, as Isa 55:1, 2, 3; Matt 6:19, 20, 33; John 6:27; 1 Tim 6:11, 19.

§. 59. Of evil self-love.

The self-love which is evil swerves in its

  • Object.
  • Measure.

1. In the object, when it is set on our corruptions, our lusts, our evil inclinations: when we desire and love them, and for their sake pursue whatever may satisfy them, as the ambitious, lustful, dissolute, gluttonous and other such persons do. This is expressly forbidden: “Make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its lusts.”574

2. In the measure, when our love is wholly and only set on ourselves, so seeking our own good that we regard no man’s good but our own, nor care what damage another receives, so long as we may gain advantage by it. This is also forbidden,575 for it is contrary to the property of true love, which “does not seek its own,” namely to the hurt of another. This has the title of576 self-love appropriated to it. It sprang from the corruption of nature, and is daily increased by the instigation of Satan for the destruction of mankind. It shows itself in the many tricks of deceit which most men use in their dealings with others; in taking advantage of others’ necessities, as in the case of usury, and of raising the price of grain and other goods in time of scarcity, and the like; in men’s slowness to help those who stand in need of their help; in want of compassion for other men’s miseries; and in many other such unkindnesses. All of these verify the proverb, Every man for himself.

But by distinguishing the forenamed points we may see that, although evil self-love is a most detestable vice, yet it is both lawful and commendable to love oneself rightly.

§. 60. Of the error of the Stoics in condemning all passion.

The folly of the Stoics, who would have all natural affection577 rooted out of man, is contrary to this pattern, and unworthy to find any welcome among Christians. For what do they aim at but to root out of man what God has planted in him, and to take away the means which God has used for the better preservation of man? That wise man whom they frame for themselves is worse than a brute beast: he is a mere log or block. Not only the best and wisest men that ever were in the world, but also Christ himself had in him those passions and affections which they account unbecoming a wise man. Their folly has long since been hissed out of the schools of the philosophers; should it then find a place in Christ’s church?

§. 61. Of using natural affection well.

Let us labor to cherish this natural affection in us, and to578 turn it to the best things: even to such as are good not only in appearance but in truth, and among good things to such as are most excellent and most necessary, such as concern our souls and eternal life. To this end we must pray to have our understandings enlightened (that we may “discern579 what differs, and approve what is excellent”), and to have our wills and affections sanctified, so that we embrace, pursue and delight in what we know to be best. So our natural affection will be turned into a spiritual affection.

Here we see how we may make nature a schoolmaster to us. For as Christ sends us to the birds of the air and the lilies580 of the field to learn from them, so the apostle here sends us to our own natural instinct. We cannot complain that we have no schoolmaster near us (as many in the country can, whose children are brought up untaught for want of one): we ourselves are schoolmasters to ourselves. Therefore, as the apostle by this teaches husbands to love their wives, so let us all learn more generally to love one another. For581 we are all mutual members of one and the same body, and our brother or neighbor is “our own flesh.”582

§. 62. Of man’s forbearing to wrong himself.

Eph 5:29.

For no man ever yet hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it.

The first particle (for) shows that in this verse an evidence and manifestation of a man’s love of himself is given. Its first part, which is set down negatively, shows that

It is against the common instinct of nature for a man to hate583 himself. It is noted as an evidence that devils were in the Gadarene, in that “he was cutting himself with stones.”584 Had the devils not forced him, he would never have done it.

Hatred is contrary to love. Since it was proved before585 that every man by nature loves himself, it follows by necessary consequence that no man hates his flesh. For two contrary effects do not proceed from the same cause: “no spring can yield both salt water and fresh.”586

Objection. Many waste their bodies with fasts, vigils, labors, toils and the like. Others tear and gash their flesh with whips, knives, swords, and even with their teeth. Others lay such violent hands on themselves that they take away their own lives.

Answer. 1. None of these things are done by the instinct of nature which God has set in man, but through the corruption of nature which the devil has caused. Now nature and the corruption of nature are two contrary causes; no wonder, then, that contrary effects come from them.

2. They think they do these things in love to themselves: superstitious persons, to merit salvation by wasting their bodies; others, to free themselves from disgrace, poverty, slavery, torment or such evils. So there is an apparent good that makes them do it, and not simply hatred of themselves. Those who do so are either possessed with a devil, or blinded in their minds, or bereft of their wits, or overwhelmed with some passion, so that they do not know what they do. Therefore they do not do it in hatred.

2. Objection. Holy and wise men, deliberately and on good advice, have “beaten down their bodies,” and yielded their lives587 to be taken away, “refusing their release.”

Answer. That was far from hatred, and done in great love to themselves, as was shown588 before.

§. 63. Of unnatural practices against oneself.

The forenamed doctrine exposes many practices used589 by various men as being against nature, and in that respect most horrible and detestable.

1. The practice of the idolatrous Baalites, who, to move their idol to hear them, “cut themselves with knives and lances … until the blood gushed over them.”590 Not much unlike them are popish hermits, anchorites, flagellant monks, Grandimontenses, various sorts of Franciscans, and other friars. Of these591 some wear shirts of haircloth, some shirts of mail next to their bodies, some go barefoot, some whip themselves daily until blood follows, and some waste their bodies with lying hard, vigils, fasting, going on pilgrimage, etc.

2. The practice of gluttons, drunkards, unchaste and pleasure-loving persons, who, to satisfy their corrupt appetites, impair their health, bring diseases on themselves and shorten their days.

3. The practice of brawlers, who by quarrels cause their flesh to be wounded and their lives taken away. Among these may be reckoned those who bring themselves into great straits, distresses and dangers for the sake of gain, and those who by felony, treason and like evil deeds cast themselves on the sword of the magistrate.

4. The practice of those who give the reins to grief, fear, wrath and other like violent passions, so that by them they weaken their bodies and shorten their days.

5. The practice of self-murderers, who in this break the rule of love (“as yourself”)592 and end their days in a most horrible sin, depriving themselves of the time, place and means of repentance. So, whatever foolish excuse they make for their sin, little better can be thought of them than that they thrust their souls headlong into hell, unless the Lord, between the act done and their last breath, extraordinarily touches their hearts. Religion, nature, sense and all abhor this fearful deed. So not only those who have been enlightened593 by God’s word, but also the heathen, who had no other light than the light of nature, have judged it to be a most desperate sin.

§. 64. Of haters of others.

2. By the affection which nature moves men to bear to their own flesh, we may see how nature prevails more with men than conscience and obedience to God’s word, yes, more than the594 Spirit. For while nature keeps all men from hating their own flesh, nothing can keep many husbands from hating their wives, and wives their husbands; nor brothers, kinsmen and neighbors (yet these are “our own flesh”); no, nor many of those595 who profess themselves to be of the mystical body of Christ, from hating one another. What shall we say of these? Is nature of greater power, and more mighty in working, than the Spirit? Surely such men either deceive themselves and others in pretending to be members of the body of Christ, or else the Spirit is very weak in them, and the flesh bears great sway. Let haters of their brethren think on this and be ashamed.

§. 65. Of man’s care in providing and using things needful for his body.

The second evidence of the love which a man bears to himself is noted in two such branches (nourishes and cherishes) as comprise596 all needful things under them. So the apostle implies by them that

Nature teaches all men to provide such things as are needful for597 them: needful for life, as food, and needful for health, as clothing. Nature is set forth here as a schoolmaster to Christians; therefore what nature teaches is a bounden duty. Solomon insists much on it, who in this respect598 says, “It is good and fitting … to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does.”

If he who does not provide for his599 own is worse than an unbeliever, what is he who does not provide for himself? Even worse than a beast, for nature has taught the brute beasts to nourish and cherish themselves. If any think that this better befits beasts, or natural men, than saints, let them tell me which of the saints, guided by God’s Spirit, has at any time wholly neglected himself. To pass over all others, it is expressly noted of Christ that, as there was occasion, he600 slept, he601 ate, he602 rested, and otherwise refreshed himself.

Objection. Though he was603 hungry, and food was prepared for him, yet he refused to eat.

Answer. 1. Forgoing one meal is no great hindrance to604 cherishing the body.

2. Extraordinary and weighty occasions may lawfully make a man neglect himself a little, so that he may show that he prefers God’s glory and his brother’s salvation before the outward nourishing of his body. To this purpose Christ says, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me”; that is, I605 prefer it before my food. And Saint Paul says, “I will most606 gladly spend and be spent for the sake of your+ souls.” We must therefore take heed here of the extremes on both sides.

1. Of undue and excessive neglect of our bodies, so that their strength is wasted and their health impaired.

2. Of caring too much for them, so that on no occasion will we lose a meal or a night’s rest. Fasting and keeping vigil, as occasion requires, are bounden duties.

But to return to the point of nourishing and cherishing our flesh:

1. For this end God has provided food, clothing and all607 things needful for our weak bodies, that they should be nourished and cherished by them. Not to use them, therefore, is to refuse God’s providence.

2. When we nourish and cherish our bodies well, they are the better enabled to do the work and service which God appoints to be done; but when we neglect them, they are disabled for it. As this is a motive, so it ought to be an end at which we aim in nourishing and cherishing our bodies.

§. 66. Of those who neglect to cherish their bodies.

Many offend against this good instinct of nature.608

1. Covetous misers, who so dote on their wealth, and so609 delight in an abundance of goods stored up, that they do not allow themselves the things needful to nourish and cherish their bodies. Solomon rebukes such men much. Of them he says that there is “wealth610 hoarded to the harm of its owner.” Daily experience gives evidence of its truth. For besides making their riches611 snares and612 hindrances that keep them from eternal life, such men make this present life very irksome,613 filling their heads full of much gnawing care and keeping them from quiet rest. Many in this case are so besotted614 that, though they have abundance, they will not allow themselves in health a good meal or decent clothing, nor in sickness the medicine they need, no, nor a fire and such common things. Their case is worse than that of those who are in want: for others will pity and help such as are in want, but who will pity and help these?

2. Those who are too intent on their business, even the affairs615 of their lawful callings (for in good things there may be excess). Many students, preachers, lawyers, tradesmen, farmers, laborers and others offend in this, when they do not allow their bodies seasonable times of refreshment and rest, but fast, go without sleep and toil too much in their calling. Those who disable themselves by such means make themselves guilty of neglecting as much good as they might have done if they had nourished and cherished their bodies. Some are so eager in their business that they think all the time misspent which is spent in nourishing and cherishing their bodies, and so they wish that their bodies needed no food, sleep or other such means of refreshment. These thoughts and616 desires are foolish and sinful in many respects, as

1. In showing a secret discontent and grudging against God’s providence, for God has so ordered our condition for the clearer manifestation of man’s weakness and of God’s care over him.

2. In taking away occasions of calling on God and giving him praise. For if we did not stand in such need of God’s providence, would we pray to him so often for his blessing? If we did not feel the sweetness and comfort of his providence by the good means which he affords us, would we be so thankful to him?

3. In taking away the means of mutual love. For if, because of our weakness, we did not stand in need of help and relief from one another, what trial would there be of our love?

3. Those who sever these two duties of nature (nourishing and617 cherishing) and make them a hindrance to one another. Some so nourish their bodies that they cannot cherish them; that is, they spend so much on eating and drinking that they have nothing to clothe themselves with. Others so cherish them that they cannot nourish them; that is, they so deck themselves out in fine clothing beyond their means that they do not have sufficient food for themselves. These fall into two contrary extremes: into excess in one thing, and into defect in another.

§. 67. Of contentment with what is sufficient.

As the apostle, by naming these two (nourish, cherish), shows that both of them are needful, so by naming them only, and no more than them, he shows that these two are sufficient. From this we learn that

Having food and clothing, we must be content with these.618

The apostle lays down this doctrine in these very words in619 another place. The620 prayer of Agur and the tenor of the621 fourth petition prove as much.

Question. Is a man then strictly bound to care for no more than food to nourish him and clothing to cherish him?

Answer. Provided this nourishing and cherishing is extended to the condition in which God has set us, to the charge which God has given us, and to the calling which he has appointed for us, we ought to care for no more.

Let us therefore take heed of the excess which arises from the corruption of nature, and content ourselves with the sufficiency which nature requires.
