Christ’s Union with His Beloved Body

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 68–78

§. 68. Of Christ’s forbearing to hate the church.

Eph 5:29.

Just as the Lord does the church.

This confirmation of the pattern of a man’s self by a like pattern of the Lord relates to both parts of the showing of a man’s love to himself. It relates to the negative, and so it shows that the Lord does not hate his church.

And it relates to the affirmative, and so it shows that the Lord nourishes and cherishes his church.

The difference made between Esau, a type of the world (“Esau I have hated”),622 and Jacob, a type of the church (“Jacob I have loved”), shows that the Lord is far from hating his church. The world, not the church, is the object of God’s hatred.

Objection. The church herself623 and the enemies624 of the church often conclude from Christ’s dealings with her that he hates her.

Answer. It is the flesh remaining in those who are of the church that makes them think so, not the spirit; and in the enemies of the church the flesh reigns altogether. But the things of God, and his mind and feelings, neither can nor may be judged by carnal eyes, eyes of flesh. The Spirit of God625 counts as evidences of God’s love those things which the flesh judges to be tokens of hatred; namely, chastisements.

It is not because there is no matter for hatred in the church626 that Christ does not hate it. For by nature all are of one and the same cursed stock, “children of wrath”;627 and even after our sanctification has begun, the flesh remaining in us, we daily give much occasion for hatred, if Christ should take the advantage against us that he might. Rather, it is the near union which Christ has made between himself and the church that keeps him from hating her. He has made her his spouse, and he will not hate his spouse. All the occasion of hatred that she gives, he will either wipe away or cover.

Wonderful is the comfort which every true member of the universal church628 may reap from this. For so long as the wrath and hatred of the Lord is turned from us, nothing can make us miserable. In this respect we may rejoice not only in prosperity, but also in every kind of affliction. No calamity can move Christ to hate his church, but rather to pity it the more, as we do our own bodies. Indeed, though he is provoked by sin and sees it needful to correct his church, yet he will correct it in love, not in hatred; in mercy, not in wrath.

What now if all the world hates us? Seeing that Christ does not hate629 us, we need not fear or be anxious. The subject who is sure of his king’s favor pays little regard to the hatred of others. This therefore is to be thought on, both to comfort us under the cross and to encourage us against the hatred of the world. So that none may pervert this comforting doctrine, let me add two cautions.

1. That men do not deceive themselves with a bare name, thinking themselves to be of the church when they are only in it.630 Such Christ may hate.

2. That those who are of the church do not grow insolent and provoke Christ too much to anger. For though he does not hate such, yet in wisdom he may correct them as severely as if he hated them, and make them repent their folly and insolence again and again.

§. 69. Of Christ’s nourishing and cherishing his church.

2. That the Lord nourishes and cherishes his church is evident from his continual providence over her in all ages. When he first created man, he631 provided beforehand all things needful to nourish and cherish him. When he was moved to destroy the earth and all living things on it, he took care of his church: he provided an ark to keep her out of632 the waters, and stored up in the ark all things needful for her. When he purposed to bring a famine on the world, he sent a man beforehand to lay up provision for his church. When633 his church was in a barren and dry wilderness, he gave them bread from heaven and water out of the rock, and kept their clothing from wearing out and their feet from swelling.634 After this he brought his church into a land flowing with milk and honey, and so long as it remained faithful he preserved it in that pleasant and plentiful land. So he dealt with the church in her childhood; and so also has he dealt with her in her riper age under the gospel, as the experience of all ages may witness. Nor has he nourished and cherished her only with temporal blessings, but also with all needful spiritual blessings. His word and sacraments, his Spirit and the graces of the Spirit, he has given her in all ages for that purpose. Yes, he has fed her with his own flesh and blood,635 and clothed her with his own righteousness.636

Let us learn from whom we receive all needful things, both637 spiritual and temporal, for soul and body, so that accordingly638 we may give him the praise for all. And let us not be like the ungrateful Israelites, who639 disregarded the means of spiritual640 nourishment, and641 ascribed the means of their temporal nourishing and cherishing to their idols. In this respect the prophet makes them642 worse than the ox and the donkey, two of the most brutish beasts there are. Oh, let us take heed that the like is not cast up against us. The Lord has nourished and cherished us in this land not sparingly but most liberally and bountifully, and that with both temporal and spiritual blessings, so that he may justly say, “What more could I have done643 for My vineyard than I already did for it?”

Let us also learn to depend on Christ for all things that we644 lack. We need not fear poverty. Though we do not have the645 plenty we could wish, yet we will have sufficiency. Christ will not allow his church to famish for lack of food, nor freeze for lack of clothing, whether temporal for the body or spiritual for the soul. He who can and will perform it has said, “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.”646 Lazarus was not forsaken; witness the angels that carried his soul into Abraham’s647 bosom. If any of Christ’s church do perish for lack of outward means, it is because Christ by that means will advance them to that place where they will need nothing; so he does not forsake them.

§. 70. Of the union between Christ and the saints.

Eph 5:30.

For we are members of His body, of His flesh, and of His bones.

The reason for the love of Christ already named, and for its fruits648 toward his church, is laid down here, as both the causal particle (FOR) and the inference of this verse from the former show. This reason is the near union between Christ and his church, set forth by a metaphor of the members of our body. By this he implies that, though there were no other reason to move a husband to love his wife than the near union between them (they being649 one body,650 one flesh,651 one self), that would be enough; for by that alone is Christ moved to love his church.

The mystery of our spiritual union with Christ is laid down here, and as fully and distinctly (though very briefly)652 as in any place of Scripture. I will endeavor to explain it as plainly as I can.

We are. Here the apostle changes both person and number.653 For before, he spoke of the church as of another, in the third person, and as of one, in the singular number. But here he speaks of the same church in the first person, including himself, and in the plural number, including all others like himself (the elect of God, and saints by calling). By this he gives us to understand what he means by the church, namely the company of saints. To this company he associates and joins himself, though he was a preacher of the gospel, an extraordinary preacher, an apostle. By this he shows that he was made partaker of the same grace, and saved by the same means, as others were. Well might he not grudge to rank himself in this privilege, because it is the highest degree of honor that can be654 to be a member of the body of Christ: much more than to be a preacher, a prophet, an apostle, or of any other eminent calling.

The metaphor used here (members of his body) sets655 forth the near union between Christ and the saints. Many other metaphors are used in Scripture for the same purpose, such as foundation656 and building, vine657 and branches, husband658 and wife, and the like. All of them are very fit, but none is more proper and pertinent to the point than this of a body, with its head and members. What nearer union can there be than between the head and members of the same body?

If the apostle had stopped here, we might have thought that he meant nothing other than what he meant659 before, where he called Christ a head, and the church a body. But in adding (of his flesh and of his bones) he declares a further mystery still.

In general there is a difference between this phrase660 (OF his body) and these (OF his flesh;661 and OF his bones). The former is a sign of the662 genitive case; the two latter are a663 preposition. For distinction’s sake the two latter might have been translated out of his flesh, out of his bones, or from his flesh, from his bones (for a like phrase is so translated664 before, from whom). But seeing these particles out of or from are ambiguous, the former translation may stand as the best, provided a difference is made in the sense, though there is none in the words.

The former (members of his body) declares the union itself.

The latter (of his flesh and of his bones) declares the means665 of making that union. This latter relates to what Adam said of Eve, “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen 2:23). That is clear from the next verse, which the apostle takes out of the same place. It implies, then, that as Eve was made a woman out of Adam’s flesh and bones, so the church is made a church out of Christ’s flesh and bones.

1. Question. Was the very substance of the saints, their flesh and bones, taken out of Christ, as the substance of Eve was taken out of Adam?

Answer. Not so, if the words are taken literally. For in that sense Christ may rather be said to be of our flesh and of our bones, because he took our nature, and that from a daughter of Adam. In this respect he is said to be “of the seed of David,”666 and667 of the Jews, “according to the flesh.” Besides, the apostle expressly says (v. 32), “This is a great mystery.” The mystery therefore must be searched out. To this end Christ must be considered as another Adam (and so the Holy Spirit calls him “the last Adam,” “the second man”),668 that is, a stock, a root that gives a being to branches sprouting out of him.

2. Question. What being is it that we receive from Christ?669

Answer. Not our natural being (that we have from the parents of our flesh), but a supernatural and spiritual being, which the Scripture calls a new birth,670 a new man,671 a new creature.672 This spiritual being is not in regard of the substance of our soul or body, or of any of their powers or parts, faculties or members. For all these we have by lineal descent from Adam, and all sorts of men have all these, those who are not of the church as well as those who are of it. It is in regard of the integrity, goodness, and divine qualities which are in them,673 even that holiness and righteousness with which the church is endowed and adorned. As we are natural men we are of Adam; as we are spiritual men we are of Christ.

3. Question. Why is mention made of flesh and bones674 in this spiritual being?

Answer. 1. In allusion to the creation of Eve, so that by comparing this with that, this might be the better understood.

2. In regard of the Lord’s Supper, where the flesh of Christ is mystically set before us to be spiritual food for us. So that, as before (v. 26) he showed the mystery of one sacrament, baptism, here he might show the mystery of the other sacrament, the Lord’s Supper.

3. In relation to Christ’s human nature, by virtue of which we come to be united to Christ. For the divine nature of Christ is infinite, incomprehensible, incommunicable, and675 there is no proportion at all between it and us, so that we could not be united to it directly. But Christ, by taking his human nature into the unity of his divine nature, made himself one with us, and us one with him; so that by his partaking of our mortality, we are made partakers of his immortality.

4. Question. Are we then united only to his human nature?

Answer. No: we are united to his person, God-man. For as676 the divine nature, in and by itself, is incommunicable, so the human nature, considered singly, in and by itself, is unprofitable. The Deity is the fountain of all life and grace; the flesh does not give life. But that spiritual life which flows originally and primarily from the Deity, as from a fountain, is conveyed into us by the humanity of Christ, as by a conduit.

5. Question. How can we who are on earth be united to his677 human nature, which is contained in the highest heaven?

Answer. This union, being supernatural and spiritual, needs no local presence for the making of it. That eternal Spirit which is in Christ is conveyed into each of the saints (as the soul of a man is into every member and part of his body), and by virtue of that Spirit they are all made one with Christ, and with one another: “by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body,”678 which body is Christ.

This is to be noted against these two errors. The first is679 this: We are united first to the divine nature of Christ, which is everywhere, and by virtue of it to his human nature.

Answer. 1. The Deity (as we showed) cannot be imparted to us directly, so this cannot be.

2. Our union with Christ is spiritual, not physical or natural, so this local presence is not needed.

The second error is this:

The human nature of Christ has all the divine properties in it,680 so that it is present everywhere, and by reason of this we are united to Christ.

Answer. This also is impossible and needless. The properties of a true body cannot possibly admit the incommunicable properties of the Deity. That implies a direct contradiction, namely that the finite should be infinite. It is needless also, because the union we speak of is (as we said) spiritual.

6. Question. What kind of union is this spiritual union?681

Answer. A true, real union of our persons (bodies and souls) with the person of Christ (God and man). For as the Holy Spirit united the divine and human natures of Christ in the virgin’s womb, and made them one person, by reason of which Christ is of our flesh and of our bones, so the Spirit unites that person of Christ with our persons, by reason of which we are of his flesh, and of his bones. There is a great difference between the kinds of these unions. The union of Christ’s two natures is hypostatical and essential: they make one person. But the union of Christ’s person and ours is spiritual and mystical: they make one mystical body. Yet there is no difference in the reality and truth of these unions. Our union with Christ is not one bit less real and true because it is mystical and spiritual. Those who have the same Spirit are as truly one as those parts which have the same soul. The effects which proceed from this union show its truth. For the Spirit that sanctified Christ in his mother’s womb sanctifies us also; the Spirit that gave him life gives682 us life; the Spirit that raised him from death raises us; the Spirit that exalted him exalts us. The many resemblances which the Scripture uses to set forth this union show its truth. But it is set forth most vividly by the resemblance Christ makes between it and his union with his Father. “I pray” (he says of all his saints) “that all of them683 may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You. May they also be in Us … that they may be one as We are one.” This note of comparison (as) is to be taken not of the kind, but of the truth of these unions: our union with Christ is as true as Christ’s union with his Father.

So true is this union that not only Jesus himself, but all the684 saints who are members of this body, together with Jesus its head, are called CHRIST, 1 Cor 12:12. Gal 3:16.

This is to be noted against the fancy of those who imagine this union to be only in the imagination and fancy; or else only in agreement of spirit, heart, and will; or at most, in a sharing of spiritual graces.

7. Question. What is the bond by which this union is made,685 namely, by which Christ and the saints are made one?

Answer. There is a double bond. One is on Christ’s part, namely the Spirit of Christ (for “by this we know that we dwell in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit”). The other is on the saints’ part, namely faith (for “Christ dwells in our hearts through faith”).686 The Spirit is conveyed into us when we are dead in sins, wholly flesh; but being in us, the Spirit breeds this blessed instrument of faith, by which we lay hold on Christ and grow into him as the graft into the stock. So, Christ laying hold on us by his Spirit, and we on him by faith, we come to be incorporated into him and made one body, as the graft and the stock are one tree.

8. Question. To what end has Christ so truly and closely687 united us to himself?

Answer. Not for any benefit to himself, but purely for the honor and good of the church. By this union the honor of Christ is imparted to the church, as the honor of a husband to his wife, and of a head to the body. Great also is the benefit which the church reaps by it. For by this means Christ is made more fit to do good to the church, as a head to the body; and the church is made more capable of receiving good from Christ, as a body from the head, being knit to it by the soul, and by veins, sinews, nerves, arteries, and other such ligaments.

Having thus laid open this great mystery by questions and answers as plainly as I can, I will further point out some of the excellent privileges which belong to the saints by virtue of it, and also some of the principal duties to which the saints are bound in regard of it.

§. 71. Of the privileges belonging to the saints even in this life because of their union with Christ.

The privileges of the saints which arise from their union with Christ concern this life, the time of death, and the life to come.

In this life, these:

1. A most glorious condition, which is to be a part of Christ, a688 member of his body. All the glory of Adam in paradise, or of the angels in heaven, is not comparable to this. In this respect the saints are said to be “crowned with glory and honor,” and to have all things put under their feet. Compare Ps 8:4, 5, etc. with Hebrews 2:6, 7, etc., and you+ will find the apostle apply to Christ what the prophet spoke generally of man. Now those two places cannot be better reconciled than by689 this union of Christ and the saints. For seeing both make one body, which is Christ, what is spoken of the body may be applied to the head, and what is spoken of the head may be applied to the body; for the same honor belongs to both. In this respect the church is more honorable than heaven, the angels, and every other creature.

2. The attendance of good angels, who are “sent to serve690 those who will be heirs of salvation,”691 because those heirs are of the body of Christ, who is their Lord. These are the “horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha”; and they are also round about every one of God’s saints in all their distresses, though we see them no more than the servant of the man of God saw them, till the Lord opened his eyes. That charge which is given to the angels over the Son of God, “to guard him in all his ways,” and “to lift him up in their hands, so that he692 will not strike his foot against a stone,” relates to this body which is Christ.

3. An honor to make Christ himself complete: for as the individual693 members make a natural body complete, so the individual saints make complete this body which is Christ. In this respect the church is said to be “the fullness of Him who fills all in all.”694 Christ fills all things, and yet the church makes him full. This is to be understood of that voluntary condition to which Christ subjected himself, to be the head of a body; so that without the parts of the body he is incomplete, as a natural body is maimed and incomplete if it lacks even the least of its members. How can we now think anything but that he will preserve and keep safe all his saints? Will he restore to us all the parts of our natural body at the general resurrection, and will he lose any of the parts of his own mystical body?

4. A kind of possession of heaven while we are on earth. For695 what the head has possession of, the body and its individual members also have possession of. In this respect it is said, “God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the696 heavenly realms.” And, “whoever … believes Him who sent Me has eternal697 life … he has crossed over from death to life.” And, “Whoever has the Son698 has life.” This is something more than hope; and it serves greatly to strengthen our hope, and to give us assurance of that heavenly inheritance.

They know neither the power of God nor the force of this union who deny that the saints have assurance of salvation. For (to follow this metaphor a little) suppose a man were cast into a river, and his head were able to lift and keep itself above water: would we not say that the man is safe enough, he is above water? This is the case of this mystical body. It is cast into the sea of this world, but Christ its head has lifted himself up and keeps himself aloft, even in heaven. Is there now any fear, any possibility, of the drowning of this body, or of any member of it? If any should be drowned, then either Christ must be drowned, or else that member must be pulled from Christ; both of which are impossible. So by virtue of this union we see how our safety depends on Christ’s safety: if he is safe, so are we; if we perish, so must he.

In this respect, “you+ may be secure, O flesh and blood: you+ have699 gained heaven in Christ. Those who deny heaven to you+ may also deny that Christ is in heaven.”

Learn here how to think of the resurrection, ascension, and safety of Christ: as of the resurrection, ascension, and safety of a head, in and with whom his body and all his members are raised, exalted, and preserved.

5. A most happy kind of government under which the saints are: even such as the members of a head are under. A head rules the body not as a cruel lord and tyrant, harshly,700 inhumanly, basely, and slavishly, but meekly, gently, with great compassion and fellow feeling. Even so does Christ rule his church, binding up what is broken, healing what is maimed, directing what wanders, and stirring up what is dull. This privilege is all the greater because it belongs to the church alone. Though he has a golden scepter of grace and favor to hold out to his church (as Ahasuerus held out his to Esther),701 yet he has also “an iron scepter” to “break” the men of this world, and to “shatter them702 like pottery.” Though he has gone to prepare a place for his saints, so that where he is they may be also,703 yet he will “make his enemies his footstool.”704

6. An assurance of sufficient supply of all needful things which705 the saints lack, and of safe protection from all things hurtful. For by reason of this union, Christ our head has a sense of our need and of our pain. On this ground he said to those who fed and visited his members, “You+ gave Me something to eat … you+ visited Me”;706 and again, to Saul, who persecuted his members, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?”

Objection. How is it, then, that the saints lack many things,707 and often suffer much pain and hurt?

Answer. Christ in his wisdom sees it needful that they should lack and feel pain (and of this we are to be persuaded), or else he would not allow them to lack or to feel what they do. Therefore in all need, in every distress and danger, let us lift up our head to this our head.

7. A right to all that Adam lost. For Christ is the “heir of all708 things”709 (“the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof”)710 indeed, as mediator and head of the church he is heir of all. His body therefore has a right to all. On this ground the apostle says, “All things are yours.”711 So the saints, and only the saints, can with a good conscience use the things of this world. Those who are not of this body (whatever right and title they have before men) are only usurpers of the things they enjoy and use. They are like bankrupts who, not being worth one penny, deceitfully borrow from others, and with it keep a great table, deck and furnish their houses very lavishly, put themselves, their wives and children into fine clothes, and are merry and riotous. What is likely to be the end of such men?

8. A right to more than Adam ever had: namely, to Christ712 himself, and to all that belongs to him: to the purity of his nature, the perfection of his obedience, the merit of his blood, the power of his death, the force of his resurrection, the efficacy of his ascension. All is ours, even as the understanding, intelligence, judgment, sight, hearing, and all that is in the head belongs to the body. If the church itself were, of itself, as pure in nature, as perfect in righteousness, as powerful over death and devil and grave and hell, as able to rise from death and to ascend into heaven as Christ, it could receive no greater benefit by this than it does by these things in the person of Christ. So truly and properly are Christ himself, and all things belonging to him, the church’s. What more can be said? What more can be desired? O blessed union! Blessed are those who have a part in it!

Question. How is it, then, that the church is so basely and miserably713 regarded in the world?

Answer. “The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him.” It does not know Christ, the head of this body; it does not know the body, which is Christ. Let us, who know both head and body, the near union between them, and the privileges which follow from it, not be daunted either by the scoffs and scorns of the world or by our own outward weaknesses, needs, and calamities. What more would he who has Christ have?

§. 72. Of the privilege of our union with Christ in the time of death.

The privilege which the saints receive by their union with Christ in the time of death (that is, all the time that passes from the departure of the saints out of this world until the general resurrection) is wonderful. For when body and soul are severed from one another, neither soul nor body is separated from Christ, but both remain united to him; even as, when Christ’s body and soul were severed from one another by death, neither his soul nor his body was separated from the Deity, but both remained united to it. This inviolable bond, which holds the saints (yes, even their very bodies as well as their souls) united to Christ in death, is the benefit of a spiritual union. If our union with Christ were bodily, it could not be so.

Objection. Is it possible that the body which is dead should remain714 united to Christ, when it receives no power from him?

Answer. 1. If a member of a natural body may do so, why not a member of the mystical body? That a member of a natural body may do so is evident from those who have a hand, arm, foot, leg, or any other member struck with a dead palsy. They are at times so struck that those parts receive no sense at all, nor any vigor or life from head or heart; and yet they remain true members of that body.

2. The very dead bodies, consumed by worms or otherwise, do receive a great present benefit from their union with Christ. For by virtue of it a substance is preserved, and they are kept from destruction. Nothing is destroyed in the saints by death but that which, if it were not destroyed, would make them most miserable, namely sin. That is utterly, totally, finally destroyed in them, together with all that goes with it, which is every kind of infirmity. But the rotting of the body is only like the rotting of grain in the earth,715 so that it may rise a more glorious body. The metaphor of sleep,716 applied to the saints when they die, shows that their bodies are not utterly destroyed.

Objection. The bodies of all men, even of those who are not717 of this union, are preserved from utter destruction. This therefore is no benefit of our union with Christ.

Answer. Though in the general thing itself, which is a preservation of the substance of the body, the same thing befalls the saints and the wicked, yet the means by which both are preserved, and the end for which they are preserved, are far different.

1. The saints are preserved by a secret influence proceeding718 from Christ as a head. In this respect they are said to have “fallen asleep in Him,” and to be “the dead in Christ.” But the wicked are reserved by an almighty power of Christ, as a terrible Lord and severe Judge.

2. The bodies of the saints are preserved to enjoy eternal glory together with their souls; but the bodies of the wicked are reserved to be tormented in hell.

Because of these differences, the grave is like a bed to the saints,719 in which they may sleep quietly, free from all disturbance, till the day of resurrection. But it is a prison to the wicked, to hold them fast until the great day of trial, so that on Judgment Day they may be brought to appear at the bar of God’s judgment seat, and there receive the sentence of condemnation.

§. 73. Of the privilege of our union with Christ after death.

The privilege which the saints receive after death by virtue of their union with Christ far surpasses all before. It may be brought under two heads.

  1. Their resurrection.
  2. Their glory in heaven.

What was said before of the difference between the preservation of the bodies of the saints and of the wicked in death may be applied to the difference of their resurrection.

Resurrection simply in itself is not the privilege of the saints, but “the resurrection of life”: to the wicked belongs the720 “resurrection of condemnation.” The benefit of resurrection arises from the glory which follows it in heaven. The apostle has excellently set forth that glory721 before, in v. 27.

§. 74. Of the duties required of the saints by virtue of their union with Christ.

As the mystery of our union with Christ is a matter of great comfort and encouragement (which arises from the privileges already named), so it is also a matter of direction and incitement to us for the performing of various duties. Those who desire assurance of these privileges, and comfort by them, must be diligent and conscientious in these duties. Some of the most principal of them are these.

1. Confidence in Christ. Christ being our head,722 so mighty, so wise, so tender, in every way so sufficient a head as he is, we would greatly dishonor him if we did not rest ourselves wholly and only on him for every good thing, and against every evil.

2. Subjection corresponding to his manner of governing us.723 The world is subject to Christ by force, as he is an absolute and almighty Lord. But since he governs us as a head, we must be subject to him as members, willingly and readily. What member will rise up and rebel against the head? Indeed, what member is not as ready to obey as the head is to command?724

3. A cleansing of ourselves from all filthiness of flesh and725 spirit. Shall we defile the members of Christ?726 The sins of the saints are in this respect the more heinous, because that body, even Christ, of which they are members, is defiled by them. Therefore, in regard of Christ the head, of the other saints their fellow members, and of themselves, all who profess themselves to be of this body must be watchful over themselves and cleanse themselves from all filthiness. Otherwise they give just occasion to think that they are no members of this body. If a lion’s foot or a bear’s paw were held out and said to be the member of a man, would anyone believe it? Can we then think that worldlings, drunkards, the profane, riotous and unclean persons, and such limbs of the devil are members of Christ?

4. A conformity to the image of Christ in true holiness727 and righteousness. It is not enough, therefore, for the members of Christ to abstain from polluting themselves, for they are “created in Christ Jesus to do good works.”728 “The one who remains in Me” (says Christ) “and I in him, will bear much fruit.”729

5. Heavenly affections. “Since you+ have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of730 God. Set your+ affections on things above, not on earthly things.” Where our head is, there also our heart ought to be. Earthly affections do not come from that head which is in heaven, nor from that Spirit which proceeds from him. “Those who731 live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit.”

6. Courage against death: seeing that in death we are Christ’s, what cause have we to fear death? “Do not be afraid of732 those who kill the body and after that can do no more.” The ancient worthies “refused their release, so that733 they might gain a better resurrection.”

So much for the union itself. The means of bringing it about remain to be handled.

§. 75. Of the regeneration of those who are members of Christ.

Eph 5:30.

—Of His flesh, and of His bones.

This clause declares the means by which we come to be members of Christ, namely by receiving a new being from Christ: to be not of the flesh and of the bones of Adam, but of the flesh and of the bones of Christ. Taken spiritually, as has been expounded734 before, this shows that

Those who are true members of Christ’s body are truly regenerate.735 “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature.” The apostle lays down these words736 so that they serve both as a demonstration and as an exhortation (he is, or let him be, a new creature): neither is expressed, but either, or both, may be understood. “All of you+ who were baptized into Christ”737 (that is, made members of this body) “have clothed yourselves+ with Christ” (that is, have been born again). The first branch points out our incorporation into Christ, the latter our regeneration.

This second man and last Adam, Christ Jesus, is “a life-giving738 spirit.”739 He diffuses life and grace into all his members. If his Spirit is in us, it will give life to our mortal bodies. If the head of our natural bodies conveys sense into all our members, and if the root of a tree diffuses sap into all the branches, shall not Christ much more give life to all his members?

This, then, is a test by which we may find out whether740 we are indeed of this body or not, and so have a true right741 to the privileges already named. Many boast of this honor, that they are members of Christ’s body, and yet they are not of his flesh and of his bones: they have no other being than what they received from their parents. These vain professing Christians are like wooden legs or arms on a man, which may be covered over with stockings and sleeves for a time, but will not be raised at the resurrection with the other parts of the man’s body. So neither will those professing Christians be raised to glory with Christ, though they may be covered over with the hose and sleeves of profession, and so seem to be members.

§. 76. Of Christ, the author of our regeneration.

This relative particle (HIS), twice repeated (of HIS flesh,742 and of HIS bones), shows that

Regeneration is from Christ.743 “The Son gives life to whom He wishes.”744

Objection. This work is attributed in Scripture to the745 Father, to the746 Spirit, to the747 word, and to the748 ministers of the word.

Answer. Christ’s part may very well stand with all these. The three persons in the Trinity are all one: one in nature and essence,749 one in will and consent, one in virtue and power; what the one does, the other does also. Yet because there is a difference in their manner of working, this work (like other works) is distinctly attributed to each of them.

The Father is (if I may so speak) the beginner of this work. It was his will that his Son should be the head of a body, and that members should be made fit for that head and have a new being (“He chose to give us birth”);750 for this end he sent his Son into the world to be made flesh. The Son carried out the will of his Father: he took flesh upon him, so that we might be of his flesh. So Christ says of himself, “I have come down from heaven … to do the will of Him who751 sent Me. And this is the will of Him who sent Me, that I shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day.” The Spirit applies to us the power and efficacy of the flesh of Christ, and so finishes this blessed work. “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing,”752 namely, of itself, without the Spirit.

So we see that ascribing this work of regeneration to Christ does not exclude the work of the Father, or of the Holy Spirit, in it, but it does exclude the work of man. It is not of ourselves, nor of our parents, nor of any other man. For we are born “not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but … of God”;753 in which respect our new birth is said to be754 from above.

Objection. How then is it attributed to the word, and to the755 ministry of man?756

Answer. As to instruments which the Lord is pleased to use. Of the word it is said that God has given us birth by the word.757 Of himself, a minister, the apostle says, “in Christ Jesus I became your+ father.”758 So God and Christ are joined with these instruments, or else they are not at all powerful and effectual for so great a work. For “neither he who plants nor he who waters is759 anything, but only God, who makes things grow.”

The work of regeneration is a new creation, a divine760 work, beyond human power. It must therefore be worked by the Lord, or it cannot be worked at all.

This is to be noted both by those who do not yet have assurance761 of this blessed work done in them, and also by those who have assurance of it.

The former may learn here where to turn for it: namely, to him who came down from heaven for that purpose, and who says, “The one who comes to Me I will never762 drive away.” In all the means that we use, let us look up to him and seek a blessing from him.

The latter must, with the tenth leper, return to763 Christ and glorify God. Whatever the means were, or whoever the minister was, the praise and glory of all must be given to him.

§. 77. Of Christ, the matter of our regeneration.

The preposition (OF), set down twice (OF his flesh, and764 OF his bones), being a proper sign of the material cause, shows that

Christ is not only the author, but also the matter of our new birth. The new spiritual being which the saints have comes out of him.765 “From Him the whole body, supported …, grows as God causes it to grow.” In this respect we are said to be766 blessed with every spiritual blessing in Christ. The metaphor of a vine,767 which Christ takes to himself, also proves as much; and so do these phrases, “My flesh is real food, and My blood is real drink.”768

Christ comes to be this by his incarnation. God in himself is like a bottomless and closed fountain:769 from him directly we can receive nothing. But Christ made flesh is “a fountain opened.”770 “God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him.”771 “From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace.”772

Behold here the benefit of Christ’s incarnation. By his taking773 part of our mortal flesh, we are made partakers of his spiritual flesh, namely of that spiritual life and grace which comes from him who was made flesh to convey it into us. To strengthen our faith in this the more firmly, the Lord has instituted the holy communion of his body and blood. With what conscience, reverence, and confidence ought this blessed sacrament to be celebrated?

By this doctrine we may further learn how to seek every774 thing from God’s hands which we desire to obtain, and how to offer that sacrifice of praise to God775 which we would have776 accepted: namely, in and through Jesus Christ, by whom alone we have all the communion which we have with God.777 Rightly therefore does the church conclude all her forms of prayers and praises with this, or some similar clause, “through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

§. 78. Of the excellence of regeneration.

The particular matter of our regeneration expressed here (the flesh and bones of Christ) shows that

Regeneration is a most excellent work. Its excellence778 will appear the better if we compare it with the great and glorious work of our creation, and show how far it surpasses it. In this I will hold close to this metaphor, and touch779 no other differences than those it points out to us.

1. In our creation Christ was only a worker; but he is the very matter of our regeneration: we are of his flesh.

2. The relation between Christ and man then was that of Creator and creature; but here it is head and body. “We are members of His body.”

The bond is now much nearer.

3. The being which we had then was from Adam; but the being which we have now is from Christ, of HIS flesh.

4. That being was only natural; this is spiritual. For “spirit is born780 of the Spirit.”

5. Then our being was different from Christ’s; but now it is the very same as Christ’s, of his flesh.

6. Then man might fall clean away from the condition in which he was created (as he did), and yet Christ remain as he was. Now it cannot be so. For if any of the saints should now fall away, either Christ must fall with them, or they must be pulled from Christ, and so Christ remain a maimed body.

Behold the riches of God’s mercy. One might think it781 enough, and more than man could ever have been thankful enough for, that God at first created man after his own image in a most happy condition. When we knowingly and willfully fell from it, God might justly have left us, as he did the evil angels. But he has not only restored us again to that former condition, but advanced us to a far more excellent and glorious one; in which his goodness appears to be, like his greatness, infinite and incomprehensible. Who can sufficiently set it forth? “For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great782 is His mercy for those who fear Him.”

The Ancient Law and Unique Bond of Marriage

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 79–89

§. 79. Of the ancient law of marriage.

Eph 5:31.

For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will be one flesh.

The same points that were laid down before, concerning the near union of man and wife and of Christ and the church, are here further confirmed by the ancient law of marriage. The apostle mentions it all the more because it follows on the text to which he alluded in the previous verse. For when Moses had recorded these words of Adam concerning Eve, “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,”783 he adds this law: “For this reason a man will leave his father,” etc. In this place these words have both a literal and a mystical sense: a literal sense of man and wife, a mystical sense of Christ and the church. The main thing the apostle aims at is to784 show how closely man and wife are linked together, so that they may be moved all the more to perform the mutual duties, and the duties proper to each, which they owe one another. But he had set before husbands and wives the examples of Christ and the church, as patterns and motives to do their duty. So he applies what was first spoken of man and wife to Christ and his church, to show that since there is so fit a likeness between these two couples, the pattern set before them is all the more to the purpose, and the reason drawn from it all the more forcible.

Because explaining the literal sense will give great light to the mystery, I will first handle this text according to the meaning of the letter.

The first clause (for this reason) implies a necessary connection785 with what went before. The near union of man and wife, as well as of Christ and his church, was noted before. A wife was said to be as the body786 of a man, indeed as himself. Adam787 called her his flesh and bones. From this both Moses and Paul draw the inference, “Therefore,” or, “For this reason a man will leave father.” Because man and wife are so near by God’s institution, they must also be most dear to each other in their mutual affection.

The man (meaning a husband) is mentioned here in particular,788 because when this law was first made, the woman was brought to him to see how he would like her. Having set his affection on her, he was to be bound by this law to continue that good liking toward her. He is also mentioned because of the preeminence which a man has above his wife. Yet the man is not the only one bound by it; the wife is bound too. The nature and rule of a relation require as much: if a man must hold fast to his wife inseparably, the wife must likewise hold fast to her husband.

These words (will leave father and mother) are not to be taken generally, of all duties, as if children owed no duty to their parents after they are married. Nor are they to be taken simply, as if parents were really to be utterly forsaken. They are meant:

1. Of the daily service which children under their parents’ government give them, seeking to please them in all things. When children are married, their daily attendance must be on their wives or husbands,789 taking care how to please them.

2. Of setting up a new family. For this purpose their parents’ house must be left, and the husband and wife must live together.

3. Of the distinction to be made between parents and wife or husband. Suppose some unavoidable occasion should arise in which a man must leave either his parent or his wife: for instance, his parent and his wife are both dying, in places so far apart that the husband cannot possibly be with both, and yet both urgently want him with them. By this law he must leave his parent and hold fast to his wife.

By this, then, the bond of marriage is declared to be the most inviolable bond there can be. For all men know that the bond between parent and child is a firm and inviolable bond. But the bond between husband and wife is more firm and inviolable.

To set forth the firmness of the marriage bond he adds this emphatic phrase, be joined (or, as the word properly means according to its root, be glued)790 to his wife. Things that are well glued together are as fast, firm and close as if they were one whole piece. Indeed, we see by experience that a table will often split in the solid wood before it will come apart where it is glued. So a husband ought to be as firm to his wife as to himself, and she to him.

This fits well with what follows (the two will be one flesh). Our English cannot well express the Greek791 word for word in good sense (word for word it is the two shall be into, or in, one flesh). The meaning is this: those who were two before marriage are brought into one flesh by the bond of marriage, to be just as one flesh, as closely united as the parts of the same body and the same flesh. This unity is not in respect of the bodily union of the two (for once they are married they are one flesh,792 even if they never know one another). Nor is it in respect of procreation, because one child comes from them both (for even if they never have a child, they are still one flesh). It is in respect of God’s institution, who has laid it down for a law, and as another nature, that man and wife should be this near to one another. Their consent in marriage (by virtue of God’s institution) makes them one flesh.

Our English rightly brings out the emphasis of the original in this word THE (the two). It shows that the bond793 of marriage knits only two together: one man and one woman, and no more.

This law sets forth the union between man and wife.794

In it three things are noted concerning the state of marriage.

1. Its preeminence (a man will leave his father and mother).

2. Its firmness (and be joined to his wife).

3. Its nearness (the two will be one flesh).

§. 80. Of preferring husband or wife to parents.

The first point shows that

A wife or a husband must be preferred before parents. The795 examples of Leah796 and Rachel, and of Michal797 too, are commendable in this respect.

1. The bond of marriage is more ancient, more firm and more798 near. There were husband and wife before there were parent and child. And there is a time when parents and children may part from one another, even while both are living. But there is no time in which man and wife may part from each other until death parts them. And children, though they come from the flesh of their parents, are yet made two (so that of one come two). But husbands and wives, though they were two before, are yet made one (so that of two comes one).

What wrong, then, do those parents do to their children who799 keep them under such strict subjection, even after they are married,800 that they cannot freely do the duty they ought to their husband or their wife! This goes beyond what a parent’s authority reaches to. Yet many think that their children owe them as much service after they are married as before. This is directly against this law.

The wrong is greater, and the practice more sinful, of801 those who keep their children from their husbands or their wives. “The match,” they say, “has turned out much worse than we expected.” But this should have been looked into more carefully beforehand. After marriage it is too late to seek such a remedy.

On the other side, there are many children who so regard802 their parents that they neglect their husband or their wife. Some husbands will give what they can to their parents and keep their wives very bare, letting them go without necessities. They do not care how they vex and grieve their wives, so long as they please their parents. Some wives also will secretly steal from their husbands to give to their parents.

Others can never stay away from their parents’ houses, but go there as often as they can. To show how unfitting this was, the ancient Romans had a custom of covering the bride’s face with a yellow veil. As soon as she was out of her father’s house they turned her round and round, and so carried her to her husband’s house, so that she would not know the way back to her father’s house. All such pretenses of love to parents are more perverse than pious, and in such people natural affection has more sway than true religion. Their pretense of piety toward parents is no just excuse for the injury they do to husband or wife.

§. 81. Of the firmness of the matrimonial bond.

The second point, concerning the firmness of the marriage knot, in these words (and be joined to his wife), yields two doctrines.

1. Man and wife must keep company together by continual803 cohabitation. For this end they leave their parents’ family and set up a new family.

2. Man and wife are joined together by an inviolable bond. It804 must never be cut apart until death cuts it. Body and soul must be separated from one another before husband and wife are.

Be careful, therefore, to preserve this indissoluble knot. And live together in such a way that you+ may live together with comfort, because you+ must not part.

§. 82. Of only two being joined together in marriage.

The third point, concerning the nearness of man and wife, in these words (the two will be one flesh), yields two more doctrines.

1. Marriage can be only between two, one man and one woman. For it is impossible that more than two should be joined together as nearly and firmly as man and wife are. Almost every word in this law proves this doctrine. For it says a man, not men; to a wife, not to wives; to his wife, not to another man’s wife; two, not more than two; the two, not any two; one flesh, not many fleshes.

Objection. This word (two) is not in the law as Moses records805 it.

Answer. It is necessarily implied there, for at that time there were only two in the world. God, speaking of them then, means only two. The same Spirit who guided Moses guided the806 evangelists and the807 apostles too. So, since they put in this word (two), it is certain that Moses intended it, just as with the word (only) which Christ puts into this text: “serve Him only.”808

Question. Why did God at first make only one man and one woman?

Answer. The809 prophet answers: “Because He seeks godly offspring.”

If, therefore, there are more than two, the offspring that comes from it is an adulterous offspring.

§. 83. Of polygamy and bigamy.

Can polygamy (having many wives) or bigamy (having two wives at once) have any good warrant against so express a law? Are not both of them against the first institution of marriage, so that we may say, “It was not this way from the beginning”?810 Are they not also against811 other particular laws? Lamech,812 one of Cain’s cursed line, was the first we read of who presumed to go against that ancient law.

Objection. Afterward many patriarchs and other saints took that liberty for themselves.

Answer. It was their sin, and a great blemish in them. The common error of the time, and their insatiable desire for many children, made them fall into it. Many troubles followed from it. Nor can anyone think otherwise than that much harm must follow from having more wives than one. For whereas God at first made a wife to be a help to man, two or more wives cannot but be a great grief and vexation to him because of the rivalry between them. Through Hagar Sarah was stirred up against Abraham, and Abraham was grieved at Sarah’s words. Though Leah and Rachel were sisters, their rivalry was great. The same is noted of Peninnah and many others.

Considering how heinous this sin is, our laws813 have justly made it a felony for a man to have more wives than one, or a woman more husbands.

§. 84. Of the close union of man and wife.

2. Husband and wife are the nearest of all to one another.814 Every clause in the law named above proves as much.

1. Parents must be left for a wife. Who are nearer than parent and child? If man and wife are nearer than the nearest, then they are the nearest of all.

2. A man is glued to his wife. This metaphor sets forth the nearness of a thing as well as its firmness, for things glued together are as one whole thing.

3. Man and wife are one flesh. Many from one are made two, but no two are made one so nearly and truly as man and wife.

Things are to be reckoned as near and as united as God has set them.815 But God has knit man and wife together this nearly, and made them one flesh. “What816 God has joined together,” says Christ of man and wife. In this respect the marriage union is called “the covenant817 of her God.” So this covenant cannot be released by anyone, no, not by the mutual consent of man and wife (“What God has joined together, let man not separate”). Yet many other covenants made between one party and another may be released and annulled by the mutual consent of both parties.

1. This shows that the transgressions of man and wife818 against one another are the most heinous of all, more than those of819 a friend, companion, brother, child, parent or anyone else. Who would not cry shame on the child who hates his parent, or shame on the parent who hates his child? The heathen and savages would not think them worthy of human society. What then may be thought of the man who hates his wife, or the wife who hates her husband? Apply this to all other transgressions, and note well how “the Lord has been a witness” to them.820

2. This also shows what a monstrous thing it is to sow821 any seeds of discord, and stir up strife between man and wife. Those who do it are the devil’s instruments in it, and a devilish spirit is in them. For Satan labors most to undo those knots which the Lord ties most firmly. Children of different mothers, and the separate friends of each party, are much at fault in this. “May they be cursed in the presence of the Lord,” every one of them.

3. This822 near conjunction between man and wife is a great823 motive to stir them both up to perform cheerfully all the duties which God requires of either of them. For by doing them they do their duty and show kindness to their own flesh. No man may turn away from his own flesh in the wider sense; that is, no man may neglect any duty of mercy or justice to his neighbor who is of the same stock as he is. Shall a husband or wife, then, turn away from one another, who are one flesh in the nearest respect that can possibly be? Not because they come from one flesh, but because they come824 into one flesh.

So much for the literal sense of this verse.

The mystical sense follows.

§. 85. Of the marriage union of Christ and the church.

The ancient marriage law named above is here applied mystically825 to Christ and the church. This is evident from the next verse, where the apostle, referring to this verse, says, “This is a great mystery.” There is, then, a mystery contained in it. But of what, or of whom, is that mystery? The apostle himself answers in these words: “I am speaking about Christ and the church.”

The mystery in general is this:

Christ and the church are to one another as husband and wife.

The particulars of this mystery are these.

The matrimonial conjunction between Christ and the church is a most preeminent, firm and near conjunction.

First, of the general.

The many titles of betrothal and marriage which Scripture gives to Christ and the church in their relation to one another clearly show that they are joined together by the honorable, inseparable and inviolable bond of marriage. He is called a bridegroom,826 she a bride; he the beloved,827 she his love; he a husband,828 she a wife; he a head,829 she the body; both one flesh.830

2. All the things required to join man and wife together fitly come together between Christ and the church.

1. They are persons fit to be joined. Though Christ is831 God, yet for832 this end he became man. And though the church was impure, yet for this end she is cleansed and sanctified.

2. They have their parents’ consent, for God is the833 common Father of both. And God has given834 Christ to the church, and the835 church to Christ.

3. They have given their836 mutual consent to each other.

4. He837 bears a husband’s affection toward her, and she is willing to yield a wife’s subjection to him.

5. He has838 given her many favors and gifts as pledges of his love. And she, in testimony of her faithfulness, was circumcised under the law and is baptized under the gospel, and binds herself with all the sacred bonds and covenants which God has sanctified for that purpose.

6. He has prepared839 dwelling places for them both together, and840 she earnestly desires to be with him.

Here is another evidence of Christ’s wonderful love to the841 church, and of the near union between Christ and her. The842 former was that she was his body; this, that she is his wife. The church might well say, as Abigail did, “Here is your maidservant, ready to serve and to wash the feet of my843 lord’s servants,” and, as the prodigal son did, “Make me like one of your hired844 servants,” or, as the Baptist did: “… the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and845 untie.” What a favor it is, then, to be made his spouse, his wife, his queen! Great was the favor which Ahasuerus showed to Esther when he made her his wife. He was a great monarch, who reigned “over 127 provinces from India to Cush,” but Esther was a poor orphan and a captive. Yet this favor was not comparable to Christ’s. For there was no such disparity and inequality between Ahasuerus and Esther as between Christ and the church. Nor is Esther’s advancement to be compared with the church’s. And yet there was some cause in Esther to move Ahasuerus to do what he did, for she was very beautiful and lovely, and worthy to be loved. But846 in the church, when Christ first set his love on her, there was no such thing. No example of love can be given that is in any way comparable to this.

Let the church, therefore, and all who profess themselves847 to be of the church, take such notice of this that they may endeavor848 to conduct themselves worthily of this honor and advancement. They must not grow proud and insolent because of it, but must despise all vain and worldly trifles. They must answer love with love, as the church is set forth in Solomon’s Song; be subject to her husband, reverence and obey him, and perform all the duties belonging to such a wife; and seek by all good means to maintain the honor of her place. The church is made a pattern of duty to all wives. If she should fail, greater harm would follow from it than from Vashti’s849 disobedience.

This is all the more to be heeded because it is not only a850 matter of instruction but also of trial. It shows both what those851 who are of the church ought to do and852 what in fact they will do. Therefore no profane person who thinks lightly of the Lord Jesus, no idolater who sets his love on other husbands, no swearer or blasphemer who dishonors the great name of Jesus, none who are in any way rebellious against him, and none who hate, scorn, scoff at or hurt any of his members, can have any comfort in this advancement of the church, because they have no part in it, nor right to it.

But great is the comfort which the true saints may receive853 from it. For by virtue of this matrimonial bond,854

1. Christ is made a yokefellow with his church, and her companion. Under all the burdens laid on her he puts his shoulder, to make them the easier. Indeed, he has so taken on himself the great burdens of God’s wrath, the curse of the law, and sin, the cause of it, that he has completely freed his church from them, because otherwise they would have crushed her down to hell.

2. Christ is as her champion, to answer all challenges sent to her; as her advocate, to plead against and answer all the complaints that will be made against her; and as her surety, to discharge all her debts. The church being under Christ’s covering, as a wife is under her husband’s in law, so that he answers for her, he is as her very self, all in all for her and to her.

3. All his honors, goods and privileges are hers. She has855 a right to them, and her share in them. She is a co-heir with him (Rom 8:17), a queen because he is a king (Ps 45:9), and all glorious, as was noted on v. 27.

4. He will surely perform all the duties of a husband: to love her, bear with her, provide for her, and the like. He is able to do all, for he is omnipotent. He must also be willing, because he has willingly taken this place on himself. He has made himself a pattern to other husbands; will he not, then, do himself what he requires of others?

If ever any wife might take comfort in a match, the church may take comfort in this match.

The benefit of this match will appear yet more vividly by considering in particular the three properties of this matrimonial bond named above: its preeminence, firmness and nearness.

§. 86. Of Christ’s leaving his Father and mother for his spouse.

I. The preeminence of the matrimonial bond between Christ and the church appears in this, that

Christ left his Father and his mother for his spouse, the church. As Christ is God, God is his Father; as man, the Virgin Mary was his mother. Now his leaving his Father must be taken only by way of likeness, in that he came from the place where his Father dwells to the place where his spouse was. The Scripture says that he was “at the Father’s side,”856 “at His side … His delight day by day, rejoicing always857 in His presence.” Yet “He also descended to the lower parts of the earth,”858 where his spouse was. He “came from the Father859 and entered the world.”

But he truly and properly preferred his spouse before his mother. For when he was instructing his spouse, and his mother came to interrupt him, he said to his mother, “Who is My860 mother?” and to his spouse, “Here is My mother!”

The861 church, and all who are of the church, must be of the same mind toward Christ. She must forget her own people and her father’s862 house. Since Christ has gone before us and given us so good an example, what a height of ingratitude it would be for us to prefer father, mother or anyone else before Christ our husband! Note what he says in this case: “Anyone who loves863 his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me.” And again: “If anyone comes to Me and does not hate his father and mother …, he cannot864 be My disciple.” To hate here is to be so far from preferring father and mother before Christ that one would rather hate father and mother than not love Christ. Or it is to love Christ so wholly above all that our love of parents, compared with it, is a hatred. So Levi “said of his father and mother, ‘I do not consider them’ …865 for he kept Your word and maintained Your covenant.”

This, then, is our duty: that we do not let any natural affection and doting on our parents swallow up the love we owe to Christ, as Pharaoh’s “cows that were sickly and thin devoured866 the seven sleek, well-fed cows.” How much less should any love of this world, of its profits, promotions or pleasures, draw our hearts away from Christ! Should we not rather say and do as the apostles did: “Look, we have left867 everything to follow You”?

§. 87. Of the indissoluble union between Christ and the church.

II. The firmness of the bond by which Christ and the church are said to be glued together is greater and more inviolable than that by which man and wife are joined together. Death parts man and wife, but death cannot make a separation between Christ and the church. So from this metaphor we may well infer that Christ and the church are inseparably868 knit together. “I will betroth you to Me forever,” says Christ to the church. The covenant which Christ makes with his church is an everlasting covenant. The mountains will be removed869 and the hills shaken before his loving devotion departs from the church.

The steadfastness and unchangeableness of his will is the870 only cause of this. Whom he loves, he loves “to the very end.”871 “God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable.”872 He is not like the hard-hearted Jews, who would put away their wives on every slight occasion. “I hate divorce,” says the Lord.873 Therefore, though the church through her weakness departs from him and plays the harlot, “yet return to Me,”874 declares the Lord.

Let us learn by this pattern to hold fast to the Lord.875 This is a duty most due to Christ, who holds so fast to us, and it is therefore often876 expressed in the Scripture.

There are three virtues of special use for this purpose: faith, hope and love.

Faith is the hand by which we lay fast hold on Christ and, as it were, knit him to ourselves, as he by his Spirit knits us to himself. This makes us rest and rely on him for all needful things, and not leave him for anything.

Hope is the anchor which holds us fast against all the storms of Satan, so that they can never drive us out of our harbor, which is the Lord Jesus Christ.

Love is the glue and solder which makes us one with Christ. For it is the property of love to unite in one those who love one another. “The souls of Jonathan and877 David were knit together.” Why? “Jonathan loved him as himself.” He who loves is well pleased with the one he loves, and also seeks to please him, so that they may delight in one another. If these three virtues were well rooted in us, we would say, “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?878 Shall trouble or distress,” etc.

§. 88. Of the equal privilege of all the saints.

III. Concerning the phrase by which the nearness of879 man and wife is set forth (the two will be one flesh), it may be asked how this can be applied to Christ and the saints, who are more than two.

Answer. Christ by one Spirit knits us all into one body,880 and so makes all of us, taken together, one spouse. The multitude of saints no more implies many wives than the multitude of members which a wife’s natural body has. This point, then, teaches us that

In the mystical marriage between Christ and the church, each and every one of the saints has an equal privilege. Some are not881 concubines and some wives, nor are some more loved or preferred above others, but all are one wife. “All one in Christ Jesus.”882

Neither the Father who gave them all, nor the Son who883 took them all, saw anything in one more than in another; their pure grace moved them to do what they did. Every one may well apply all the privileges named above to themselves, and not one envy another.

This gives instruction to the more eminent in the884 church, that they should not, like proud ladies, lord it over others as if they were their maidservants. And it gives consolation to the lowlier sort, that they may hold themselves up and possess their souls with patience, and not envy or grieve at the outward prosperity and privileges of others. In the greatest privilege they are equal to the greatest.

So much for the parties joined to Christ. For these words (the two) show that all the saints are only one; Christ is the other of the two. The next words (will be one flesh) show how near those saints are to Christ.

§. 89. Of the close union between Christ and the church.

The main point to be noted here is that

Christ and the church are most nearly linked together. What885 can be nearer than for two to come into one flesh?

This is something more than to be of Christ’s flesh. That shows that we are, as it were, cut out of Christ; this shows that we are knit to him again. That was a preparation for this; this is, as it were, the consummation and perfection of all.886 Many metaphors are used to set forth the near union between Christ and his church, but this surpasses them all. As here we and Christ are said to be one flesh, so in another place we are said to be one spirit. Well, therefore, might the name and title Christ be given to this spouse of Christ.

It887 was noted on a ground like this that, of all other persons,888 the transgression of a wife against her husband is the most heinous. What, then, are the transgressions of the church against Christ? We are much more bound to Christ for the privileges we receive from him as a head and husband, our Savior having made an everlasting covenant of marriage with us, than for those we received from him as our Creator, Lord and master. So the rebellions now committed against him are the more monstrous. To Adam, who broke the first covenant, and so sinned against his father and master like a rebellious child and servant, mercy and pardon were given. But for those who now break the bond of this everlasting covenant, and make a total and final desertion, utterly renouncing this husband, or by their adultery causing him to give them a certificate of divorce, “no further sacrifice889 for sins remains, but only a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume all adversaries.” This is to be noted to make us the more watchful over our ways. We must resist sin at its beginning; we must “see to it that no890 one falls away from the grace of God”; and we must “not give891 the devil a foothold” at all. Satan will strive most to dissolve the nearest bonds that God makes. Since this is the nearest of all, we ought to be most careful to preserve it.
