The Mystery and Practice of Marriage

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 90–95

§. 90. Of the mystery of the union of Christ and the church.

Eph 5:32.

This is a great mystery, but I am speaking about Christ and the church.

This verse is the conclusion of that excellent digression which the apostle has made concerning the close union of Christ and the church.

Two points are to be noted in it.

1. A moving exclamation (“This is a great mystery”).

2. A particular application of the law named before (“but I am speaking about Christ and the church”).

Here first note that

The union between Christ and the church is a great mystery.

The apostle could not have said more of it than to call it a mystery, a great mystery.

A mystery is a divine secret.892

It is a secret in two respects.

1. Because it is not known.

2. Because it is unsearchable: its depth cannot be fathomed.

It is a divine secret, for two other reasons.

1. Because it could not have been opened except by divine revelation.

2. Because, when it is opened, it cannot be grasped except by the illumination of the Spirit. The Spirit who opens and reveals the mystery must also open the eyes of our understanding to discern it rightly.

It is further said to be a great mystery.

1. Simply, in itself, because its matter is deep,893 difficult, weighty, and of great importance.

2. Comparatively, in relation to other mysteries: no mystery revealed in God’s word is comparable to it.

Let us not presume to measure it with the line of our own reason. Since it is a great mystery, it is above our capacity. Yet because it is revealed, we must believe it, as we believe the mysteries of the Trinity, of Christ’s eternal generation, of the personal union of his two natures, of the procession of the Holy Spirit, and the like. We believe them because the word has revealed them, though we cannot fully see the reason of them. Here lies a chief difference between our condition in this world and in the world to come. Here we must believe what we know only in part; there we shall perfectly know whatever is to be believed. Preachers can make this mystery known only in part, and hearers can grasp it only in part. Let us therefore wait for a perfect understanding of it until all things are perfected in Christ. But in the meantime let us believe, without doubting or wavering, what is revealed of it.

In our meditation on this mystery, let us conceive nothing carnal,894 nothing earthly of it, because it is a mystery: it is altogether spiritual and heavenly. From the natural union of our head and body, and from the marriage union of man and wife, we may and ought to take occasion, by way of likeness, to help our understanding of the union of Christ and his church. It is for this end that these likenesses are used, and by this means our understanding may be much helped, as it is by the outward elements and rites used in the sacraments. But if, because of these comparisons, we drag this, which is only and wholly spiritual, into any carnal matter, we shall make a thick mist and a dark cloud of what is given for a light.

The folly of our adversaries is plainly exposed here. They make our union with Christ purely carnal. For they imagine it to consist in a bodily mingling of Christ’s flesh with ours: by our eating his flesh with the teeth of our bodies, drinking his blood down our throats, and digesting both895 in our stomachs as our bodily food, so that it may turn into our substance. In this they show themselves like the dull-headed people of Capernaum, and like ignorant Nicodemus. There is a great deal of gross absurdity in that notion, but no great mystery.

§. 91. Of the pope’s usurping the title of spouse of the church.

The apostle’s application of this mystery to Christ and the church exposes two gross errors of the papists.

One is that they make the pope a spouse of the church. How can anyone have the face to apply to the pope and the church what the apostle says so expressly is meant of Christ and the896 church? Indeed, what arrogant presumption it is to attribute to a mortal, sinful man what belongs to the eternal and holy Son of God alone! Is not this to confer Christ’s prerogatives on himself, and so make himself an outright Antichrist? Who gave the church to the pope, or the pope to the church? When did she give her consent? (I speak of the true universal church of Christ.) What has he done for her? Or rather, what has he not done against her? The897 distinction between an imperial and a ministerial spouse cannot serve their turn here. The metaphor of a head will not allow a ministerial head, and much less will the metaphor of a spouse allow a ministerial spouse. As he is an adulterer who takes it on himself to be a ministerial husband, so she is an adulteress who yields herself to such a one. The apostle says, “I promised you+ to ONE husband.”898

§. 92. Of the false sacrament of marriage.

The other error is that marriage is a sacrament. The main ground of it they have taken from this text. Yet that ground is removed by the apostle’s application of this mystery to Christ and the church as plainly as if the apostle had framed his words on purpose to forestall this wrong inference. It is as if he had said, So that no one may mistake this mystery and apply it to the joining of man and woman in marriage, know that I mean no such thing: the mystery I speak of concerns Christ and the church. I wonder how they dare misapply what is expressed so plainly. Even if the apostle had not shown his mind and meaning so clearly, the very thing itself would lead us to judge so of it. For “that which in Christ899 and the church is a great mystery is only a small matter in man and wife.” The Latin Vulgate first led them into this error, for it translates the word mystery as a sacrament. But a translation is no sufficient ground to prove a doctrine. Besides, the word sacrament used by that translator has as wide a range as mystery. If they were to make everything he translates sacrament a proper sacrament of the church, there would be many more sacraments than the papists themselves make.

1. As for this supposed sacrament, no papist could ever show when or where God ordained it to be a sacrament. Indeed, they do not agree among themselves about the time, how long it has been a sacrament.900 Some of them hold that it has been a sacrament ever since the first institution of marriage in Paradise. But the greater number of papists hold it to be a sacrament901 of the New Testament, under the gospel, because their Council of Trent has so decreed. Here we may note how the greater number of them, when two absurdities are in question, are ready to fall into the worse. Under the law the church in its childhood needed, and had, more sacraments than under the gospel. Yet this thing, which was in use as much under the law as under the gospel, and had as much then to make it a sacrament as it has now, was no sacrament then, and yet is one now.

2. As they cannot show where it was ordained as a sacrament, neither can they show what its sacramental sign is. Some make the bodily union of man and wife the sign. But there may be a true marriage though the parties married never come together.

Others make the parents’ giving the sign. But they hold that a marriage made without the parents’ consent is a true marriage.

Others make it the priest’s blessing. Yet they hold that the marriage of infidels and heretics, who have no priests, is a true marriage.

Others make it the consent of the parties themselves. Then a party would administer a sacrament to himself.

Others make it other things. So, lacking the light of God’s word, one strays down one bypath and another down another, and none of them hits on the right one.

3. There is a similar disagreement about the form of this sacrament.

4. If the other positions they lay down concerning marriage are noted, one would think they would be far from making it a sacrament. They prefer virginity to it. Indeed, they count it a kind of pollution. They hold it unlawful for priests, monks, nuns, and such holy orders (as they esteem them) to marry. So there is a sacrament in which their holy ones may not share. The order of priesthood is a sacrament (in their account), yet that order keeps men from marriage; so one sacrament fights against another. Indeed, infidels may partake of a sacrament, and so their holy and precious things are denied to their holy ones and cast to swine. So we see a rotten building raised on a sandy foundation: a false sacrament established on a false application of this text. Can it then stand?

§. 93. Of the sum of husbands’ and wives’ duties.

Eph 5:33.

Nevertheless, let each one of you+ in particular so love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she reverences her husband.

The apostle, having made a long digression about the mutual relation between Christ and the church, whom he set forth as patterns to husbands and wives, now returns to the main point he intended, namely the duties of husbands and wives. The first word (Nevertheless) implies as much, as if he had said, Though I have digressed a little902 into the mystery of the union of Christ and the church, yet nevertheless, O husbands and wives, call to mind what I chiefly aimed at, namely your+ duties.

This verse, then, contains the conclusion of the apostle’s discourse concerning the duties of husbands and wives.

Two points are especially to be noted in it.

  1. A declaration of their separate and distinct duties.
  2. A direction to each of them to apply their own proper duties to themselves.

Their distinct duties are noted in two words

  • Love.
  • Fear.

These two, as they are distinct duties in themselves, so they are also common conditions that must be joined to all other duties. Love is as sugar to sweeten the duties of authority that belong to a husband. Fear is as salt to season all the duties of subjection that belong to a wife. The apostle has therefore set them down as two marks for husbands and wives to aim at in everything in which they have to deal with one another.

I will speak of these more distinctly in the treatises on the particular duties of husbands and wives.

§. 94. Of applying the word to ourselves.

The direction for each of them to apply his own proper duties to himself in particular is especially to be noted here. Two things are to be observed in this direction.

1. That every particular person apply to himself what a minister delivers to all in general. “Each one903 of you+ in particular,” says the apostle. This is as much as if he had expressed his mind more fully in this way: I have laid down such general duties as all husbands and wives, without exception, of whatever rank or degree they are, are bound to. I have not delivered them by name to every one separately, one by one, but generally to you+ all; yet let every one of you+ apply these things to yourselves+ in particular.

2. That every one apply his own special duty to himself. Since love belongs especially to a husband, to him he says that he must “love his wife.” And since reverence belongs especially to a wife, to her he says, “let the wife see that she reverences her husband.”

There is a direction in each of the separate letters sent to the seven churches of Asia, in these words: “He who904 has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” It teaches every member of any of those churches to apply to himself what was delivered to the whole church. So does a similar905 exhortation which Christ called out to the people whom he taught in parables. So does this declaration of how far Christ’s counsel reaches: “What I say to906 you+, I say to everyone.” To this purpose many precepts given to whole churches, and to all sorts of people, are set down in the singular number, as if given to one: “Wake up, YOU [singular] who907 sleep.” “YOU [singular] stand by faith. Do not be arrogant,” etc.908

The life and power of God’s word lies in this particular909 application of it to ourselves. This is to mix faith with hearing. I mean a faith by which we not only believe the truth of God’s word in general, but also believe it to be a truth concerning ourselves in particular. In this way every precept in it will be a good instruction and direction to guide us in the way of righteousness. Every promise in it will be a great encouragement and consolation to us, to uphold us and make us hold on. And every judgment threatened in it will be a curb and bridle to hold us in, and to keep us from the sins against which the judgments are threatened. But otherwise, if we do not bring the word home to our own souls, it will be as a word “spoken into the air,”910 vanishing away without any profit to us. Nothing makes the word less profitable than putting it off from ourselves onto others, thinking that it concerns others more than ourselves.

That we may make the better use of this doctrine, let us observe both what general duties belong to all Christians, and apply them to ourselves as particular; and also what duties belong to persons of our own place, calling and condition, and apply them to ourselves more especially. Let all manner of husbands and all manner of wives, of whatever rank or degree they are, who read the duties that follow, know that they are spoken to them in particular. Let kings and queens, lords and ladies, ministers and their wives, rich men and their wives, poor men and their wives, old men and their wives, young men and their wives, all of every sort, take them as spoken to them in particular. It is not honor, wealth, learning, or any other excellence, nor lowliness of place, poverty, lack of learning, or any other such thing, that can exempt a husband from loving his wife, or a wife from reverencing her husband. He who says each one excepts no one. Therefore, each one in particular, do you+ so. The same application may be made to all parents and children, masters and servants, concerning their duties.

§. 95. Of everyone’s looking especially to his own duty.

In this application we must look rather to the duty which we owe and ought to perform to others than to what is due to us and others ought to perform to us. For the apostle does not say to the husband, “See that your wife reverences you,” but, “See that you love her”; and so to the wife.

For this purpose the Holy Spirit presses particular duties on the particular persons who ought to perform them: subjection on wives, love on husbands, and so with others. So this is what you must especially consider: how you911 may show yourself blameless. I do not deny that one ought to stir up another, and one help another as far as they can to perform their duty, especially superiors who have charge over others. But the chief care of every one ought to be for himself, and he ought to make the greatest conscience of performing his own duty.

1. It is more acceptable before God, and more commendable912 before men, to do duty than to exact duty. As in matters of free charity, so also in matters of bound duty, “It is more blessed to913 give than to receive.” In particular, it is better for a husband to be a good husband than to have a good wife; and so for a wife. To have others fail in their duty to us may be a heavy cross; for us to fail in our duty to others is a fearful curse.

2. Every one is to give an account of his own particular914 duty. What the prophet says of father and son may be applied to husband and wife, and to all other sorts of people: “If a father does what is just and right, he is righteous; he915 will surely live. If he has a son who does not do so, he will surely die; his blood will be on his own head.” Again: “If a father does what is not good, he will die in his iniquity; but if his son does what is just and right, he will surely live. The righteousness of the righteous man will fall upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked man will fall upon him.” That it will be so between husband and wife may be gathered from these words: “Two people916 will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left.”

Let this be noted against the common, empty excuse made for neglecting duty, which is this: Duty is not performed to me; why should I do my duty? “When my husband does his duty, I will do mine,” says the wife. “And I mine,” says the husband, “when my wife does hers.” What if he never does his duty, and so is damned? Will you never do yours? This looking for duty at others’ hands makes us all the more careless of our own.

Therefore, you+ husbands, look especially to your+917 own duties: love your+ wives. And you+ wives, look918 especially to yours+: reverence your+ husbands. For this end, let husbands read most diligently the duties which concern husbands, and wives those which concern wives. Let not the husband say of the wife’s duties, “There are good lessons for my wife,” and neglect his own; nor the wife say the same of the husband’s duties, and not regard her own. This is what makes the subjection of many wives very harsh and irksome to them: their husbands, who urge and press them to it, show little or no love to them at all. And this is what makes many husbands very slow to show love: their wives, who expect much love, show little or no reverence to their husbands. Therefore, “let each one of you+ in particular so love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she reverences her husband.”

892. On a mystery, see more in The Whole Armor of God, Treatise 3, §. 168, on Eph 6:19.

894. 2. Use. Nothing carnal in our union with Christ. Ecclesia Christo in occulto vxor est. For secretly and inwardly, in a hidden, spiritual secret, the human soul cleaves to the Word of God, so that they are two in one flesh.] Aug. contr. Faust. Man. lib. 22. cap. 38.

The Child’s Duties to His Parents

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 96–114

§. 96. Of the meaning of the first verse of the sixth chapter.

From the particular duties that concern husbands and wives, the apostle proceeds to lay down those that concern children and parents. As before he laid down wives’ duties before husbands’, so here he begins with children’s (who are inferior to their parents), and that for the same reasons that were given919 before.

Besides, children are the fruits of the joining in marriage, and so they are fitly placed next to man and wife.

What concerns children is laid down in the sixth chapter of Ephesians, vv. 1, 2, 3. We will open the meaning of it point by point.

Eph 6:1.

Children, obey your+ parents in the Lord, for this is right.

The first word (children) is in the original as fitting a word920 as could be used, for by its derivation it means those who are begotten and born. The other word (parents) answers to it: it means those who beget and bring forth921 children. Yet the words are not to be taken so strictly, as if none were meant but those who begot and brought forth, or those who were begotten and brought forth by them. For under the title parents he includes all who are in the place of natural parents, such as grandfathers and grandmothers, stepfathers and stepmothers, fathers-in-law and mothers-in-law, foster-fathers and foster-mothers, guardians, tutors, and other such governors. And under the title children he includes grandchildren, stepchildren, sons-in-law and daughters-in-law, wards, pupils, and the like. For an honor and a subjection is due from all who are in the place of children to all who are in the place of parents, though in a different kind, as we will922 show later. This word children, which in the original is of the neuter gender, also includes both sexes, males and females, sons and daughters. So each of them is to apply the duties set out here to themselves as carefully as if both kinds had been named in particular.

He speaks of parents in the plural number to show that he923 means both sexes here too, father and mother, as the law names both. And he adds this relative word your. By way924 of restraint, it shows that not every child is bound to every parent. By way of extent, it shows that whatever the condition of the parents may be, honorable or lowly, rich or poor, learned or unlearned, etc., their own children must not be ashamed of them, but must give them every duty they are bound to. If they are parents to children, they must be honored by children.

The word (obey), under which all the duties of children are925 included, means, by its Greek derivation, to listen with humble submission. That is, to attend and give heed to the commands, reproofs, directions and exhortations given to them, and that with such reverent respect for the persons who give them that they make themselves conform to them.

It is a duty proper to inferiors, and it implies both reverence and obedience. The926 verb points to obedience; the927 preposition, to reverence.

Under this word (obey) the apostle includes all928 the duties that Scripture everywhere requires of children. This is plain from his own illustration of it in the second verse, by the word honor, which the law uses. So this word (obey) is to be taken in as large an extent as that word (honor).

Question. Why is obedience put for all the rest?

Answer. 1. Because it is the hardest of all the rest, and the one children are most unwilling to perform. Those who yield to this willingly will balk at no duty.

2. Because it is the surest evidence of the honor a child owes his parent, and so of keeping the fifth commandment.

3. Because children are bound to their parents. The duties they perform are not matters of courtesy, but of necessity. Their parents have power to command them and to demand them.

The added clause (in the Lord) is in effect the same as929 the one used930 before (as to the Lord). It points to a limitation, a direction and an incentive. It is a limitation, showing that children’s obedience to their parents is to be kept within the obedience they owe to Christ, and may not go beyond its limits. It is a direction, showing that in obeying their parents they must have an eye to Christ, and so obey them that Christ may approve of it. It is an incentive, showing that parents bear the image of Christ, and in that respect children must obey their parents all the more.

The last clause of this verse (for this is right) is an express931 reason to enforce the obedience just named. It is drawn from equity, and shows that this obedience agrees with all law; indeed, that it is due by way of repayment. If children are not obedient to their parents, they do what is most unjust: they defraud their parents of their right.

The former phrase (in the Lord) implies one reason; this one plainly points to another, as the first word (for) declares.

§. 97. Of the meaning of the second verse.

Eph 6:2.

Honor your father and mother (which is the first commandment with a promise),

The very words of the fifth commandment are cited here932 by the apostle to confirm the reason just given, that it is just and right to obey parents, because God requires as much in the moral law. The law is more general than the apostle’s precept. For the law includes under it all the duties that every kind of inferior owes to his superiors, whether in the family, the church or the commonwealth; but the apostle’s precept is given to only one kind of inferior in the family. Yet the argument from a general to a particular is very sound and good, thus: All inferiors must933 honor their superiors; therefore children must honor their parents.

By adding the express words of the law, the apostle shows that the subjection he required of children is no yoke he put on their necks on his own authority, but one the moral law has put on them. So this may be noted as a third reason, namely, God’s express charge in his moral law.

If I were to handle this law in its full extent, I would wander too far from the apostle’s purpose. I will therefore open it no further than it concerns the point in hand, that is, the duty of children.

Honor includes here all the duties that children in934 any respect owe to their parents. It implies both an inward reverent esteem and an outward dutiful submission. Indeed, it also implies repayment and maintenance.

Honor is used in relation to parents for two reasons especially.

1. To show that parents bear God’s image. For honor is properly due to God alone; it is due to the creature only as it stands in God’s place and carries his image.

2. To show that it is an honor to parents to have dutiful children, just as it is a dishonor to them to have disobedient children.

Both father and mother are expressly named, to take away935 from children every pretense for neglecting either of them. For through the corruption of nature we are prone to look for many excuses to exempt ourselves from the duty we are bound to; and if not wholly, then in as large a part as we can. Some might think that if they honor their father, who is their mother’s head, they have done what the law requires. Others may think they have done as much if they honor their mother, who is the weaker vessel. But the law, naming father and mother, condemns the one who neglects either of them. Yet the father is set in the first place. This shows that if a conflict should arise between them, so that both could not be obeyed together, the father commanding what the mother forbids, the father is to be preferred (especially if it is not against the Lord).

The words that follow, (which is the first commandment936 with a promise), are fitly set in a parenthesis, because they are not the words of the law. The apostle inserted them as a reason to enforce the law, and so they make a fourth reason.

Question. In what respect is this commandment called the first with a promise?

Answer. 1. The word the apostle uses here properly937 means an affirmative precept, as our English word (commandment) does. Now of the affirmative precepts, it is the first with a promise.

2. Scripture often applies the word law to the second table in particular, as where he says, “he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the938 law,” and so in other places.

Now this is the first commandment of the second table.

3. It is true in general of all the commandments: among the ten, it is the first with a promise.

Objection. The second commandment has a promise attached939 to it.

Answer. 1. What is attached to the second commandment is not expressly a promise. It is rather a declaration of God’s justice in taking vengeance on transgressors, and of his mercy in rewarding those who keep the law. Yet I do not deny that a promise is implied by consequence; but here it is expressed.

2. The promise implied there is only a general promise made to those who keep the whole law, and that is why he uses the plural number, commandments. But here a particular promise is made to those who keep this commandment in particular.

2. Question. Why then is it called the first, when no other commandments with a promise follow?940

Answer. This word (first) does not always refer to some other that follows. It is often taken simply, to show that none was before it. So the word firstborn is used in the law,941 and so Christ is called the firstborn son of Mary.

The word promise shows that this fourth reason includes some benefit that comes to the children themselves who honor their parents. The benefit is expressly named in the next verse, which we will consider point by point later.

§. 98. Of aiming at our own good in seeking the good of others.

Here in general we may note that

It is not unlawful to aim at our own good and benefit in doing the duties to others that God requires at our hands. For what God himself sets before us, we may seek and aim at. There are many similar promises in Scripture, and many approved prayers grounded on those promises, by which the truth of this doctrine is confirmed to us. Hezekiah942 makes the good service he had done to God and his church a ground for obtaining a longer life, and so do others.

For God lays no duty on any man without aiming in it at the good of the one who performs the duty, as well as of the one to whom it is performed. By this he would show that his commandments are no tight yokes and heavy burdens, but means of procuring the good of those who fulfill them.

How highly this commends the kind regard that943 God has for all the sons of men, seeking their good in every place where he sets them, whether of authority or of subjection!

How this ought to stir us up to keep willingly and cheerfully944 the laws God commands us, and to perform the services he requires of us, since by doing so we procure our own good!

How fully this may satisfy, and even stop the mouths of,945 all who are discontented with their places and grumble against the subjection God requires of them!

What a good direction and resolution this may be to many946 who are moved in conscience to seek the good of others, and yet doubt whether in doing so they may aim at their own good or not! To make this case clear by one instance, which may serve for many: a minister is faithful in his place and very hardworking, and in that respect has a good conscience, but he also has a tender and weak conscience. He doubts whether by his work he may seek a living for himself, fearing that in this he seeks himself, and not simply the building up of God’s church. But by the doctrine just stated we see that both may be aimed at: for God commands the one and promises the other. As we have one eye on God’s commandment for direction, so we may have the other on his promise for encouragement.

Yet because through the corruption of our nature we are too947 prone to seek ourselves, some cautions are to be carefully observed in this point.

1. That we do not seek our own good by any transgression, for it is promised to obedience.

2. That we do not seek ourselves and our own good so wholly that we neglect others. For God has joined both together, and no man may put them apart.

3. That we aim at our own good as a reward that follows the duty God commands, and so are as willing to do the duty as we are eager for the reward.

4. That our own benefit is not the only thing, no, nor the chief thing, we aim at in doing our duty. Rather, it should come in as a motive to add an edge to other motives of greater weight and sharpen them. And this is what the order the apostle keeps in setting down his reasons points out to us. For the three former reasons concern God, and the good conscience children ought to keep toward him. The first points to God’s image, which parents carry (in the Lord). The second sets out the right that God has prescribed to children. The third declares God’s charge. Only this fourth, which is the last, concerns the profit and benefit of the children themselves.

§. 99. Of preferring what is honorable to what is profitable.

From the order just described we may further gather that Equity and a good conscience ought to move us to do our duty more than our own profit and the benefit that comes to us from it. Suppose such a conflict should arise between these that they could not both stand together. Suppose that for doing what is right, and what God has commanded, our prosperity must be hindered and our life shortened. Then we should so hold to what is right and commanded by God that prosperity, life and all are let go. All the exhortations in Scripture to forsake goods, lands, life and everything else for righteousness’ sake tend to this purpose. This point is so clear948 that the heathen saw it by the glimmer of the light of nature they had. For they could say that what is honorable and right is to be preferred before what is advantageous and profitable.

There is no comparison between what is honorable and what is advantageous, between right and profit. The one is absolutely necessary for attaining eternal salvation; the other gives only a little quiet and contentment in this world. No, if profit is without right, it can give no true contentment or quiet at all.

They are unworthy, therefore, of the name of Christians949 who aim so wholly and only at their outward profit and prosperity that they do not regard what is right and what God has commanded. If by obeying God and doing what is right they may reap some benefit for themselves, they can be content950 to yield to it. But if not, farewell all right, farewell all God’s commandments. Though they think everything that is profitable is good, whether it is right or wrong, God’s word counts nothing good but what is honorable. Such people therefore can look for no blessing from the Lord.

§. 100. Of the meaning of the third verse.

Eph 6:3.

that it may go well with you, and that you may live long on the earth.

The promise mentioned before in general is set down here in particular. The first words (that it may go well with you) are not in the Hebrew text951 where the law is first recorded. That is why they are not set in the usual form of the ten commandments that we use. Yet in952 another place, where the law is repeated, they are set down. And the Greek translation commonly called the Septuagint (which the church in the apostles’ time probably used) has them expressly in both places. Now this part of the promise (that it may go well with you) is placed first to enlarge the other part, concerning long life, which is the chief thing intended. This appears from the fact that long life alone is mentioned where the law is first recorded. It shows that the long life953 God promises will not be a life of woe and misery (for then it would be no blessing, but the longer life lasted, the worse it would be), but a life full of comfort and happiness. That is why Moses sets this former clause in the latter place, after long life, thus: “so that your days may be long and that it954 may go well with you.” He does this to show that the well-being spoken of here enlarges the benefit of long life.

The apostle sets down the place where the benefit of this promise is to be enjoyed in the broadest phrase, (on the earth). The law brings it into a narrower compass, “in the land that the Lord your God is giving you,” meaning the land of Canaan, which God gave to the Jews as their own special inheritance. So the promise, as the law sets it down for the Jews in particular, implies long life and prosperity in their own inheritance; for to the Jews long life out of their own country was counted no life. But the apostle, writing to all nations, leaves out that description of Canaan and keeps only the general substance in this phrase (on the earth). He sets it down to show that even outward prosperity, and a long life in this world, is promised here.

§. 101. Of prosperity: how far it may be a blessing.

To clear this text further and to apply it better, I will resolve various questions arising out of it, and gather such profitable instructions as it offers.

The promise has two branches.

The first branch (that it may go well with you) is very ample955 and large. All good things, all manner of blessings whatever, spiritual and temporal, belonging to soul and body, concerning this life and the life to come, make for a man’s well-being. So the first question may be asked:

1. Question. What is the extent of this phrase in this place?956

Answer. It may be extended in general to all manner of good things. For “godliness … holds promise for the present life and for the one to come.” But (as I take it) temporal prosperity is chiefly intended here, and that for these reasons.

1. It is joined with long life, which is a temporal blessing.

2. The last words (on the earth) may be referred to this branch of well-being as well as to the other, of long life.

3. In the law (from which this clause is taken) it is expressly set down thus: “that it may go well with you in the957 land,” etc.

2. Question. Is outward temporal prosperity, then (such as honor,958 health, peace, liberty, goods, etc.), a token of God’s love and favor?

Answer. Yes. In itself it is a blessing and a fruit of God’s love, as appears from these reasons.

1. As it was first made and ordained by God, it is a good thing.

2. It tends to man’s good if it is rightly used.

3. It was given to man before he had sinned.

4. It is promised by God as a reward to those who fear him959 and keep his commandments.

5. The saints have prayed for it and have been thankful960 for it.

6. Its contrary was first inflicted as a punishment of sin,961 and is often threatened as a token of God’s wrath, and so it has also been inflicted on transgressors.962

§. 102. Of prosperity bestowed on the wicked, how it proves a curse.

3. Question. Why then is it given to the wicked, even to those who are963 haters of God and are hated by him? And why are God’s friends, those who are964 loved by him and love him in return, deprived of it? This painful doubt made David stumble,965 and moved other prophets to complain. But the answer is ready.

Answer. Outward prosperity is of such a nature that it may turn to the good or the harm of the one who enjoys it. And in this God’s wonderful and unsearchable wisdom is seen, in that he is able to turn blessings into curses and curses into blessings.966 He can work by contraries.

4. Question. How is prosperity a curse to the wicked?

Answer. Purely by consequence, through their abuse of it. God gives it to them to show the riches of his mercy; and so that all may taste of it, he does good to the evil and the good.967 Besides, he tests them in this way, to see whether by any means they may be brought to repentance. Because they do not have that gift, their prosperity proves to be a means of making them the more inexcusable, and of increasing their just condemnation the more. For the more God’s blessings abound toward them, the more they abuse them, adding to all their other sins that most odious sin of ingratitude, which completes the heap. And in these respects I may say of the prosperity of the wicked what the prophet said of their king: God gives it in his anger, and takes it away in968 his wrath. For by their abuse of it, it proves to be Satan’s bait to lure them, his snare to catch them, and his hook to drown969 them in ruin and destruction. In a word, then, the wicked are fed in a fair pasture, like oxen appointed for the slaughter. They are raised up high, as on a ladder or scaffold, like thieves and traitors, to be brought down with shame and destruction, as Pharaoh’s baker was lifted up.970

§. 103. How both having and lacking prosperity is a blessing to the saints.

5. Question. How is the enjoying or the lacking of prosperity a blessing to the righteous?

Answer. God in his wisdom knows what is best for them and deals with them accordingly. He gives them prosperity as far as he sees it will turn to their good, and withholds it from them as far as he sees it will turn to their harm. Whenever God gives any temporal blessing to his saints, therefore, it is a token of his favor; and whenever he withholds any, the very withholding is also a fruit of his favor. In this the word is made true that “God works all things together for the good of those971 who love Him.” So if they abound, it will go well with them; if they lack, it will go well with them; if they are in high place, it will go well with them; if in lowly place, it will go well with them. Whether they are at liberty or in prison, whether in health or sick, in whatever condition, it will go well with them.

6. Question. How is it, then, that saints are often brought to such extremities that they are forced to complain that it goes very972 badly with them?

Answer. There is flesh and blood in them, and because of its weakness they are forced to complain. But the present impression of weak flesh is not enough to call the truth of God’s promise into question. In their present extremity they do not consider what God’s mind is, what his manner of dealing with them is, how needful it is that they should be dealt with so, and what end and outcome the Lord will give. In truth it is better with them than they know. There are some weighty reasons that move God to bring them to the extremity they are in. These concern his own glory,973 or the building up974 of others, or their own good: as975 curing some dangerous disease,976 displaying the grace of God given to them,977 drawing them nearer to God,978 making them long the more for heaven, and the like.

§. 104. Of long life: how far it is a blessing.

Concerning the second branch of God’s promise (long life), other questions are to be resolved.

1. Question. Is long life a blessing?979

Answer. Yes. Otherwise God would not have promised it as a reward, here and in other places, nor have given it to his saints.

The reasons proving it to be a blessing may be gathered under three heads: 1. God’s glory. 2. The good of the church where they live. 3. Their own good.

1. God’s glory is much advanced by the long life of the saints. For the longer they live, the more they themselves observe God’s wonderful works, and the more they make them known and declare them to others. But in the grave all980 is forgotten.

2. God’s church is greatly built up by it. In this respect the apostle says, “it is more necessary for981 you+ that I remain in the body.” In the saints, what Elihu says should be is true, namely that “age should speak, and many years should teach wisdom.”982 The longer the saints live, the more good they do; but after death they do none: “Night is coming, when no one can work.”983984 On this ground the apostle exhorts us to do good while we have time.

3. By living long, the saints gain for themselves great honor and dignity among God’s people, and a strong, steadfast confidence in God. Men value a good old servant; much more will God. Old saints have two strong props to establish them and make them bold. One is the remembrance of God’s former favors, by which their hope of eternal life is made more sure to them. The other is a kind of present expectation of the fulfillment of God’s promises, which they have long waited for.

By this it appears that this particular promise is no light matter of small weight, but a strong motive to stir up children to obedience.

§. 105. Of long life proving a curse to the wicked.

2. Question. Why then is long life given to many wicked people? And why are many saints cut off?

Answer. Long life is of the same kind as prosperity: it may be turned into a curse as well as prove a blessing.

By living long on earth the wicked make their sins grow to the full (as is implied of the Amorites).985 They make their name stink the more on earth, as a carcass stinks the more the longer it remains above ground. And they bring the greater torment in hell on themselves: for as986 sin is increased, so that torment will be increased.

The righteous have their days shortened for their good, when they are shortened, and that in these and similar respects:

  1. That they may be987 taken away from the evil to come.988
  2. That they might be made an989 example to others.
  3. That990 by a temporal death eternal condemnation might be avoided.
  4. That their991 chief and greatest reward might be hastened.

§. 106. Of limiting the promises of temporal blessings.

So we see that there may be just cause to alter the latter branch of this promise, long life, as well as the former, prosperity, and yet no wrong comes to the righteous by it, nor any benefit to the wicked.

3. Question. Is not the truth of the promise called into question by this?

Answer. Not in the least. For first, all promises of temporal blessings are limited by a condition such as this: if keeping it may stand with God’s honor and the good of the person to whom it is made. 2. God never simply deprives his saints of what is promised, but only gives them something better in its place. In taking away wealth, he gives a greater store of grace; in restraining liberty of body, he gives freedom of conscience; with affliction he gives patience; by taking away this temporal life, he gives eternal life. In this God deals like one who, having promised so much iron, gives as much silver instead, or gold for silver, and so for one pound gives the value of hundreds or thousands.

§. 107. Of applying prosperity and long life to the obedience that children give their parents.

4. Question. Why are long life and prosperity assigned to this kind of righteousness in particular?

Answer. They are not so assigned to this as if they belonged to no other. For elsewhere they are promised in general to the992 keepers of the whole law, and to other particular branches of it besides this one. Yet in these and similar particular respects993 they are applied to the obedience of children.

1. Because obedience to parents is one of the surest evidences of our conformity to the whole law. By it we show our regard for God’s image, and lay a good foundation for performing every duty to man.

2. Because a child’s performing his duty to his parents is, under God, a special means of their doing well and living long. (For as rebellious children make their parents go to their graves the sooner with grief, so dutiful children make them continue the longer in prosperity.) Therefore the Lord in return promises such a child prosperity and long life.

3. Because parents are a special means of procuring the welfare and long life of their children. Partly they do it by their provident care, as Naomi said to Ruth, “Should I not seek a resting place for you,994 that it may be well with you?” And partly they do it by their earnest prayer: for the faithful prayer of parents for dutiful children has great force with God. From this the custom has arisen of children asking their parents’ blessing, and of parents blessing their children. In this respect the law sets forth the blessing of the fifth commandment thus: they will prolong your days.995

4. Because disobedience to parents brings much harm on children’s heads, and often shortens their days, and that in many ways.

1. Parents are often provoked by their children’s disobedience996 to disinherit them, or at least to allow them a smaller portion, so that it does not go so well with them. Indeed, some are provoked to bring their rebellious children before the magistrate, who by God’s law was to cut them off,997 so that their life is shortened by it.

2. Parents are provoked to complain to God of their children’s disobedience, and God is moved by this both to lay heavy judgments on such children in their lifetime and to shorten their days. For parents’ complaints make a loud cry in God’s ears. It is said that God, by cutting off Abimelech with an untimely death,998 “repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done to his father.”

3. When parents are too indulgent toward their children, God punishes the sin of both parent and child by shortening the child’s days. Take for example Hophni999 and Phinehas, Absalom,1000 and Adonijah.1001

4. Disobedience to parents is a sin that seldom goes alone, for an undutiful child is commonly a very wicked person in many other ways. Considering how prone our nature is to every sin, it cannot be avoided that those who shake off the yoke of government at the beginning should run headlong into all wild living, looseness and licentiousness. So with sin added to sin, it must bring harm upon harm, until at length life is cut off.

Since these harms are avoided by giving due obedience to parents, it may well be said that it will go well with obedient children, and they will live long.

§. 108. Of God’s ordering his favors so that they may appear to be true blessings.

Now that the particular branches of God’s promise have been1002 opened one by one, we will consider them jointly, for they greatly enlarge one another. Prosperity sweetens long life and makes it welcome; otherwise to live long, that is, in misery and wretchedness, is very tiresome and grievous. Again, long life added to prosperity makes it so much the greater blessing. For the longer a good thing lasts, the better it is. If prosperity were only like a flower, soon gone, the very thought of how fleeting it is would greatly lessen its joy and comfort. But both of them joined together show that what is promised is no small blessing.

From the joining of them both together, I observe that

God so orders his favors that they appear to be true blessings,1003 tending indeed to the good of those on whom he bestows them. So when God gave Abraham a son, he established his covenant with him, that this gift might be a true blessing.

I might give the same instance in all the children of promise, such as Samson, Solomon, John the Baptist, etc. So in other favors. When God added fifteen years to Hezekiah’s life, he also promised1004 him deliverance from his enemies, and peace and truth all his days. And when God gave David a kingdom, he gave him1005 great victories and long life, and established his kingdom for his descendants; and he dealt in the same way with Solomon. But not to dwell on any more particulars, this doctrine is excellently confirmed in Psalm 128.

In this way God will show that he gives in love even the temporal blessings he gives to his saints, so that they may value them accordingly, and that their hearts may be the more enlarged both to wonder at his goodness and to be thankful for it.

This is the use we must make of the things the Lord is1006 pleased to give us, such as long life, good health, honor, peace, plenty, liberty and all prosperity. We must receive and use them as God gives them, namely, as tokens of his favor, and be the more stirred up by them to perform the duties he requires of us. We must not abuse them to his dishonor and our own harm, but use them rather so that he may have honor and we profit by them.

§. 109. Of God’s high regard for dutiful children.

More particularly, by this promise we may learn what high1007 esteem and great regard God has for dutiful children, and for the obedience they give their parents. This ought all the more to move children to complete obedience, if at least they have any care for God’s favor and the tokens of his love. Oh, consider this, all you+ who have parents to honor! Consider how concerned and how earnest God is, in every way and by all means, to draw you+ to obedience. He does not content himself with urging the justice of the point, the place of your+ parent, and the charge he himself has given. He presses your+ own profit most of all, and that not only in hope for the time to come, but in present enjoyment in this life. And he does so because we, in our childishness, are moved most by things that are present and that we can see and feel. He deals with us as a tender father who provides for his child not only a good calling and a fair inheritance, but also gives him plums, pears and such things as delight him for the present, the more to draw him on.

§. 110. Of children’s doing good to themselves by honoring their parents.

Children may further learn from this promise that in1008 performing their duty they do good not only to their parents, but also to themselves: they procure their own welfare and long life. What utter fools, then, disobedient children are! They regard neither God, nor their parents, nor themselves. They deprive themselves of their eternal happiness, hinder their welfare and shorten their days. So I may fitly apply to undutiful children these words of the psalmist: “Mark the obedient child, for the end of him is peace;1009 but the rebellious will be destroyed; he will be cut off.” And these of the wise man: “I know that it will go well with the dutiful1010 child, but it will not go well with the disobedient; he will not prolong his days.” And these of the prophet: “Tell the obedient child that it will be well with him;1011 he will eat the fruit of his doings; but woe to the transgressor; it will be ill with him.”

§. 111. Of parents doing good to their children by keeping them under obedience.

From this promise parents may learn how to do good1012 to their children, how to provide for their welfare and to preserve their life long on earth (a thing most parents are naturally inclined to, and greatly desire). It is done by teaching children their duty and keeping them under obedience. Then they have God’s promise to assure them that it will go well with their children and that they will live long. When parents are on their deathbeds, they may rest more securely on this promise than on a great store of treasure laid up for their children, or great revenues reserved for them. Many parents neglect themselves. They toil and drudge, they fret and worry, they pinch and save, to leave their children a store of wealth, thinking by this to do good to their children. Yet at the same time they pamper their children too much, give them free rein, and do not care how little duty they perform. God’s curse will lie on all the store laid up for such children, like a fire to consume it all. Does not daily experience prove the truth of this? The judgments laid on some such children plainly show God’s just indignation against them all. So let rich men not think they have left their children well provided for if they leave them a large portion, but rather if they have seen to it that they are obedient children. And if poor men’s children are such, let them not fear: it will go well with them.

It is said that a good trade is better than house and land; but by virtue of this promise we may say that obedience in a child is better than trade and all. This is the trade of a child’s1013 way that parents should teach their children. So as parents desire their children’s good, they ought to be wise in procuring it, and that is by teaching them this trade of obedience. So they will bring much comfort to themselves while they live, and good to their children after them.

§. 112. Of the lasting substance of things whose circumstances concerning the Jews have passed away.

In laying down this particular promise, the apostle puts in place of its limitation to the Jews, in these words, “in the land that the Lord your God is giving you,” a general phrase that extends it to all nations, namely this, (on the earth). From this I gather that

The substance of those things that in some circumstances were1014 restricted to the Jews in a special manner remains in force for all Christians. The substance of this promise was that it should go well with obedient children while they lived here on earth, and that in this welfare they should live long. The circumstance was that they should enjoy that blessing in Canaan. Though Christians do not live in Canaan, which is the circumstance, yet it will go well with them, and they will live long, which is the substance. So too, though the circumstance of God’s covenant with Abraham (which was circumcision) is abolished, yet the substance (which is that he will be our God, and the God of our descendants) remains. This might be illustrated further by many hundreds of instances. For the substance of all the Jewish sacrifices and sacraments, both ordinary and extraordinary, of their sabbaths, their fasts, their feasts and the like, remains, though the circumstances, like shadows, have vanished away. That is why many promises made to them are applied by the apostles to Christians, such as this: “Never will I leave you,1015 never will I forsake you.” And in general it is said, “This promise belongs to you+ and your+ children and to all who are far off.”

By this we may learn what use to make of the Old Testament,1016 even of those promises and privileges that in some particular respects were assigned to the Jews: namely, by observing the substance and distinguishing it from the circumstance. In this way we will find true what the apostle says of all things written in former times, namely, that they were “written for our instruction.”1017 In this respect the same apostle says of the things recorded of Abraham that they “were written not only for Abraham,”1018 and again of the things recorded of the Israelites, that they “were written down as warnings for us.”1019 By this we may learn how to apply the preface to the ten commandments, which mentions the deliverance of Israel out of the bondage of Egypt.

Pray, therefore, for the spirit of illumination to discern between substance and circumstance, especially in reading the Old Testament.

§. 113. Of the appointed term of man’s life.

Having declared the orthodox points this text affords, I will further point out two heretical positions that our adversaries raise from it. One is held by those who call themselves Lutherans, to the dishonor of the man whom God raised up to be a worthy instrument in dispelling the mist of popery, which had greatly darkened the light of the gospel. The other is held by the papists.

The former is this: God has not determined the set limit of1020 man’s days, but it is in man’s power to lengthen or shorten them. For if it were otherwise, they say, this promise of long life and others like it would be to no purpose, and so would the contrary threats of shortening man’s days.

To answer this fully, I will first show that the position itself is directly contrary to the whole current of Scripture, and then expose the unsoundness of their inference.

Concerning the determined limit of man’s days, Scripture speaks thus: “Is there not an appointed time for man on1021 earth? Are not his days like those of a hired hand?” Note with what emphasis the point is set forth, as if it were so clear that no one could doubt it. Note also the two metaphors used here, which greatly clear the point: one taken from soldiers, the other from hired servants. The one from soldiers is implied in the meaning of the original word translated appointed time, which properly means one who has1022 his time appointed for warfare, or the time itself so appointed; the other is expressed. Now we know that these times are appointed to the hour; so is the time of man’s life. In this respect Job says again, “All the days of my appointed time I will1023 wait,” etc., where he uses the same word as before, in the same sense. To this purpose such phrases as these are often used in Scripture: “determined days,” “the number of days,”1024 “hour,” etc. Did not the prophet expressly declare to Hezekiah that he would live exactly fifteen years after his sickness?1025 He could not have told it if the Lord had not set that limit beforehand. Christ says that “the very hairs of your+ head are all numbered”;1026 are not our days much more numbered? Again he says, “Who … can add one cubit to his stature?”1027 Can anyone, then, add to his days? This point is so evident that the heathen noted it.

As for their inference (if a man’s time is determined, all the promises of long life are to no purpose), I answer that God, who has set down the exact time and limit of man’s life, has also set down the means of reaching that limit. Now the time he has kept secret to himself; the means he has revealed to us. With regard to us, then, who do not know the time appointed by the Lord, it may be said that by using such and such means we prolong our days, or by doing such and such things we shorten them. Now because these means only show our days to be long or short, God’s decree remains firm and stable and is not altered by them. Yet this work of lengthening or shortening is attributed to us, because we do what lies in us toward it, and do it freely, without any compulsion. For though God’s decree causes a necessity in the outcome, it imposes no constraint on the will of man, but leaves it as free (with regard to the manner of working) as if there were no decree at all. And in this God’s wonderful wisdom is displayed: that notwithstanding his determined purpose in things, man has no ground for an excuse to say he was forced to this or that.

The knowledge of this determined limit of man’s life is of great use, for it teaches us:

1. To submit ourselves wholly to God, and to be prepared1028 either to depart out of this world soon or to live in it long, as God orders our time; neither desiring to live longer than God has appointed, nor grieving to live as long as he has appointed.

2. Not to fear the threats of any man, so as to be drawn away1029 from God by them.

3. To do God’s work while we have time,1030 etc.

§. 114. Of the reward promised to obedience, and that it implies no merit.

The other heresy, which the papists gather from this text, is1031 this: Man’s obedience is meritorious.

Answer. The reward promised here is no matter of wages and what is deserved, but of pure grace and favor.

I have spoken more fully of this error1032 elsewhere.

The Parents’ Duty towards Their Children

The First Treatise: On Ephesians 5:21–6:9 · §§. 115–122

§. 115. Of the connection of parents’ duty with children’s.

Eph 6:4.

And you+ fathers, do not provoke your+ children to wrath, but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.

The apostle, having urged children to perform their duties to their parents, turns his speech to parents, saying, “AND you+ fathers,” etc. That joining word AND, which joins an exhortation to parents to perform their duties to the exhortation made to children before it, gives us to understand that

Parents are bound to duty as well as children. Their duties1033 are indeed different; yet (notwithstanding their superiority and authority over their children) they are bound to duty. All the directions and exhortations throughout Scripture given to parents concerning their duty, and all the threatenings pronounced and judgments executed on parents for neglecting their duty, are clear proofs of this point.

Though parents are over their children and cannot be commanded by them, yet they are under God, and it is he who has laid their duty on them. So they are bound to it, as they will answer for it to their Father in heaven.

The authority which parents have is not so much for their own advancement as for the better governing of their children. That being so, their very government is a duty.

Objection. In the moral law only the duty of children is expressed.1034

Answer. The duty of parents (like the duties of many others) is implied by just and necessary consequence, which is equivalent and binds as much as if it were expressed. It is implied in this way. Those who have honor must carry themselves worthy of honor. Now the way to carry themselves worthy of honor is to be careful in doing their duty to those who honor them. This is so fair that it needed no expressing.

Therefore let ministers follow this pattern of the apostle,1035 and deal evenly with all of every sort. Let them not be partial, laying all the burden of duty on children’s necks and none on parents, holding children in very strictly but leaving parents to their own will. Parents are flesh and blood as well as children, and as prone to transgress in their place as children in theirs. Indeed, of the two, ministers ought to be more earnest in urging parents to perform their duty, because parents are under no such power and authority as children are. Fear of their parents’ authority keeps children much in awe. There is no such thing to keep parents in awe. They will therefore be all the readier to take the greater liberty, if they are not kept within bounds by the fear of God and by a good conscience.

Now you+ parents, as you+ look for honor, carry yourselves+1036 worthy of honor; as you+ look for duty from your+ children, perform duty to them. Know that one day you+ too will be called to account before the highest Judge. Your+ authority will then be no pretext to excuse your+ fault, but evidence to aggravate it. For you+, being older in years and more eminent in place, of more experience, and having a charge over your+ children, ought to be a light to show them the way and an example to draw them on. Then, seeing you+ careful and conscientious in performing your+ duty, they may be the more stirred up to perform theirs, or at least be made ashamed of neglecting their duty. But if you+ are careless of your+ duty, how can you+ expect duty at their hands? Indeed, if by your+ bad example they have been made negligent, their blood will be required at your+ hands.

§. 116. Of the extent of these words, Fathers, Children.

The word (fathers) is used here, which properly1037 means natural parents, and of natural parents the male sex. Yet (as in many other places) it is to be taken more widely: as widely as the word (children) was taken before, so that there may be a just and equal relation between children1038 and parents. So both sexes of natural parents are included under it, mother as well as father. So also are those who are in the place of parents, whether by marriage, as stepparents and all sorts of fathers- and mothers-in-law, or by appointment, as all who by right have the custody and charge of children, such as guardians, tutors, and other such governors. So it answers in every way to the word (parents) used in the first verse; and the word (children) is also to be taken here in the same extent as it was there.

§. 117. Of parents provoking children.

The next phrase (provoke to wrath) is the rendering of one1039 Greek word, which, being a compound word, cannot be fully expressed by one English word. The best and nearest that I can think of is (exasperate). The word signifies an extreme in the use of authority: too much austerity and severity, by which children are provoked to wrath. Because that is a fault, it is expressly forbidden here (do not provoke, etc.) There is a figure of speech in this word: the effect is put for the cause. The apostle’s meaning is that parents should take such care over their conduct toward their children that they give them no occasion to be stirred up to wrath. So under this word are forbidden1040 all such things as may kindle wrath in children: too much austerity in conduct, sourness in look, threatening and reviling in words, too hard handling, too severe correction, too much restraint of liberty, too small an allowance of things needful, and the like. Parents, being flesh and blood, are prone in this respect to abuse their authority. Indeed, even those who fall into the other extreme, of too much indulgence and pampering of their children, are very prone to fall into this extreme also. Many who for the most part let their children run into all kinds of wild living, without due restraint and correction, will at times suddenly fly at them like lions and correct them “at their own pleasure,” and so greatly provoke1041 their children. Those who pamper the most are the most prone to provoke to wrath. For, 1. such parents least know how to keep the middle way: one will sooner leap out of one extreme into the other than go from an extreme to the middle way. 2. The children of such parents are the soonest provoked.

Question. Is it lawful and justifiable for children to be provoked to wrath by their parents?

Answer.1042 No. This prohibition intends no such thing. The apostle is dealing here with parents, and instructs them how to prevent such harms as their children may fall into through their weakness. So here he shows only what is unlawful for parents, not what is lawful for children. From this, then, I observe by the way that

Parents must be so watchful over their conduct that by it they1043 do not make their children sin.

If they do, they make their own sin the more heinous. They also pull down on their own heads a far heavier vengeance: the vengeance of their own sin, and the vengeance of their child’s sin. For every parent is made a watchman over his child. If a watchman1044 does not do what he can to hinder the sin of those under his charge, he brings their blood on his own neck. What then do those do who, being watchmen, give occasion of sin to those under their charge?

§. 118. Of parents seeking the good of their children.

So that parents, in avoiding the rock of provoking, do not fall into the gulf of pampering, the apostle adds a BUT, which is1045 as a check to them, and teaches them that

It is not enough for parents to prevent such harms as1046 their children may fall into; they must also seek their good. All the precepts in Scripture charging parents to seek their children’s good prove the point. Here lies a chief difference between the affection which parents and strangers ought to bear toward children, and the duty which each owes to them. Mere strangers ought not to provoke them; but parents ought, moreover, to seek their good in every way.

The main good which parents ought especially to seek for their children is set out in these words: “Bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.”

The word translated (bring up) properly means to feed1047 or nourish with all needful things. It is the same word used before in chapter 5, verse 29, and translated there nourishes. It would not be unfitting to keep the proper meaning of the1048 word here, as the best Latin translations, the French, and others have kept it.

This word, joined with the others that follow, may seem1049 at first sight to be placed here only to fill out the sense, as if he had said, nurture your child in the ways of God. But if the apostle’s aim and the meaning of the word are well weighed, we shall find that it further implies a general duty, which nature itself teaches parents, namely this, that

Parents ought to provide all needful things for their children:1050 that is, such things as serve to nourish their bodies and preserve their health and life. For this phrase (to translate it word for word), nourish them in discipline, or in instruction, is a concise expression implying as much as if he had said, nourish and nurture them, or feed and instruct them. But the apostle has joined them together this closely and concisely to show that nurture and instruction are as needful and profitable as food and clothing.

§. 119. Of parents nurturing their children.1051

The word translated nurture signifies correction as well as instruction: as in Heb 12:7, “If you+ endure chastening,” and 2 Tim 3:16, Scripture is profitable “for instruction in righteousness.” Both senses will stand here, and our English word (as well as the Greek) will bear both: for to nurture children is to correct them as well as to instruct them. This advice, in this wide sense, very fitly follows the prohibition before it. For lest parents should take occasion from that to lay the reins on their children’s necks and let them run wherever they please, the apostle teaches by this that

Parents, as they must not be too severe, so neither must they be too lax.1052 They must not provoke their children to wrath, yet they must keep them under discipline. The word translated nurture, by the1053 derivation of the Greek, further sets out the middle way between the two extremes named before. For it signifies such discipline as befits a boy, or a young child. So the thing itself, discipline, by instruction and correction, keeps parents from the one extreme of laxness; and the kind or manner of discipline, being such as befits a child, keeps them from the other extreme of rigor and cruelty. Extremes on either side are dangerous and harmful, and that to both parent and child. For laxness will make children careless of all duty to God and parent; rigor will make them desperate. But virtue and safety lie in the middle way between both.

§. 120. Of parents fixing precepts in their children’s minds.

This word (admonition), by its1054 derivation, has a particular relation to the mind, and points to the informing and instructing of it. It is taken either for the act of admonishing (as in Titus 3:10, “Reject a divisive man1055 after a first and second admonition”), or for the1056 thing admonished, which is the sense most take it in here. Yet I would not have the former wholly excluded; for, by the full meaning of the word, I take this much to be intended.

As parents deliver good precepts and principles to their children,1057 so they must take care, by forceful and frequent admonitions, to fix and settle them in their children’s minds.1058 The law expresses as much by another metaphor which it uses, in a direction it gives to parents, saying, “You shall whet, or sharpen, God’s laws upon your children,” that is,1059 “you shall teach them diligently to your children.”

The more pains are taken in this, the less labor will be lost. What is little heeded at first will, by much urging and pressing, be held forever, as a nail that scarcely enters at one blow is driven in up to the head with many blows.

§. 121. Of adding information to discipline.

The addition of this word admonition to nurture is not (as some take it) a mere explanation of the same point, but also a declaration of a further duty, which is this:

As parents by discipline keep their children in check, so by information1060 they must direct them in the right way. Solomon both delivers the point and adds a good reason to enforce it. For he says, “Train up a child in the way he should go”: there is the duty. “And when he is old he will not depart from it”1061: there is the reason. Keeping a child in check by good discipline may make him dutiful while his father is over him; but informing his understanding and judgment well is a means to uphold him in the right way as long as he lives.

§. 122. Of parents teaching their children the fear of God.

The last word (of the Lord) points to the best duty that1062 a parent can do for his child. Admonition of the Lord means such principles as a parent has received from the Lord and learned out of God’s word: such as may teach a child to fear the Lord, such as tend to true piety and religion. From this I further observe that

Parents must especially teach their children their duty to1063 God. “Come, children,” says the psalmist, “listen to me; I will teach you+ the fear of the Lord.” I will speak of this particular more fully1064 hereafter.
